# Building an Agent Control Plane

## A Clean-Room Build Specification

*Everything we learned building one, written so an AI coding agent can build another
without ever seeing the original source.*

---

### What this is

A complete specification and lessons ledger for a local-first, browser-based control
plane that runs many AI coding-agent sessions in parallel against a codebase.

It is written to be handed, as-is, to a competent AI coding agent. The test it was
written against: *if you gave an agent this document and nothing else, and let it work
autonomously, would you get back an application that works substantially the same way?*

**It contains no source code from the original implementation.** What it contains is the
layer above code — product concept, feature inventory, interaction rules, and the
decisions behind them — and the layer below code — data schemas, API and event
contracts, state machines, algorithms in prose, timing and caching rules, and an
exhaustive catalogue of what broke and why.

Names of endpoints, events, database columns, states, and configuration keys **are**
included. Those are interface specification, not implementation.

### How to read it

- **A human should read Parts 0–3 and Appendix A.** They contain the decisions that are
  cheap to make on day one and expensive to reverse later.
- **Part 11 should be copied into your project's standing-instructions file before the
  first line of code is written.**
- **Part 12 is the operating manual** — an ordered sequence of paste-ready prompts.
- **Parts 13 and 14 are the UI reference**, to be kept open while building the front end.

### Table of contents

- Part 0 — How to use this document
- Part 1 — The product
- Part 2 — Architecture and the consequential decisions
- Part 3 — Launch, process management, and resilience
- Part 4 — The session daemon
- Part 5 — The web tier: HTTP and WebSocket surface
- Part 6 — Persistence and the data model
- Part 7 — The front end: shell, chat panel, realtime client
- Part 8 — The workflow board
- Part 9 — Compose and the agent library
- Part 10 — Surrounding tools
- Part 11 — The rule catalogue
- Part 12 — Build order and the prompt sequence
- Part 13 — The design system *(not yet written)*
- Part 14 — Screens, modals, and interactions
- Appendix A — The backend transport decision

# Building an Agent Control Plane

## A Clean-Room Build Specification

*Everything we learned building one, written so your coding agent can build another without ever seeing our source.*

---

## Part 0 — How to use this document

### 0.1 What this is

This document is a **specification and lessons ledger**, not a codebase and not a tutorial. It describes an application we built over roughly a year: a desktop-launched, browser-based control plane for running many AI coding-agent sessions in parallel against a codebase.

It is written for two readers at once:

1. **A coding agent** (Claude Code or equivalent) that will do the actual implementation.
2. **A human engineer** who will review that agent's work and make the judgment calls the agent should escalate.

The test we held ourselves to while writing it: *if you handed this document, and nothing else, to a competent coding agent and let it work autonomously, would you get back an application that works substantially the same way?* Every section was written against that bar. Where we could not meet it — where a section describes a thing we built but does not fully specify how — we say so explicitly rather than leaving a silent hole.

### 0.2 What this is not, and the clean-room rule

**No source code from our implementation appears in this document.** That is deliberate and it is a hard constraint on how you use this.

What you are getting instead is the layer above code and the layer below code:

- **Above:** the product concept, the feature inventory, the interaction rules, the decisions we made and why.
- **Below:** the data schemas, the API and event contracts, the state machines, the algorithms in prose and pseudocode, the timing and caching rules, and — most valuable of all — the catalogue of things that broke and why.

Names of endpoints, WebSocket events, database columns, session states, and configuration keys **are** included. Those are interface specification, not implementation. Two teams can independently write completely different code against the same interface names, and it is far better for you to inherit a coherent, battle-tested naming scheme than to invent one that will drift.

Your implementation should be written from scratch against these descriptions. Do not treat any passage here as something to transcribe.

### 0.3 The document's structure and why it is ordered this way

| Part | Title | What it gives you |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | How to use this document | You are here |
| 1 | The product: what you are building and for whom | Concept, personas, complete feature inventory, screen and modal inventory |
| 2 | Architecture overview and the consequential decisions | The ten or so choices that determine everything downstream |
| 3 | Launch, process management, and resilience | How a non-technical person actually starts and keeps the thing running |
| 4 | The session daemon | The long-lived process that owns every agent session |
| 5 | The web tier: HTTP and WebSocket surface | Complete API and event contracts |
| 6 | Persistence and the data model | Full schema, on-disk layout, storage philosophy |
| 7 | The front end: shell, chat panel, realtime client, design system | The UI spec, and the realtime-recovery lessons |
| 8 | The workflow board | Cards that launch and mirror real agent sessions |
| 9 | Compose and the agent library | Multi-agent authoring, and reusable prompt-template agents |
| 10 | Surrounding tools | Files, git, preview, search, voice, mobile, bridges |
| 11 | The rule catalogue | Every hard-won engineering lesson, grouped and portable |
| 12 | Build order and the prompt sequence | The ordered set of prompts to hand your agent |
| 13 | The design system | Color tokens, typography, spacing, shape, motion, the status visual language |
| 14 | Screens, modals, and interactions | Every screen, every dialog, every menu, every micro-behavior and timing constant |
| A | Appendix A — the backend transport decision | Whether to drive the agent CLI directly instead of through a vendor SDK, and what a POSIX-only build buys you |

Parts 1–3 are orientation and should be read by the human. Parts 4–10 are the buildable specification. Part 11 is the section to paste into your project's persistent instructions file on day one. Part 12 is the thing you actually operate. Parts 13 and 14 are the visual and behavioral reference that Parts 7–10 point into whenever they say "render this" or "the user sees" — build the UI with them open beside you.

A note on Parts 13 and 14: together they are the longest section of this document, and that is deliberate. A rebuild that gets the architecture right and the interaction detail wrong produces something that technically works and feels nothing like the original. The hover reveals, the scroll rules, the empty states, the exact button copy, the timing constants, and the status colour language are what make the difference between "a working clone" and "the same product."

**Read Appendix A before you write the first line of daemon code.** It covers the one decision we would most likely change if we started over: whether to drive the agent CLI directly instead of through a vendor SDK, and what you gain if you are willing to target Linux only. It is short, and it is cheap to act on at the start and expensive to retrofit later.

### 0.4 How to run the build

The intended workflow:

1. **Read Parts 1, 2, and 3 yourself.** They contain the decisions that are expensive to reverse. If you disagree with one of our choices, this is the moment — not month three.
2. **Create the project's standing-instructions file first** (the file your coding agent reads at the start of every session — `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, or whatever your tool calls it). Seed it from Part 11. Do this *before* the first line of code. Rules that arrive after the code exists get violated by the code that already exists.
3. **Work through Part 12's prompt sequence in order.** Each prompt is self-contained: it references the chapter that specifies its slice, states its acceptance criteria, and does not assume the agent remembers earlier conversation. Hand one prompt per session where practical.
4. **Do not let the agent reorder the sequence.** The order encodes dependency. In particular, the daemon and its IPC contract must exist before the web tier, and the web tier before the front end, because the interesting failure modes are all at those seams.

### 0.5 Scope control: what to build, and what to skip

The application described here is large. Not all of it is load-bearing. Every feature in Part 1's inventory is tagged:

- **CORE** — the product is pointless without it. Roughly the first third.
- **IMPORTANT** — the product is usable but noticeably worse without it.
- **NICE-TO-HAVE** — real value, but safely deferred to a second pass.

A reasonable v1 is: the launcher, the daemon, the session lifecycle, the chat panel, the realtime client, and the session list. That alone is a genuinely useful product. The workflow board (Part 8) is the second thing to build and is what turns it from a session viewer into a development platform. Compose (Part 9) is a separate product bolted onto the same substrate and can wait indefinitely.

If your timeline is tight, build Parts 3–7 completely and correctly rather than building all of Parts 3–10 partially. The failure modes in the realtime and lifecycle layers are subtle, user-visible, and extremely expensive to debug after the fact — which is most of what Part 11 is about.

### 0.6 A note on the lessons

Roughly a third of this document is failure analysis: things that worked in development and broke in the hands of a real user, optimizations that turned out to be correctness bugs, recovery mechanisms that caused worse problems than the ones they fixed.

Those sections are the highest-value content here, and they are also the sections a coding agent is most likely to skim past on its way to the implementable parts. When a passage says *"do not simplify this"* or *"we tried this and reverted it,"* that is not stylistic preference — it is a description of an outage. Several of these mechanisms look redundant, over-defensive, or plainly wrong until you have hit the failure they exist to prevent.

If your agent proposes removing one of them because it looks unnecessary, the correct response is to make it explain the failure mode first.

### 0.7 Conventions used throughout

- `<repo-root>/` stands in for wherever the project lives on disk. No absolute paths from our machines appear anywhere.
- **"The daemon"** always means the long-lived session-owning process (Part 4). **"The web tier"** always means the HTTP/WebSocket server (Part 5). **"The client"** always means browser JavaScript (Part 7).
- **"Agent backend"** means the underlying coding-agent tool being driven (in our case a CLI-based coding agent accessed through its SDK). Part 2 explains why you must abstract this on day one.
- A **session** is one conversation with one agent backend process. A **task** is a card on the workflow board. A **composition** is a Compose document. These three nouns are used precisely and never interchangeably.
- Tables labelled **Consequential decisions** appear at the end of each part and follow the same shape: *what we chose, why, and what breaks if you choose differently.*
- Lists labelled **Non-negotiable rules** are numbered and each states its failure mode. These are the ones to copy into your standing-instructions file.

### 0.8 The reference stack

The body of this document is deliberately written in vendor-neutral terms — "the agent backend," "a hosted Postgres backend," "the WebSocket library" — because the architecture is portable and we did not want you inheriting our vendor choices by accident.

That neutrality is unhelpful when you actually have to start typing, so here is exactly what we used. Treat it as a known-good default, not a requirement.

| Layer | What we used | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Language (both server processes) | Python 3.10+ | The agent SDK is Python; that decided it |
| Agent backend | Claude Code, driven through the Claude Agent SDK | A Node CLI binary, one subprocess per session, spoken to over stdio. This is the thing being orchestrated |
| Web framework | Flask | Chosen for simplicity; nothing depends on it |
| WebSocket layer | Flask-SocketIO in **threading** async mode | See Part 5 for the consequences of this choice — they are significant and mostly bad |
| Production server | The framework's own development server | Correct for a localhost single-user tool; do not add a WSGI server |
| Daemon concurrency | asyncio, one event loop, one task per session | Part 4 |
| IPC between processes | Raw TCP on loopback, newline-delimited JSON | Deliberately boring; it is easy to debug with a socket client |
| Local database | SQLite (WAL mode) | Zero-config default for the task board |
| Optional cloud database | Hosted Postgres with row-level security enabled and no policies, accessed with a service-role key | Only for the shared-board story |
| Full-text search | A second, disposable SQLite database using FTS5 with BM25 ranking | Rebuilt from transcripts on any corruption |
| Front end | No framework, no build step, plain scripts | **We recommend against this** — see Part 2 §2.14 and Part 7 §7.2 |
| Rich text / editor widget | A standard open-source rich-text editor component | Only used in the authoring surface |
| Browser target | Chrome/Chromium launched explicitly | Forced by browser speech APIs being Chromium-only — Part 10 §10.7 |
| Remote access | A mesh VPN's reverse-proxy mode (not its public-tunnel mode) | Part 10 §10.8 |
| Local speech-to-text | A local Whisper model in an isolated virtual environment | Optional, opt-in |
| Tests | pytest, plus Selenium with a page-object layer for end-to-end | Part 3 |

Two notes on substitution:

- **The agent backend is the one choice that is load-bearing but should still be abstracted.** Whatever coding agent you drive, put it behind the interface described in Part 2 §2.5 on day one. The whole point of that boundary is that this row of the table can change without touching anything else.
- **Language choice follows the SDK.** If your agent backend ships a TypeScript SDK and you would rather build in TypeScript, that is a perfectly good decision and nothing else in this document changes — the two-process split, the IPC contract, the entry schema, and every lesson in Part 11 are language-independent.

### 0.9 What we would tell you if we only got one sentence

Build the two-process split and the normalized message schema first, get the realtime reconnect semantics right before you add any feature that depends on them, and write down every bug's root cause in a standing-instructions file the moment you fix it — because the second and third occurrences of that bug will be introduced by an agent that had no idea the first one happened.

# Part 1 — The Product: What You Are Building and For Whom

## 1.1 Elevator pitch

A development platform for agentic programming. It runs as a persistent session daemon plus a browser-based control plane that together orchestrate many coding agents working in parallel on the same codebase: sessions that are aware of each other and avoid conflicts automatically, a hierarchical task board whose leaf nodes are literal working agent sessions, a unified library of reusable agent instructions, plus private phone access and local voice input.

It replaces the thing every serious user of CLI coding agents ends up building badly by hand — a wall of terminal windows, a separate to-do list, and a folder of prompt snippets nobody can find.

## 1.2 The three problems it solves

Everything in this document exists to address one of these three. If a feature you are considering does not serve one of them, it is probably scope creep.

**1. Session sprawl.** Running eight or more coding-agent sessions across terminal windows becomes unmanageable fast, and permission prompts are the worst part — each one blocks its session until a human finds the right window and answers it. Even three monitors run out of room. The product runs a *fleet* of agents graphically, with a single surface that shows what every session is doing and lets you answer any of them from one place.

**2. Velocity without direction.** Coding agents produce enormous throughput, but throughput does not move a roadmap. Sessions drift off task, two agents build the same thing, and nothing connects what an agent is doing to what you actually need delivered. The product couples every session to a task in a plan, so every agent is working toward a named deliverable with its position in the hierarchy injected into its prompt.

**3. Scattered, invisible reusable instructions.** The ecosystem has converged on two nearly identical concepts — "skills" (injected into the current session) and "agents" (spawned as a subprocess). Both are a markdown file with instructions; they differ only in invocation mechanism. The files scatter across hidden configuration directories with no way to browse what exists or invoke it without memorizing a name. The product presents them as one thing, organized into named collections, browsable and clickable.

## 1.3 The thesis: why a GUI around a CLI agent is worth building

The terminal is an excellent interface for *one* agent and a terrible interface for *many*. Specifically, the following are all natural in a GUI and effectively impossible in a terminal multiplexer:

- Seeing the state of twelve sessions at a glance, including which ones are blocked on you.
- Answering a permission prompt with a click, from any session, without hunting for its window.
- Injecting structured context into a new session automatically, based on where it sits in a plan.
- Telling every session what the other sessions are touching.
- Rewinding, forking, or duplicating a conversation.
- Doing any of the above from a phone.
- Keeping all of it alive across a server restart.

There is also a second-order effect worth naming because it changes how fast you can build: **because session ownership is split into a separate process, the application can modify its own source code while running.** Multiple agent sessions edit the app's own files, restart the UI tier to load the changes, and continue working — the daemon holds every session in memory while the web server restarts around it. Most of our application was built this way, from inside itself.

## 1.4 Personas

**The fleet operator (primary).** A developer running many agents at once. Lives in the session view and the task board. Cares about: speed, being able to see everything at a glance, never losing a session, and not having to remember which window a question came from. Has deep muscle memory — start, stop, resume, rewind, compact are reflexes, not decisions. Will notice a 200ms regression.

**The planner.** Same person, different mode. Works in the task board: decomposes an epic, uses the AI planner to break a natural-language request into a task tree, drags cards, reads reports. Wants the roadmap and the execution to be the same artifact, not two artifacts that need reconciling.

**The non-technical operator (explicitly supported, and constraining).** Uses the application without reading diffs and without a terminal. Presses a one-click "Update" button that commits and pushes. Cannot diagnose a dead process, cannot read a stack trace, and will not find a workaround.

This third persona is not an afterthought — it constrains the whole design:

- Every failure must degrade to a plain-language status with a next action, never a traceback.
- The application must survive unattended for days and self-heal when it does not.
- The commit-and-push button makes *every file in the repository a potential publication*, which is why Part 11 opens with public-repository safety rules.
- Nothing important may require explanation. If a feature needs documentation, it is probably designed wrong.

## 1.5 The product's shape: three pillars plus a fourth surface

The application opens on a home screen that acts as a command center, offering three pillars:

**Sessions** — run and interact with agent sessions. This is not a list; it is where the work happens. Live transcript panel, answering the agent's questions with clickable options, session tools (auto-name, duplicate, fork, rewind, delete, summarize, extract code, compare), and a choice of grid-card or compact-list presentation.

**Workflow** — a hierarchical task board with configurable columns and drag-and-drop. Arbitrary nesting depth; each level tracks status independently with completion propagating upward. At any branch a task may break into either subtasks *or* agent sessions, so the leaves of the hierarchy are running work. Includes an AI planner, reports and analytics, tags, and validation-issue tracking.

**Workforce** — the library of reusable instruction files, organized into named collections rather than by file type, with automatic discovery from the ecosystem's conventional directories, dual invocation (injected into the current session, or spawned as a subprocess) chosen by context rather than by the user, and three complexity tiers from one-paragraph personas to multi-phase pipelines.

**Compose** — a fourth view, and effectively a second product built on the same substrate: multi-agent authoring of long-form documents, with a root orchestrator agent and per-section agents. Genuinely useful, entirely optional, and safely deferred.

## 1.6 The signature features

These are the things that make the product distinctive rather than merely convenient. If you build only the obvious parts, you will produce a session viewer; these are what make it a platform.

### Cross-session awareness (CORE)

At session start, each session's system prompt receives a live snapshot of every other active session in the same project: auto-generated name, current status, how long it has been running, and the last few files it edited. Where two sessions are touching the same files, the overlap is flagged explicitly.

The agent then avoids the conflict on its own — it re-reads a file before editing, and if the file appears to be mid-refactor by another session, it backs off and surfaces the incomplete work to the user rather than producing a merge conflict inside the working tree.

There is no inter-session messaging and no coordination protocol. Just awareness and avoidance. Make it toggleable, because it costs context budget and some users want isolation.

### Session scoping into the task tree (CORE to the platform thesis)

Sessions are part of the task hierarchy rather than bolted alongside it. Spawning a session from a task card automatically injects: the full breadcrumb path up the tree, the parent's description, sibling task statuses, which siblings currently have sessions running and for how long, and any open validation issues.

This layers on top of project-wide cross-session awareness, so a session launched from the board gets both a task-neighborhood view and a bird's-eye view of everything running.

### The AI planner (IMPORTANT)

Describe work in natural language; an agent breaks it into a hierarchical task tree. Because it runs through a real coding-agent session, it reads the codebase while planning — so the breakdown reflects the actual architecture rather than the user's description of it. The user iterates on the proposed breakdown, then accepts to bulk-create.

### Permission handling as a first-class surface (CORE)

Tool-permission prompts are intercepted and surfaced in the UI — answerable with a click, from a persistent panel, for any session, without navigating to that session. This is the single biggest quality-of-life win over terminal use and should be built early.

### Local, project-aware voice input (NICE-TO-HAVE, distinctive)

Browser-native dictation is Chromium-only and produces unpunctuated run-ons that mangle project vocabulary. A local speech-to-text engine fixes all of it: works in any browser via standard audio capture, streams words in real time as you speak, detects end-of-speech using the model's own voice-activity detection rather than microphone volume (so it works in a loud room), biases recognition toward the project's own identifiers and file names, adds punctuation and capitalization, cleans up restarts and filler words, and runs entirely on the user's machine with no cloud call and no per-use cost.

Ship it opt-in behind a one-click enable that checks the machine is a good fit and downloads a small model once.

### One-click startup (CORE — and the first thing every user judges you on)

Most of your users will be on a Windows host, and a meaningful share of them will never open a terminal. The startup experience is not packaging polish; it is the first ninety seconds of the product, and it is where a non-technical user decides whether this thing works.

**The contract, stated as four requirements:**

1. **One icon, one click.** A desktop shortcut is created for the user — they never type a command.
2. **Visible feedback within about a second.** Not a spinner in a terminal; a real window.
3. **Continuous, honest progress** through named steps until the browser opens on a working app.
4. **The thing they clicked can be closed without killing anything.**

Requirement 4 is the one that quietly dictates architecture: it is why the server must be spawned genuinely detached, and why the launcher targets a *windowless* interpreter. Get this wrong and a user closes what looks like a leftover window, the server dies, and the browser tab they're looking at becomes a corpse — with no error, no explanation, and nothing to act on. That exact failure reached a real user.

**The boot splash is a product surface, not a loading indicator.** Ours is a borderless, always-on-top, screen-centred window rendered as an animated canvas at roughly 60fps, fading in from transparent, with drifting ambient particles over a dark gradient matched to the app's own theme, a live step list, and an eased progress readout.

The ambient motion is the part people skip, and it is the part that matters: **a frozen splash is indistinguishable from a hung application.** The animation must run independently of progress, so that a slow step still looks alive. A static image with a progress bar fails this test the first time dependency installation takes ninety seconds.

Two rules that came out of real incidents and are worth inheriting:

- **Announce every step when it begins — including the slow, invisible ones.** We originally had no marker for the heavy module-import phase, so a freeze there kept displaying the *previous* step and misdirected debugging. A progress indicator that lags reality is worse than none.
- **The splash must never be load-bearing.** Pre-flight the GUI toolkit in the parent process before spawning it (the child's own import failure exits silently, so without the check a machine lacking the toolkit shows *nothing at all*), fall back to a native OS notification carrying the same message plus the install hint, suppress native crash dialogs in the splash process, and start the application normally whether or not any of it works.

The whole experience, end to end: click the icon → an animated window appears within a second → seven named steps advance → the browser opens on a working app → the splash dismisses itself. **At no point is there a blank screen or an unexplained wait.**

Part 3 §3.2 specifies all of it — shortcut creation and self-healing per platform, the splash's visual and animation spec, the status protocol between the app and the splash window, and the degradation path.

### Private mobile access (IMPORTANT)

The whole application on a phone — sessions, board, library, voice — without exposing anything to the public internet. Answer a session's question from the couch; start a task from the train.

The mechanism matters: the server stays bound to loopback. A mesh VPN's proxy bridges the phone to it, so only the user's own authenticated devices can reach it, end-to-end encrypted. Because that proxy provides real TLS certificates, the phone treats the page as a secure context, which is what unlocks microphone access on iOS.

Make it a persistent toggle that re-arms on every startup, with a guided, self-verifying setup wizard that reads live VPN state — it should tell the user the exact account to sign the phone into (the number-one first-time mistake) and show a positive confirmation the instant the phone joins. Every failure path degrades to a clear status with a next action.

## 1.7 Feature inventory

Tagged **CORE** (product is pointless without it), **IMPORTANT** (usable but noticeably worse), **NICE** (defer safely).

- Live transcript panel streaming the agent's work in real time — **CORE**
- Send messages to a running session — **CORE**
- Answer the agent's questions with clickable option buttons — **CORE**
- Start, stop, sleep, resume sessions — **CORE**
- Delete sessions, with trash and tombstones so deletions stick — **CORE**
- Auto-generated session names — **IMPORTANT**
- Manual rename — **IMPORTANT**
- Duplicate a session — **IMPORTANT**
- Fork a session from a point in its history — **IMPORTANT**
- Rewind a session to an earlier point — **IMPORTANT**
- Compact a session's context — **IMPORTANT**
- Summarize a session — **NICE**
- Extract code from a session's output — **NICE**
- Compare two sessions side by side — **NICE**
- Grid-card and compact-list presentations, switchable — **IMPORTANT**
- Per-session model selection, changeable mid-session — **IMPORTANT**
- Per-session permission mode — **IMPORTANT**
- Queue messages while the agent is busy — **IMPORTANT**
- Cross-session awareness injection, toggleable — **CORE to the thesis**
- Session search across transcripts — **IMPORTANT**
- Project switching; sessions scoped per project — **CORE**

### Permissions
- Intercept tool-permission requests and surface them in the UI — **CORE**
- Persistent side panel listing all pending approvals across sessions — **CORE**
- Approve / deny with one click — **CORE**
- Remembered decisions and permission modes — **IMPORTANT**

### Workflow board
- Configurable columns (default: Not Started, Working, Validating, Remediating, Complete) — **CORE**
- Drag and drop between columns — **CORE**
- Arbitrarily deep task hierarchy with independent per-level status — **CORE**
- Completion propagating up the tree — **IMPORTANT**
- Launch a session from any task card, with hierarchical context injected — **CORE to the thesis**
- Task chooser on a new task: break into subtasks, spawn sessions, or let AI plan — **IMPORTANT**

- Breadcrumb navigation that stays visible inside a session opened from the board — **IMPORTANT**
- Progress bars on parent tasks — **NICE**

- Gap-numbered ordering for cheap drag-reorder — **IMPORTANT**

- Collections ("departments") as the organizing unit rather than file type — **IMPORTANT**

- Three complexity tiers in one tree — **NICE**

### Compose

### Surrounding tools
- File drag-and-drop onto the window, with destination picker, that tells the running session about the file — **IMPORTANT**
