### The ordering principle

**Build in incident order, not in architectural order.**

Every item above exists because something broke in a specific way on a specific day, and the sequence of the prompts is roughly the sequence in which those failures actually hurt: first the user could not start the application, then they could start it but closed a window and lost it, then they could keep it running but their browser silently dropped a feature, then they could restart it but the restart killed the wrong process, then everything worked until they walked away from the machine.

You will be tempted to build the resilience layer early because it is the interesting part. Do not. **A healer built before the failure it heals is a guess** — and the eight mechanisms in §3.11 are valuable precisely because each one is shaped around an observed incident rather than an imagined one. Ship §3.1–§3.10 first, run it on real machines, and let the incidents tell you which healer to build next.

And when you build them, hold every one of them to the single rule that governs this entire chapter:

> **A safety net must never be able to break what it protects.**

A watchdog that kills healthy long turns, a reaper that matches too loosely, a supervisor that restart-loops, a socket healer that cycles a working connection, a duplicate instance that hijacks a mutex port — each of these converts a rare failure into a frequent one, and each of them is a *plausible* implementation of a *correct* idea. The difference between the two is always the same thing: an invariant that is stated, justified with its incident, and pinned with a test.


---

# Part 4 — The Session Daemon

---

## 4.1 What this part covers, and why the daemon exists

### 4.1.1 Definitions used throughout this chapter

Read these before anything else. Every term is used with exactly this meaning for the rest of the chapter.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Agent CLI** | A third-party command-line program (in the reference implementation, a Node binary) that wraps a large-language-model coding agent. It is spawned as a child process, speaks a bidirectional JSON control protocol over stdin/stdout, executes tools (file edits, shell commands, searches) on the local machine, and streams messages back. You do not control its source. |
| **Agent SDK** | The vendor-supplied client library that spawns and drives the Agent CLI. It exposes an async client with `connect / query / receive_response / interrupt / disconnect`, plus a "can use tool" permission callback. |
| **Session** | One long-lived conversation with the Agent CLI, bound to one working directory, with a durable transcript on disk and a stable identifier. |
| **Transcript** | The append-only JSONL (one JSON object per line) file the Agent CLI writes for a session. It is the source of truth for conversation history and is what a *resume* replays. |
| **Daemon** | The long-lived process specified in this chapter. It exclusively owns every live session. |
| **Web tier** | The HTTP + WebSocket server the browser talks to. It owns no session objects. |
| **Entry** | One normalized record in the daemon's in-memory conversation log for a session. This is what the browser renders. Distinct from a transcript line. |
| **Turn** | One user message → agent work → terminal `RESULT` message cycle. |
| **`<agent-home>`** | The Agent CLI's per-user state directory (a dot-directory under the user's home directory). Never hardcode a user path; derive it at runtime. |
| **`<repo-root>`** | The root of the application you are building. |
| **`<APP>_*`** | Environment-variable prefix. Choose one for your product and use it consistently. |

### 4.1.2 What you are building

A single long-lived Python process, listening on a loopback TCP port, that owns every live agent session in the product. The web tier holds a **proxy object** whose method names are byte-identical to the daemon-side session manager, so the web tier literally cannot tell whether it is talking to a local object or a remote process. That symmetry is load-bearing: the application factory calls `session_manager.start(socketio, app)` in both configurations without a branch. Preserve it. It is what lets you run the whole system in-process for tests and split for production without a second code path.

### 4.1.3 Why it must be a separate process

Do not co-host session management inside the web server. Every row below is a concrete failure that was observed, not a hypothetical.

| Failure if co-hosted | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Every web restart kills every session | Non-technical users press a one-click "Update" button that restarts the web tier. The restart endpoint takes a `scope` parameter (`web` / `daemon` / `both`); `web` is the only safe value, and it *exists* precisely because the daemon survives it. Restarting the daemon destroys every running agent. Treat that as an absolute prohibition for automated agents in your own product. |
| Turn latency collapses under concurrency | A threading-mode WSGI server serializes handlers. An attempted client-side heartbeat (`client_ping` / `client_pong`) had to be reverted because pongs took **>8 s** behind concurrent IPC — direct proof that the request layer cannot host anything latency-sensitive. |
| The permission callback deadlocks | Tool-permission approval blocks inside an SDK async task group for **up to one hour**, waiting on a human. That cannot occupy a request worker. |
| "Stop session" kills the whole application | Session teardown uses `killpg(getpgid(cli_pid), …)` on POSIX. If the CLI shares the host process's process group, the kill blasts the host. **This regression shipped to Linux users.** Preventing it requires controlling *every* `subprocess.Popen` in the process — only feasible in a process that does nothing else. |
| Shared-state corruption | Session registry, message queues, permission policy, and UI preferences are single-writer JSON files. Two web workers race them. |
| Browser backpressure stalls the model | If the SDK stream and the WebSocket write share a thread, a slow browser throttles the agent. The split forces an explicit queue between them. |

Additional daemon-only responsibilities that independently justify the split: orphan-process reaping, runaway external-search reaping, a stall watchdog, OS keep-awake pulsing, crash-recovery replay, and JSONL transcript repair. Each needs a process whose lifetime is measured in days.

### 4.1.4 Singleton and boot discipline

Exactly one daemon per port. Enforce it in layers, because either layer alone has a known hole:

1. A kernel-managed **named mutex** on Windows, or a **`flock` lockfile** on POSIX.
2. A **socket bind** with `SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE` (Windows) or `SO_REUSEADDR` + `SO_REUSEPORT` (POSIX).
3. **Stale-mutex override:** if the mutex is held but the port is *not* listening, declare the mutex stale and start anyway.

`SO_REUSEADDR` is not optional. A `kill -9`'d daemon leaves the port in `TIME_WAIT` for ~60 s, and the replacement daemon otherwise fails to bind. The user-visible symptom was *"restart didn't restart the daemon."*

Write a PID file at `<agent-home>/gui_daemon.pid`, or `gui_daemon_<port>.pid` for non-default ports.

**Boot hardening must run before any third-party import.** Two specific measures:

- **Pre-seed the platform uname cache.** On Windows, `platform.system()` issues a WMI query that hangs *forever* if the WMI service is wedged, and the HTTP-library import chain calls it. Prime the cache with a hardcoded value first.
- **Arm a hang-dump.** Install a `faulthandler` timeout with a **120-second** fuse that dumps all thread stacks, and disarm it once the socket binds. Without this, a boot hang produces no artifact at all.

---

## 4.2 Process architecture and IPC

### 4.2.1 Transport and framing

- TCP, **loopback only**, `127.0.0.1:5051` by default, overridable via `<APP>_DAEMON_PORT`.
- `listen(1)`; **exactly one client at a time**. A new connection *replaces* the old one — close the previous socket. This is correct because there is exactly one web server.
- `TCP_NODELAY` on both ends.
- `SO_KEEPALIVE` on **both** ends with aggressive timers: idle **15 s**, interval **5 s**, count **3**. (macOS exposes only `TCP_KEEPALIVE`; set it to 15.) Kernel defaults of ~2 hours are useless for laptop sleep/resume. Without keepalive **on the daemon side**, a resumed Linux host leaves the daemon blocked in `recv()` on a dead socket forever, refusing to release its single client slot. Build this in Stage 1; it is nearly undebuggable once real sessions are live.
- **Framing:** newline-delimited JSON, UTF-8. Both readers must accumulate **raw bytes**, locate the last newline, decode only up to it, and retain the remainder. Decoding each `recv()` chunk independently raises the moment a multi-byte character straddles a chunk boundary. Log and skip undecodable chunks; log and skip unparseable JSON lines.

### 4.2.2 Wire shapes

```
request:  {"req_id": "<8 hex chars>", "method": "<name>", "params": { ... }}
response: {"req_id": "<8 hex chars>", "result": <any JSON>}
error:    {"req_id": "<8 hex chars>", "error": "<message string>"}
push:     {"event": "<name>", "data": { ... }}          // no req_id
```

`req_id` is the first 8 hex characters of a UUID4. A push event is distinguished purely by the presence of `event` and the absence of `req_id`.

**Contract subtlety you must design around.** A `null` result is indistinguishable from a timeout on the client side, because the client stores `msg["result"]` into a holder initialized to `None` and treats `None` as "no response yet." Therefore: **any handler that can legitimately return a falsy or absent value must normalize `None` to `{}` before returning.** The subsession-metadata handler is the canonical case.

### 4.2.3 Concurrency model — daemon side

There are **both** OS threads and **one** asyncio event loop, explicitly bridged.

| Thread | Role |
|---|---|
| main | `accept()` loop with a **1 s** socket timeout so shutdown stays responsive |
| `ipc-client` (one per connection) | reads and frames lines; dispatches |
| one ephemeral thread **per request** | every dispatch runs on its own thread so a single slow handler can never stall the pipeline. Safe because socket writes are serialized by one write lock. |
| `session-manager-loop` | the dedicated asyncio loop that owns all SDK clients |
| `session-recovery` | one-shot crash recovery at startup |
| `session-health-monitor` | stall / sleep-detect / keep-awake watchdog, **30 s** tick |
| `runaway-reaper` | POSIX-only external-search process reaper, **60 s** sweep |
| `signal-forensics` | POSIX-only; captures the *sender PID* of shutdown signals |
| timer threads | orphan sweep (**60 s**), wake-up queue watchdog (**30 s**), registry save (**3 s** debounce), queue save (**1 s** debounce) |
| `snap` pool | bounded `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8)` for file-snapshot hashing |
| default executor | `run_in_executor` for transcript repair, mtime scans, snapshot writes |

**Bridging rule.** Every public session-manager method is **synchronous** and is called from a dispatch thread. Work that must touch the SDK is submitted with `asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe`. A helper waits on the resulting future with a **30 s** default timeout. Fire-and-forget submissions (start, send, close, interrupt) do not wait.

**Locking.** All of these are non-reentrant unless stated. Each has a documented deadlock attached to it:

- **Manager lock** — guards the session dictionary. `start_session`, when it decides to forward a prompt to `send_message`, **must do so outside the lock**, because `send_message` re-acquires it.
- **Per-session lock** — guards the entries list. Append and index-capture must happen *together* under it.
- **Queue lock** — the push-update helper re-acquires it, so it must be called **outside** any held block. This was a real production deadlock.
- **Per-parent inbox locks**, keyed by parent session id.
- **Hook-pending map lock.**

**Cross-thread event signalling.** Permission waits use a plain `threading.Event`, polled from the coroutine with `anyio.sleep(0.1)` (falling back to `asyncio.sleep`). Do not "improve" this to an async event plus `loop.call_soon_threadsafe`: that combination did **not** reliably wake the waiter. Poll ceiling: 36 000 iterations × 0.1 s = **1 hour**.

### 4.2.4 Concurrency model — web side (the proxy client)

Five threads: `daemon-reader`, `socketio-emitter`, `daemon-heartbeat`, `daemon-reconnect`, `daemon-resync`.

- **Reader** is the *only* thread that reads the socket. It correlates responses by `req_id` into a pending map `{req_id: (Event, holder)}` and pushes events onto an internal queue.
- **Emitter** drains that queue and calls `socketio.emit`. This decoupling is deliberate: WebSocket write latency must never delay IPC response correlation.
- **Heartbeat**: every **20 s** send `ping` with an **8 s** timeout. On failure, force-disconnect. Constraint (pin it with a test): `HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT < HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL`, with sane bounds of 5–60 s for the interval and 2–30 s for the timeout.
- **Force-disconnect must call `shutdown(SHUT_RDWR)` *before* `close()`.** On Linux, `close()` alone does not reliably wake a `recv()` already in flight; the shutdown does.
- **Reconnect loop**: 2 s cadence. Emit a `daemon_reconnect` progress event to browsers with `status` ∈ `connecting` / `connected` / `restarting` / `disconnected`. After **5** failed rounds (~10 s), **respawn the daemon process** detached (Windows: `CREATE_NO_WINDOW | CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP`; POSIX: `start_new_session=True`), logging to `<repo-root>/logs/daemon_debug.log`.
- **Connect**: up to 50 attempts with 100–200 ms sleeps.
- **Resync on connect**: fetch `get_aliases` and `get_permission_policy`.

**Startup ordering is a real trap.** `start()` must (1) connect *without* resync, (2) start reader, emitter, and heartbeat, and only then (3) resync on a background thread. Resyncing before the reader is running blocks for the full 30 s waiting on a response that no thread is reading.

**Stale-disconnect guard.** The reader snapshots the socket object it is reading. When its inner loop exits, it sets `connected = False` **only if the current socket is still that same object**. Otherwise a reconnect already happened and the exiting reader would clobber a healthy state.

**Initial push.** The instant a client connects, the daemon pushes `state_snapshot` carrying `{sessions, queues}` — a full session-state list plus every non-empty queue. (Historical bug worth guarding: after the queue was extracted into its own component, the snapshot builder read a stale attribute name, raised, and silently dropped the snapshot; the UI only recovered via later polling. See §4.15 rule 20.)

### 4.2.5 Signal forensics (POSIX)

Standard `signal.signal()` handlers cannot see `siginfo_t.si_pid`, so every prior investigation of *"stop session crashed the daemon"* dead-ended at "Received signal 15" with no sender.

Build this instead: **block** `SIGTERM` / `SIGINT` / `SIGHUP` at process level, and run a dedicated thread on `sigwaitinfo()`, which *does* preserve `si_pid`. On receipt, log: signal name, `si_code`, `si_uid`, sender pid/ppid/comm/cmdline, own pid/pgid/sid/ppid — **plus an explicit diagnosis line**:

- sender == self ⇒ a bug in the daemon's own kill path;
- sender is a Python process ⇒ the web tier's restart endpoint;
- otherwise ⇒ external (service manager, OOM killer, user).

Then unblock and re-raise the signal to itself so the normal graceful handler runs on the main thread.

---

## 4.3 The IPC command surface (complete table)

All methods are synchronous request/response except where noted. Every method returns a JSON value; most return `{"ok": true}` or `{"ok": false, "error": "..."}`.

| Method | Key params | Returns | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `start_session` | `session_id, prompt, cwd, name, resume, model, system_prompt, max_turns, allowed_tools, permission_mode, session_type, extra_args, parent_session_id, subsession_origin_turn, parent_deleted_at, auto_report_on_idle` | `{ok}` | Returns immediately; the driver coroutine runs async. |
| `send_message` | `session_id, text` | `{ok}` or `{ok, queued}` | Auto-queues if the session is not IDLE. |
| `resolve_permission` | `session_id, allow, always, almost_always` | `{ok}` | Unified: auto-detects hook vs SDK-callback permission. |
| `resolve_hook_permission` | `req_id, action` (`allow` \| `deny`) | bool | |
| `hook_pre_tool` | `tool_name, tool_input, session_id` | `{action: "allow"\|"deny"}` | **Blocking**, dispatched on its own thread; waits up to 3600 s. |
| `interrupt_session` | `session_id`, `clear_queue` (default `true`) | `{ok}` | |
| `set_session_model` | `session_id, model` | `{ok, model}` / `{ok, model, resumed}` / `{ok:false, error}` | Honesty contract, §4.4.6. |
| `cancel_auto_retry` | `session_id` | `{ok}` | |
| `retry_now` | `session_id` | `{ok}` | |
| `close_session` | `session_id` | `{ok}` | Forces STOPPED synchronously, cleans up async. |
| `close_session_sync` | `session_id`, `timeout` (default 5 s) | `{ok}` | Blocks on the cleanup future. |
| `remove_session` | `session_id` | `{ok}` | Drops from the in-memory map only. |
| `save_registry_now` | — | `{ok}` | Forces immediate persistence. |
| `get_all_states` | — | list of state dicts | Filters out `planner` / `title` session types. |
| `get_entries` | `session_id, since` | list of entry dicts | |
| `get_entry_count` | `session_id` | int | O(1), no serialization. See §4.15 rule 6. |
| `has_session` | `session_id` | bool | |
| `get_session_state` | `session_id` | state string or `null` | |
| `get_dormant_states` | — | `{sid: {last_state, name, cwd, session_type, last_activity}}` | Restart memory; display only. |
| `get_permission_policy` | — | `{policy, custom_rules}` | |
| `set_permission_policy` | `policy, custom_rules` | `null` | |
| `get_ui_prefs` / `set_ui_prefs` | `prefs` | dict / `null` | `set` **merges**, never replaces. |
| `queue_message` | `session_id, text` | `{ok, queued}` (+ `deduped`) | |
| `get_queue` / `remove_queue_item` / `edit_queue_item` / `clear_queue` | `session_id`, `index`, `text` | list / `{ok}` | |
| `get_aliases` | — | `{old_id: new_id}` | |
| `get_subsession_meta` | `session_id` | dict, **never `null`** — normalize to `{}` | |
| `mark_inbox_dirty` | `session_id` | bool | |
| `orphan_children_of` | `parent_sid` | list of child sids | |
| `detect_rewind_orphans` | `parent_sid, new_line_count` | list of child sids | |
| `reanchor_subsession` | `child_sid, new_origin_turn` | bool | |
| `detach_subsession` | `child_sid` | bool | |
| `set_auto_report_on_idle` | `session_id, on` | bool | |
| `ping` | — | `{ok, pid}` | Heartbeat. |

Unknown method ⇒ `{"req_id": …, "error": "Unknown method: <name>"}`.

### 4.3.1 Push events (daemon → web tier → browser)

| Event | Payload | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| `state_snapshot` | `{sessions: […], queues: {sid: […]}}` | Each new client connection. |
| `session_state` | full state dict (§4.4.2) | Every state transition. |
| `session_entry` | `{session_id, entry, index}` | Every new transcript entry. |
| `session_permission` | `{session_id, tool_name, tool_input}` | A tool needs manual approval. |
| `session_usage` | `{session_id, usage}` | Per-call usage extracted from a `message_start` stream event. |
| `stream_event` | `{session_id, event}` | Raw partial-message streaming. |
| `system_message` | `{session_id, subtype, data}` | Any unrecognized SDK system subtype (debug channel). |
| `session_id_remapped` | `{old_id, new_id}` | The SDK assigned a different session id. |
| `queue_updated` | `{session_id, queue}` | Any queue mutation. |
| `queue_dispatched` | `{session_id, text, remaining}` | A queued message was auto-sent. |
| `inbox_updated` | `{parent_session_id, undelivered_count, from_child_session_id, auto\|marker}` | A subsession reported to its parent. |

`daemon_reconnect` is emitted by the **web-side proxy**, not the daemon.

### 4.3.2 Documentation-drift lessons

Our published IPC reference drifted from the implementation in four ways: a wrong signature (`resolve_hook_permission`), a wrong event name (`id_remap` vs the actual `session_id_remapped`), a phantom parameter (`send_message` documented a `voice` field the proxy accepts but never transmits — voice handling belongs entirely at the WebSocket layer, which appends a timestamp tag and a *"transcribed from voice — may contain transcription errors"* note to the prompt text), and eight missing methods.

**Generate the IPC table from the dispatch map at build time, or add a test that diffs the documented method set against the registered handlers.** A hand-maintained protocol table will drift, and the drift is invisible until an integrator wastes a day on it.

---

## 4.4 Session lifecycle: states, transitions, triggers

### 4.4.1 States

Five primary states, serialized lowercase: **`starting`**, **`working`**, **`waiting`**, **`idle`**, **`stopped`**.

Orthogonal to state:

- **`substatus`** ∈ `""`, `"compacting"`, `"auto-resuming"`. **Always emit it**, including the empty string — an absent key and an empty string must be distinguishable so the client can tell "cleared" from "not provided".
- **Dormant** — *not a state*. A session absent from the daemon's map but present on disk. Naïvely the UI renders it "sleeping"; **restart memory** (§4.4.7) lets it render "was idle/working before restart" instead.

### 4.4.2 The state payload

Always present: `session_id`, `state`, `cost_usd`, `error`, `name`, `cwd`, `model`, `session_type`, `working_since` (0 unless WORKING), `created_ts`, `tracked_files` (**last 5 only**), `substatus`, `retry_at`, `retry_attempt`, `retry_max`, `retry_reason`, `entry_count`.

Conditional: `usage`; `permission` (`{tool_name, tool_input}`) when WAITING with a pending tool — **this is what lets a reconnecting browser re-render an in-flight permission prompt**, so do not omit it; `parent_session_id` + `subsession_origin_turn`; `inbox_dirty`; `auto_report_on_idle`; `queue` (merged in by the emitter).

**Countdown design.** The browser computes the live "Auto-retrying in 12m…" text locally from `retry_at`. **There is no per-second emit.** A per-second push per session is a self-inflicted load problem and it degrades badly on mobile.

### 4.4.3 Transition table

| From | To | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| — | STARTING | `start_session` creates the record |
| STARTING | WORKING | SDK client connected |
| STARTING | IDLE | bare resume with no prompt (after draining the startup `init`) |
| STARTING / WORKING | STOPPED | event loop dead; connect failure with failed reconnect |
| WORKING | WAITING | permission callback needs a human |
| WAITING | WORKING | permission resolved (allow, or deny **without** interrupt) |
| WAITING | IDLE | permission denied **with** interrupt (the interrupt path already set IDLE; the callback must not re-emit WORKING) |
| WORKING | IDLE | `RESULT` message processed |
| WORKING | IDLE | stream ended with no `RESULT` (safety net) |
| WORKING | IDLE | drive-loop `finally` catch-all when still WORKING and no result was handled |
| WORKING | IDLE | user interrupt (set **synchronously**, before the async cancel) |
| IDLE | WORKING | `send_message`, queue auto-dispatch, auto-retry fire, or auto-resume entry (a wake-up fired) |
| IDLE | WORKING + `compacting` | a pre-compaction hook fires, or a `compact_boundary` system message |
| any | STOPPED | `close_session` (forced synchronously) |
| STOPPED | STARTING | `start_session` on a stopped session is allowed (record deleted and recreated) |
| WORKING/STARTING with a finished task | STARTING | **zombie detection**: the task object is `done()` but state never left WORKING/STARTING ⇒ force-clean the record so a restart is possible |

**Special case — start on a live session.** If `start_session` targets a session that is alive (IDLE / WORKING / WAITING / STARTING) **and a prompt was supplied**, forward to `send_message` rather than erroring. This covers the extremely common front-end case of stale "running" bookkeeping. With no prompt, return `{ok:false, error:"Session already running"}`.

### 4.4.4 Start / resume — the driver coroutine

Ordering here is both a correctness and a performance contract:

1. If resuming: run **pre-resume transcript preparation** (repair + media eviction, §4.12.5) in a worker thread.
2. Compute the effective SDK permission mode: an explicit per-session mode always wins; otherwise the global policy's override; otherwise `default`.
3. Build session options and create the SDK client.
4. **Start the pre-turn mtime scan in an executor *before* awaiting connect.** (See §4.15 rule 5.)
5. `await connect()` — spawns the CLI, 700–1000 ms.
6. Capture the CLI subprocess PID for orphan cleanup.
7. State → WORKING; emit.
8. Reset per-turn flags (direct-edit, the whole wake-up family, post-compact).
9. `await` the mtime task.
10. If there is a prompt: append a `user` entry (display-capped, §4.6.4), emit it, send the query, then stream.
11. If there is **no** prompt (bare resume): consume **at most one `init` system message within a 3-second window**, then go IDLE.
12. Post-turn drain (§4.5.5), or — if a retry was flagged — arm the retry and **skip** the drain.

**Step 11 is a fix, not an optimization.** Skipping it leaves the CLI's startup `init` sitting in the SDK buffer. The post-turn drain's 100 ms peek then reads it as an auto-resume signal, flips to WORKING, and waits forever for a `RESULT` that will never come. Reported symptom: *"session appears working after model switch."*

**Do not write a pre-turn file snapshot on the first turn.** The SDK has not yet issued a `RESULT`, so the session id has not been remapped to the CLI's real UUID, and the snapshot would target the wrong transcript file.

### 4.4.5 Stop, sleep, delete

**Interrupt ("Stop").** Synchronous part first, in this order: clear the queue (default), set the interrupted flag, set state IDLE, clear the entire wake-up flag family and the substatus, cancel any pending auto-retry, **capture the current task object**, emit. Then async: resolve any pending permission as deny-with-interrupt; cancel the **captured** task (not the current `info.task`, which a new send may already have replaced); and send the SDK interrupt **only if no new task has started**. Finally append a "Session interrupted by user" system entry, unless the CLI already produced an equivalent one within the last 3 entries.

**Sleep / Close.** Force STOPPED **synchronously**, so a subsequent `start_session` is not rejected. Clear wake-up state and substatus; cancel auto-retry; erase the restart-memory entry (§4.4.7); emit; then run async cleanup.

**Async cleanup** is a seven-step, individually fault-isolated sequence:
1. resolve pending permission as deny + interrupt;
2. cancel the task;
3. **capture the CLI PID before the SDK disconnect destroys the handle**;
4. SDK disconnect;
5. kill the process tree;
6. force `state = STOPPED` and drop the client;
7. emit state and schedule a registry save.

**Contract: this coroutine must never let an exception escape.** Its future is observed by the synchronous close path, and an exception raised inside the cleanup's own error handler would break the STOPPED invariant.

**Delete** is a web-tier operation, sequenced: `close_session_sync` → `remove_session` → `orphan_children_of` → inbox removal, then **soft-delete** the transcript into a per-project trash folder with 30-day retention rather than unlinking it.

### 4.4.6 Model switch — the honesty contract

This exists because the UI once lied about which model was in use.

- `info.model` changes **only after the CLI confirms** via the control protocol. On any failure the recorded model is untouched and the error is returned to the caller.
- All model writes funnel through **one sink**, which also records the model into a "confirmed models" list that backs the model picker.
- The CLI's `init` message is the **ultimate authority** and overwrites anything the switch recorded.
- A **dormant** session (the daemon restarted since it went idle) is auto-resumed with the *requested* model rather than erroring.
- **After a successful switch, deliberately do not emit state.** An emit on an IDLE session unconditionally attempts queue dispatch, which would fire a queued message the user did not expect and make the first post-switch turn look hung.
- Before issuing the switch, set a `model-switch-in-progress` flag, because the CLI emits an `init` as a side effect and the post-turn listener must not mistake that for an auto-resume.

### 4.4.7 "User stopped" intent, and restart memory

**User-stopped** is a *derived predicate*: state is STOPPED **or** the interrupted flag is set. Check it in four places:

1. Before any reconnect (defence in depth for every caller).
2. Before the stream-heal reconnect.
3. **Again after the heal's backoff sleep** — the user can sleep the session *during* the 2/4/8-second wait.
4. In the browser client, mirroring the same intent in its own ghost-recovery guard.

Rationale: a transport death and a user sleep both leave the session looking dead. Without an intent discriminator, a reconnect scheduled the instant the stream died **resurrects a session the user just slept and re-sends the last message**. That is the "Sleep won't stick" bug, and it is maddening to users because the session appears dead on disk yet keeps reappearing in the UI.

**Restart memory** is a separate concept. At daemon startup, *before the first registry write*, capture a snapshot of previously-active sessions. Recovery deliberately re-launches only mid-task sessions, so merely-idle ones vanish from live state and would render as "sleeping," losing a distinction users rely on. `get_dormant_states` serves that snapshot, **omitting any session that has since gone live** (live state wins). An explicit stop **must** call a `forget_dormant` operation that removes the id under **both** its raw and alias-resolved forms — otherwise the sidebar keeps reporting the stopped session as idle on every page load, and the stop appears to undo itself on refresh.

### 4.4.8 Fork, rewind, compact

- **Fork** and **fork+rewind** are web-tier operations: slice the transcript JSONL up to a chosen line, rewrite every embedded session id to a fresh UUID, append a custom-title entry, and start a new session on it. The daemon is not involved beyond the normal start.
- **Rewind** restores files from two sources: reversing `Edit` old/new strings found in the transcript after the target line, and restoring from the daemon-written file-history snapshot backups (§4.12). It returns `files_restored`, `files_skipped`, and `rewind_orphans` (the last obtained from the daemon, §4.9).
- **Compact** is user-initiated by sending the literal text `/compact`. The daemon special-cases it: the echoed slash command is suppressed from the transcript, and `substatus` is optimistically set to `compacting`.

---

## 4.5 Message flow end to end

### 4.5.1 `send_message` — the ordered algorithm

```
resolve session id through the alias map
if session not in memory:
    if a transcript file exists on disk:
        read cwd / name / model from the registry
        start_session(resume=True) and re-enter
    else:
        return not-found
# ---- inbox drain: MUST sit here, above everything below ----
if info.inbox_dirty:                    # in-memory bool; zero disk I/O when false
    drained = drain_undelivered(sid)    # atomic read-modify-write of inbox.json
    text = format_drain_block(drained) + "\n---\n[Your message]\n" + text
           (or just the block, when text is empty — the "pull updates" path)
    info.inbox_dirty = False            # cleared even on failure
with info.lock:                         # atomic check-and-set
    if state is STOPPED: return error
    if state is not IDLE: return queue_message(...)
    if this is not a self-heal:  reset stream-heal counters
    if this is a genuinely new user message: clear API-retry budget and error banner
    read (do NOT clear) the interrupted flag
    capture any live post-turn listener task
    if interrupted or a listener exists: set drain-stale (quick variant for a listener)
    if a listener exists: set listener-superseded    # same lock as the state flip
    append the user entry (skip bare slash commands); emit it only if post-interrupt
    clear the model-switch flag; state = WORKING; substatus = "" (or "compacting" for /compact)
emit state
cancel the captured listener task (outside the lock, via the loop)
schedule the send-query coroutine on the loop
```

Three details are non-negotiable:

- **The interrupted flag is read but not cleared here.** Clearing it from the caller thread races the old task's cancellation handler, which checks the same flag on the loop; the old task would then believe it was a normal cancel and reset state to IDLE. Clear it inside the send-query coroutine, on the loop, *after* the old task has processed its cancel.
- **The supersede flag is set inside the same lock as the state flip.** This guarantees the listener cannot observe WORKING without also observing supersede, so a straggling auto-resume `RESULT` cannot clobber the new turn's state back to IDLE.
- **Cancel the listener before launching the new query**, so two consumers never race the single shared SDK buffer.

### 4.5.2 The send-query coroutine — ordered algorithm

```
await sleep(0)                       # let the old task's CancelledError land first
clear interrupted; clear listener-superseded
if no client: reconnect; else force IDLE and bail
pre-flight liveness: if the CLI process is dead:
    increment the shared crash counter
    if counter > 3 -> circuit-break with a "context is probably too large, run /compact"
                      message and stop
    else            -> post a visible "CLI process exited — reconnecting (n/3)" entry,
                       then reconnect
prepopulate tracked files (executor)
reset: turn-had-direct-edit, turn-content-started, awaiting-compact-drain,
       the entire wake-up family, post-compact-init-seen        # BEFORE the gather
await gather( write_file_snapshot(pre-turn), record_pre_turn_mtimes )    # in parallel
if drain-stale: drain the SDK buffer (two variants, §4.5.4)
send the query
stream: for each message -> process_message
        wrap EACH message in its own try/except so one bad message cannot kill the
        stream before RESULT arrives
        bail immediately if a newer task has taken ownership
run the CLI watchdog concurrently for the duration of the turn
after RESULT: either arm the API retry (and skip the drain), or run the post-turn drain
safety net: stream ended with no RESULT and still WORKING -> force IDLE
finally: catch-all IDLE; stream-heal; API-retry arm; post-turn snapshot
```

### 4.5.3 The CLI watchdog

Runs **only** for the duration of a WORKING turn (it auto-returns when state leaves WORKING, and is also explicitly cancelled). It polls at **1 s**:

- If the CLI subprocess PID reads as 0 (dead): increment the heal counter, set the heal-needed flag, log `STREAM_HEAL_TRIGGER site=cli_watchdog`, **disconnect the transport so the response iterator raises**, and return — handing off to the existing heal path.
- **Long-turn heartbeat**: if the turn has produced *no visible content* for **75 s**, emit exactly one `system` entry saying the model is still working, with an elapsed-minutes hint and a `/compact` tip. Motivation is measured, not theoretical: single legitimate turns of **465 s** and **1084 s** were observed on an 8.2 M-token session, during which the UI looked frozen and users assumed a crash.

It deliberately **does not** run during the post-turn listener.

### 4.5.4 Stale-buffer draining

The SDK uses **a single shared bounded message stream for the client's whole lifetime**, and it is **not** flushed by `interrupt()`. Two situations leave garbage in it, and they need *different* strategies:

- **After an interrupt.** The CLI acknowledges and emits a `RESULT` for the abandoned turn that nobody consumed. The next query's response loop reads it immediately and terminates — the UI flashes WORKING then instantly IDLE. **Strategy: one full response cycle with a 5 s overall timeout**, because it must block until the interrupt-ack actually arrives.
- **After superseding a post-turn listener.** Usually the buffer is empty, but it can hold a partial auto-resume cycle. **Strategy: adaptive multi-cycle** — a **0.1 s** timeout for the *first* message of a cycle (empty-buffer detection), **30 s** for subsequent messages (let an in-flight cycle finish), at most **10** cycles (real life is ≤ 2). Using the 5 s variant here would add a five-second penalty to *every* ordinary follow-up message.

Defence in depth: both `CancelledError` handlers and both `finally` blocks re-check **task identity** *and* the **supersede flag**, so a stale task that somehow reaches state-mutating code bails out.

### 4.5.5 Post-turn drain and the extended listener

The post-turn drain runs after every successful turn. Its **critical invariant: it must hand control to the extended listener at the end** (or be cancelled/superseded). **Every error path must `break` toward the listener rather than returning** — returning would leave the SDK buffer with no consumer, and future auto-resume content would then be read as the *next* user query's response.

Loop:
1. **Peek** with a **100 ms** timeout. Inside the peek, a *pre-detect* runs before processing: if state is IDLE and the message is anything other than a `compact_boundary` system message or a `RESULT`, treat it as an auto-resume and flip to WORKING **first** — unless a model switch is in progress, in which case clear that flag and stay IDLE.
2. If `compact_boundary` was seen: wait for `init` with a **300 s** timeout; on timeout, clear substatus and fall through to the listener.
3. If auto-resume was seen without a result: stream until its `RESULT`.
4. If a result was consumed inside the peek: loop again to catch chained activity.
5. Otherwise: exit the peek phase.
6. Enter the extended listener.

The **extended listener** sets its in-post-turn flag **before** the initial IDLE emit (so that emit cannot dispatch a queued message that would then race wake-up content), emits IDLE, and then sits on the response iterator. Its bail predicate checks **both** task identity **and** the supersede flag, because there is a window in which `send_message` has set the flag but the new task has not yet claimed ownership. It clears the in-post-turn flag on **every** exit path, but only if it still owns the task. Anti-tight-loop guard: if a cycle yields zero messages, sleep **0.5 s** before retrying.

**The listener must never flag a stream-heal.** Production logs showed this site firing on healthy idle sessions because of an unrelated "command failed with exit code 1", producing the *"Reconnected — retrying last message automatically"* loop users complained about repeatedly. The reasoning is decisive: by the time the listener runs, the turn's result already shipped and the user already saw their answer, so resending is **always** wrong. Genuine stream death during a real turn is still caught by the four in-turn trigger sites.

### 4.5.6 Wake-ups

A **wake-up** is a deferred continuation the agent schedules for itself: an explicit scheduled-wake tool, or a background shell command whose completion later produces a notification. When one is pending, the SDK will deliver a *later* auto-resume cycle (`init` → content → `RESULT`) into the shared buffer, so the queue must not dispatch into it.

Detection: tool names matched against a small exact set plus case-insensitive substrings (e.g. `schedulewake`, `wakeup`, `backgroundtask`) so vendor renames are caught without a code change.

Flags per session: `wakeup_pending`, `wakeup_is_scheduled` (true only for a *real* timer tool), `wakeup_max_delay` (per-turn accumulator of the longest expected delay), `wakeup_deadline`, `wakeup_queue_blocked_since`, `force_queue_dispatch`.

Rules — all of these cost an entire night to learn:

- **Flag wake-ups at tool-use time, but apply the "awaiting" substatus only at `RESULT`.** Setting it during the turn made the working bar read "Awaiting wake-up…" while the agent was still actively running tools.
- **Only a real scheduled-wake tool earns the label.** A background shell command is *not* a timer — it resumes if and when its process exits, possibly never. It still briefly gates the queue for race safety, but the UI must stay honestly Idle. **Promising a timer that does not exist was the root of the phantom-hang bug.**
- **Clear the substatus when the wake-up fires**, not at the next result. Leaving it latched showed "Awaiting wake-up…" and a sleeping indicator while the spinner was already running.
- **Arm a phantom deadline at `RESULT`**: `now + longest expected delay this turn + 120 s grace`. If the expected delay is unknowable (background shell), assume a ceiling of **1800 s**. A scheduled delay is clamped at **3600 s**. Past the deadline, clear the awaiting state back to plain Idle — the listener stays alive so a late wake-up can still resume; you only stop lying.
- **Reset the per-turn delay accumulator at `RESULT`**, and clear a stale deadline when no wake-up is pending.
- **Every user-driven turn start clears the whole wake-up family**, including the force-dispatch override, so it cannot latch or double-fire.

---

## 4.6 The normalized entry schema

There are **two** normalization layers. Layer 1 converts SDK objects into a backend-neutral message. Layer 2 converts that into transcript entries. Keep them separate: Layer 1 is the seam that lets you swap agent backends; Layer 2 is the seam that lets you change the UI.

### 4.6.1 Layer 1 — the normalized message

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `kind` | `assistant` \| `user` \| `system` \| `result` \| `stream_event` |
| `blocks` | list of dicts, each with a `kind` of `text` \| `tool_use` \| `tool_result` \| `thinking` |
| `is_sub_agent` | user messages only; true when the SDK set a parent-tool-use id |
| `subtype` | system messages: `init`, `compact_boundary`, `turn_duration`, `task_notification`, … |
| `data` | system payload; for stream events `{event, data}`; for results `{result: <error text>}` |
| `cost_usd`, `is_error`, `session_id`, `usage`, `duration_ms`, `num_turns` | result only |
| `raw` | the original SDK object — escape hatch, never used in core logic |

Block shapes: text `{kind, text}`; tool_use `{kind, name, id, input}` (**a non-dict input must be coerced to `{}`**); tool_result `{kind, text, tool_use_id, is_error}`; thinking `{kind}` **with no text** — chain-of-thought is deliberately not forwarded.

### 4.6.2 Layer 2 — the log entry

Fields: `kind`, `text`, `name`, `desc`, `id`, `tool_use_id`, `is_error`, `timestamp` (float). Serialization **omits empty-string fields**; `timestamp` is always present; `is_error` appears only when true.

| `kind` | Produced by | Populated fields |
|---|---|---|
| `user` | initial prompt, follow-up send, non-duplicate CLI-echoed user text | `text` |
| `asst` | assistant text block | `text` (truncated at 50 000) |
| `tool_use` | assistant tool-use block | `name`, `desc`, `id` |
| `tool_result` | user tool-result block | `text` (20 000), `tool_use_id`, `is_error` |
| `system` | interrupt markers, compaction notices, heal/retry status, model switches, watchdog announcements, SDK-injected system content | `text`, `is_error` |
| `permission` | auto-approval audit lines and the question-tool intercept | `text`, `name`, `is_error` |

**No entry is produced for thinking blocks or stream events.** Stream events are forwarded as push events only. Do not document a kind you never produce — our docstring listed a `stream` kind that nothing emits, and it misled readers.

### 4.6.3 The tool one-liner (`desc`)

Derived by **first match**, in this order: `description` when *both* `description` and `prompt` are present (that combination identifies the sub-agent tool) → 200 chars; else `command` → 300; else `file_path` (plus "write N chars" when content is present); else `path` (same); else `pattern` → 200; else `first_key: value` → 200.

### 4.6.4 Truncation is asymmetric and intentional

Assistant text **50 000**; user text and tool-result text **20 000**; the user *display* cap is **20 000**, with one exception.

**Display-cap exception.** A message that embeds an "invoke" envelope (a skill body wrapped in opening/closing markers) **must never be sliced through the closing marker**: the client renders a compact pill by matching that marker, and a blind slice dumps a multi-thousand-character skill body into the chat. Rule: keep the envelope whole regardless of size and cap only the user's own trailing text. The entry text is also what the self-heal path re-sends, so mangling the body is doubly wrong.

### 4.6.5 Message dispatch

**Resolve the session id through the alias map first.** The post-turn listener is launched with the **pre-remap** id; without alias resolution, every later lookup finds nothing and returns silently — the wake-up's `RESULT` never sets IDLE and the queued message is stranded forever.

**ASSISTANT.** Clear `compacting` when a post-compact `init` was seen; set the content-started flag. Per block:
- *text*: run the "modified thinking block 400" detector (§4.11.6). Otherwise append an `asst` entry.
- *tool_use*: append a `tool_use` entry; if the tool is `Edit` / `Write` / `MultiEdit` / `NotebookEdit`, add its file path to `tracked_files` and set the direct-edit flag; if the tool creates a wake-up, set the wake-up flags and accumulate the expected delay.
- *thinking*: skip.

**USER.** For tool-result blocks: detect `Stream closed` **or** `Tool permission request failed` inside an error result and flag stream-heal. The second string matters — it is what the CLI writes when its *permission channel* breaks while stdout is still alive, and it produces 10+ failed tools in a single turn without any other detector firing. For text blocks: skip sub-agent text; skip bare slash-command echoes; render SDK-injected system content as a collapsed `system` entry with a short label (deduplicated against the last 3 entries); otherwise append a `user` entry **without emitting** (the client already shows an optimistic bubble), and only if it is not a duplicate of the last user entry.

SDK system-content markers to recognize: continuation-summary text, a system-reminder tag, a local-command-stdout tag, a local-command-caveat tag, command-name / command-message / command-args tags, and `[Request interrupted by user]`.

**SYSTEM.**
- `compact_boundary` — **discard as stale** if the turn has produced no content *and* substatus is not already `compacting`. (The SDK delivers it *after* `RESULT`, so it sits in the buffer and reappears at the start of the next turn.) Otherwise set WORKING + `compacting`, record the pre-compaction token count, emit, and append a "Compacting context (Nk tokens, auto|manual)…" entry.
- `turn_duration` — log only.
- `init` — record the CLI's resolved model id (**ground truth**). Clear substatus unconditionally and reset the post-compact flag. If we were compacting **and** the post-turn drain flag is set, go IDLE. Emit; if we were compacting, append "Context compacted".
- anything else — forward as a `system_message` push event for debugging.

**RESULT**, in this order: clear stale substatus (preserving `auto-resuming` when a wake-up is pending); apply the wake-up substatus and arm the phantom deadline; record cost; merge usage (**per-call usage from a `message_start` stream event wins over the cumulative result usage**); record duration and turn count; set the "ever got a result" flag; classify errors and flag an auto-retry or surface the error; **remap the session id** if the SDK assigned a different one; then, under the per-session lock, set IDLE **unless superseded**, and set the awaiting-compact-drain flag so the IDLE emit is deferred.

The **remap** must fan out to: the in-memory session map, the alias map, the message queue, the persisted user-set name, a "remapped" marker so stale ids are filtered from listings, any task↔session links in other subsystems, and a `session_id_remapped` push event. Miss any one of these and you get a class of bug where a session is half-visible under two identities.

**STREAM_EVENT.** Extract per-call usage from `message_start` — this is the **authoritative** context-window size, whereas the result's usage is cumulative — push a `session_usage` event, and forward the raw event.

---

## 4.7 Message queueing

### 4.7.1 Why

The frontend cannot reliably know whether a session is idle at the instant of a submit. Rather than returning an error on that race, `send_message` **auto-queues** whenever the state is not IDLE and returns `{ok:true, queued:true}`. The queue is also what makes unattended overnight operation work: messages typed mid-turn are delivered in order when the turn finishes.

### 4.7.2 Guarantees

- **FIFO per session.** Dispatch pops index 0.
- **Adjacent-duplicate suppression.** If the tail of the queue is byte-identical to the incoming text, drop the add — but **still emit a queue update** so the client's optimistic cache converges. This defends against Enter+click double-fire, client double-tap, and a send/auto-queue race with a wake-up state flip.
- **Re-queue at the front on dispatch failure**, so a lost race never loses a message.
- **Remapped with the session** when the SDK reassigns an id.
- **Cleared on interrupt by default** (`clear_queue=True`), so the post-interrupt IDLE does not immediately fire a message the user just stopped. The health monitor's watchdog interrupt deliberately passes `clear_queue=False` — there, the queue *is* the continuation.

### 4.7.3 The dispatch gate

Suppress dispatch on an IDLE emit when **any** of the following hold:

1. The interrupted flag is set.
2. An API-retry countdown is pending (`retry_at > 0`). The retry is the continuation of the failed turn and must run first; otherwise a queued follow-up jumps the queue and the failed work is silently abandoned. **This guard must live at the single chokepoint**, not at each call site, because the starvation watchdog explicitly bypasses per-call-site gates.
3. The in-post-turn flag **and** a pending wake-up are *both* set — **unless** the force-dispatch override is set.

`queue_message` must **duplicate** gates (2) and (3), because it dispatches directly when the session is already idle; without the duplicate, it is the bypass that reintroduces the bug.

**Deferred re-emit safety net.** After a dispatch attempt on IDLE, arm a **3-second** timer that re-checks: if the session is still IDLE and still ungated, try dispatch again (covering a message queued in the exact instant the session went idle) and re-emit the IDLE state (covering a silently dropped WebSocket push). The timer must apply the same retry gate, because it fires *before* a longer backoff would.

**Starvation watchdog.** Sweep every **30 s**. Arm a `queue_blocked_since` timestamp the first sweep that sees a live, non-stopped session with an undrained queue, and **keep the armed timestamp across sweeps** until the queue empties. Past **120 s** (env-overridable), set the force-dispatch override so the gate falls open. Two rules, both learned the hard way:

- **The watchdog must bet on nothing about wake-ups.** It arms purely on "a live, non-stopped session has an undrained queue." A self-perpetuating wake-up loop re-arms `wakeup_pending` at *every* `RESULT`, so a wake-up-aware condition never fires. In the incident, four queued messages sat dead overnight behind 38 consecutive background-shell wake-ups.
- **Resetting the armed timestamp each sweep means the timeout is never reached** — that flicker *was* the original starvation. Keep it armed.
- **Force-dispatch only when IDLE.** A WORKING session just gets the flag and drains at its next IDLE emit, so an in-flight turn is never interrupted.

### 4.7.4 Persistence and debouncing

File: `<agent-home>/gui_message_queues.json`, a flat `{session_id: [text, …]}` map; empty queues are omitted. Saves are **debounced on a 1-second timer** — if a timer is already alive, skip, because the pending save will capture the newest state. Shutdown cancels the timer and writes synchronously.

**Rule: never call the immediate save from a queue operation.** Before the debounce existed, every add/edit/remove/clear/dispatch rewrote the entire queue state, and auto-dispatch chains produced measurable I/O contention.

Recovery reads this file at startup: **a session with a non-empty queue is recovered even if it was merely idle**, because otherwise the message sits orphaned with no task to consume it.
