# Part 6 — Persistence and the Data Model

---

## 6.1 What this part covers, and the storage philosophy

### 6.1.1 Definitions used throughout this chapter

Read these first. Every term below is used with exactly this meaning for the rest of the chapter.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Agent CLI** | A third-party command-line program wrapping a large-language-model coding agent. It runs as a child process, edits files on the local machine, and writes its own conversation files to its own private state directory. You do not control its source, its file format, or its release schedule. |
| **Agent SDK** | The vendor-supplied client library that spawns and drives the Agent CLI. |
| **`<agent-home>`** | The Agent CLI's per-user state directory — a dot-directory under the user's home. Derive it at runtime from the home directory; never hardcode a user path. |
| **`<home>`** | The operating-system user's home directory. |
| **`<repo-root>`** | The root of the application you are building. |
| **`<app>`** | A short lowercase token identifying your product, used as a filesystem prefix (e.g. `<app>-media/`). Pick one and never change it. |
| **`<APP>_*`** | Environment-variable prefix for your product. |
| **Transcript** | The append-only JSONL file (one JSON object per line) the Agent CLI writes for one conversation. It is the source of truth for conversation history and is what a *resume* replays back to the model. |
| **Session** | One long-lived conversation, bound to one working directory, identified by a session id, backed by one transcript. |
| **Project** | One working directory the user runs sessions in. Projects partition almost every store in the system. |
| **Board** | The task-tracking feature (columns, cards, hierarchy, status transitions). This is the only domain that lives in SQL. |
| **Embedded engine** | A single-file, in-process SQL database with write-ahead logging. |
| **Hosted Postgres** | A managed Postgres service reached over HTTPS through a REST-over-SQL gateway, with row-level security and server-side stored procedures. |
| **Repository** | The abstract data-access interface over the board's storage. |
| **Distinctive ownership prefix** | A fixed string (this specification uses `gui_`) that every file *your application* writes into `<agent-home>` must carry, so ownership is unambiguous at a glance. |
| **Derived state** | Data that can be regenerated in full from a more authoritative source, and may therefore be deleted at any time. |

### 6.1.2 What you are building

A persistence layer for a local-first desktop web application that drives a third-party coding agent. The application stores its own structured data, reads and writes another program's private files, and must survive crashes, antivirus file locks, concurrent writers it does not control, and a one-click "Update" button pressed by people who do not read diffs.

There is one fact from which the entire design follows:

> **The application does not own its most important data.** Conversation transcripts belong to another program, live in that program's private directory, and are written concurrently by a process you cannot coordinate with.

Everything in this chapter is a consequence of managing that relationship safely. If you are building a system where you own the conversation store outright, large parts of §6.3, §6.10, §6.11 and §6.13 collapse into something much simpler — and you should take that option if it is available to you. Read §6.3.4 and §6.13.5 before deciding.

### 6.1.3 The storage philosophy in five sentences

1. Use SQL only where the data is genuinely relational, genuinely yours, and genuinely queried in aggregate.
2. Use flat files where the format is dictated externally, the access pattern is append-mostly, or interoperability with the foreign tool is required.
3. Put every file your application owns **outside the repository tree**, in the user's home directory, because a gitignore rule is a policy and a directory outside the repository is a mechanism.
4. Treat every read of foreign state as untrusted input: tolerate missing, locked, truncated, and malformed data on every single path.
5. Make every write atomic, and make every destructive operation reversible or preceded by a tombstone.

---

## 6.2 The three storage tiers and why the split is drawn where it is

| Tier | Location | Contents | Owner | Consistency requirement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Relational** | `<agent-home>/gui_kanban.db` (embedded engine) **or** a hosted Postgres database | Board data: tasks, columns, tags, issues, status history, task↔session links, preferences | Your application, exclusively | Strong. Transactions, foreign keys, cascade deletes. |
| **Derived relational** | `<agent-home>/gui_search_index.db` (embedded engine + full-text extension) | Full-text index over transcripts | Your application | None. Disposable; delete and rebuild on any error. |
| **Flat files** | `<agent-home>/…` and `<repo-root>/…` | Transcripts (foreign), per-project session bookkeeping, daemon runtime state, configuration, logs, caches, composed documents, backups | Mixed | Per-file atomicity; tolerant reads. |

### 6.2.1 Why the board is in SQL

The board has every property SQL is good at, and no property that argues against it:

- A **recursive parent/child hierarchy** with cascade delete and ancestor walks.
- **Ordered positions** within a column, needing midpoint insertion and range renumbering.
- Two **many-to-many** relationships (tasks↔sessions, tasks↔tags).
- An **append-only audit trail** (status history) that is the substrate for every analytics view.
- **Aggregate queries** — velocity per day, cycle time, throughput heatmaps — that want `GROUP BY`, `JOIN`, and date functions.

Decisively: the board is also the only data you fully own. It has no external writer, so you can guarantee its invariants. Never put data with a foreign writer behind a schema you enforce; you will lose that fight.

### 6.2.2 Why sessions are flat files

1. **The format is dictated externally.** A transcript is JSONL written by the Agent CLI. You can read it, append to it, and occasionally rewrite it. You cannot choose its shape.
2. **The access pattern is append-mostly.** Transcripts are appended thousands of times per session and read either start-to-end or tail-only. A line-oriented file is exactly the right structure. A row per message would put a write barrier on the hot path and buy nothing, because search is served by a separate index.
3. **Interoperability is required.** The user can open the same session in the Agent CLI's own terminal interface. Migrating transcripts into a database breaks that, permanently.
4. **Crash tolerance is better.** A truncated JSONL costs you one line, and every reader in the system already skips unparseable lines. A truncated database page costs you the database.

Small per-project bookkeeping maps (display names, tombstones, remaps, access timestamps) are also flat JSON. They are small, read on every sidebar render, and benefit from mtime-keyed caching. Putting a dictionary behind a schema, a connection pool, and a migration runner is a poor trade.

### 6.2.3 Why your own state lives in the user's home, not the repository

State that lives inside the repository tree is one missing ignore rule away from being published. In the reference product the repository is public and a one-click "Update" button commits and pushes without a diff review, pressed by non-technical users. Home-directory state is *structurally* incapable of being committed.

**Adopt this wholesale.** Give every file you place in `<agent-home>` the distinctive ownership prefix `gui_` (or your own equivalent) so a maintainer of the foreign tool can tell at a glance which files are not theirs, and so your own cleanup code can never target a foreign file by accident.

---

## 6.3 The path-encoding contract (and why you should avoid needing one)

### 6.3.1 The problem

The Agent CLI stores each project's transcripts in a directory whose name is a **lossy encoding of the project's absolute working directory**. To find a session, you must reproduce that encoding byte-for-byte. Get it wrong and sessions do not appear "missing" with an error — they appear *not to exist*, while the daemon is happily running them.

### 6.3.2 The encoding rules

Apply these as ordered literal replacements over the raw path string. There is no escaping and no reserved character.

| Replace | With |
|---|---|
| `\` | `-` |
| `/` | `-` |
| `:` | `-` |
| `_` | `-` |
| `.` | `-` |

Worked examples:

```
C:\Users\<user>\code\Foo        →  C--Users-<user>-code-Foo
/home/<user>/code/Foo           →  -home-<user>-code-Foo
<home>/<agent-home>/_system     →  C--Users-<user>--<agent-dir>--system
some_project.v2                 →  some-project-v2
```

**The underscore and dot rules are the ones people omit, and both caused production incidents.**

- Omitting `_` → `-`: any project whose path contains an underscore silently fails every project filter. Sessions run but are invisible.
- Omitting `.` → `-`: the reference implementation runs internal utility sessions in a working directory under the agent's own dot-directory. Without the dot rule, the filter that hides that internal project built the wrong directory name, so **the internal project leaked into the user-facing project list**, *and* its stale transcripts were never pruned because the cleanup sweep looked in a directory that did not exist. One missing character, two bugs.

Write an exhaustive encoding test matrix before you write anything that consumes it: Windows drive letters, POSIX roots, underscores, dots, hyphens already present in the path, mixed separators, empty string, drive-letter-only, and a round-trip case.

### 6.3.3 Decoding is ambiguous and must probe the filesystem

Because `-`, `_`, `/` and `.` all encode to `-`, decoding cannot be a pure function. Implement it as a search:

```
DECODE(encoded):
  if encoded contains "--":                    # Windows: drive separator
      drive, rest = split on first "--"
      candidate = drive + ":/" + rest with all "-" → "/"
      if candidate is a directory: return candidate
      # otherwise rebuild segment by segment
      parts = rest split on "-"
      path = drive + ":/"
      i = 0
      while i < len(parts):
          for lookahead in 4..1:                # longest match first
              for sep in ["_", "-", "/"]:
                  cand = sep.join(parts[i : i+lookahead])
                  if (path + cand) is a directory:
                      path += cand + "/" ; i += lookahead ; goto next
          path += parts[i] + "/" ; i += 1       # give up on this segment
      if path (stripped) is a directory: return it
  else if platform is not Windows:              # POSIX: leading "-"
      ... identical algorithm rooted at "/" ...
  else:
      return encoded unchanged                  # Windows, no drive marker

  # Final fallback: scan likely parents, re-encode each child, compare
  for scan_dir in [<home>/Documents, and on POSIX <home>/{projects,src,code,dev,repos}]:
      for child (and one level of grandchildren) in scan_dir:
          if ENCODE(child) == encoded: return child
  return best-effort reconstruction
```

Cap the lookahead (4 tokens is sufficient in practice) or the search becomes exponential on deep paths. Tolerate permission errors on every directory iteration.

### 6.3.4 What you should do instead

If you own the transcript store, **do not build this.** Key directories by a UUID or a hash of the working directory, and store the real working directory as a field inside the file. The ambiguous encoding exists here only because it is imposed by a foreign tool. Reproducing it in a greenfield system would be self-harm.

### 6.3.5 The project-id aliasing escape hatch

Because the board's `project_id` is derived from an absolute filesystem path, two users on different operating systems pointing at the same shared hosted-Postgres board land in **different silos** — their paths differ, therefore their project ids differ, therefore they see empty boards.

Provide an alias map in the application config: `project_id_aliases: {local_project_id: remote_project_id}`. Consult it **only** on board routes. Sessions, file paths and version-control operations must keep using the real local-derived id, because those legitimately depend on the actual folder on this machine.

Provide a discovery endpoint that lists the distinct `project_id` values present in the remote database and fuzzy-matches them against the local one, so the user can adopt an alias from a picker instead of hand-editing config. A sufficient heuristic:

- Compare the trailing `-`-delimited segment of each id (that is the original folder's basename).
- Score 100 for an exact case-insensitive basename match, 60 if either full id contains the other's basename, 0 otherwise.
- Score 0 for an exact full-id match — that means no alias is needed.

---

## 6.4 The relational schema (complete, final state, table by table)

This is the final combined state after all migrations. Types are given in embedded-engine terms with the hosted-Postgres equivalents noted in §6.4.10.

All timestamps are **ISO-8601 UTC strings** in the embedded engine. All surrogate keys are **UUID4 strings**.

### 6.4.1 `schema_version`

| Column | Type | Null | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `version` | INTEGER | no | — | Primary key. One row per applied migration. |
| `applied_at` | TEXT | no | — | ISO-8601 UTC timestamp of application. |

### 6.4.2 `preferences`

A global key/value store. Not per-project.

| Column | Type | Null | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `key` | TEXT | no | — | Primary key. |
| `value` | TEXT | no | — | Stored stringified. |
| `updated_at` | TEXT | no | — | ISO-8601 UTC. |

Seeded on install: `kanban_backend` = `sqlite`, `kanban_auto_advance` = `false`, `kanban_page_size` = `50`.

**Design note, stated as correction:** in the reference implementation this table overlaps with the JSON application-config file, and the JSON file is what the runtime actually reads. The table therefore survives mainly as migration payload. **Choose one preferences store.** If you keep this table, read from it; if you keep the JSON file, drop this table. Two stores for one concept guarantees divergence.

Also: store typed values, not `str(value)`. Stringifying booleans produces `"true"` from one writer and `"True"` from another, and every reader then needs a normalization function.

### 6.4.3 `board_columns`

One row per column per project.

| Column | Type | Null | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | TEXT | no | — | Primary key, UUID4. |
| `project_id` | TEXT | no | — | Encoded-working-directory project key. |
| `name` | TEXT | no | — | Display label, e.g. "Not Started". |
| `status_key` | TEXT | no | — | Machine key, e.g. `not_started`. Joins to `tasks.status`. |
| `position` | INTEGER | no | `0` | Left-to-right order. |
| `color` | TEXT | yes | `#8b949e` | Hex swatch. |
| `is_terminal` | INTEGER (boolean) | yes | `0` | Column means "done". |
| `is_regression` | INTEGER (boolean) | yes | `0` | Column means "went backwards". |
| `sort_mode` | TEXT | yes | `manual` | `manual` or `last_updated`. |
| `sort_direction` | TEXT | yes | `desc` | `asc` or `desc`. |

Constraint: `UNIQUE(project_id, status_key)`.

**Default columns**, created lazily the first time a board is read for an unknown project:

| Name | `status_key` | `position` | `color` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Not Started | `not_started` | 0 | `#8b949e` |
| Working | `working` | 1 | `#58a6ff` |
| Validating | `validating` | 2 | `#d29922` |
| Remediating | `remediating` | 3 | `#f85149` |
| Complete | `complete` | 4 | `#3fb950` |

Define this list **once**. The reference implementation defines it in three places — twice inside the two storage backends and once in a higher-level defaults module — and the copies already disagree about `sort_mode` (the backends use `manual` for all five; the defaults module marks the last three `last_updated`/`desc`). Which one you get depends on which code path created the project. Do not reproduce this.

### 6.4.4 `tasks`

The core entity. A self-referencing tree.

| Column | Type | Null | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | TEXT | no | — | Primary key, UUID4. |
| `project_id` | TEXT | no | — | Project key (subject to aliasing, §6.3.5). |
| `parent_id` | TEXT | yes | NULL | FK → `tasks(id)` ON DELETE CASCADE. NULL = root task. |
| `position` | INTEGER | no | `0` | Gap-numbered order within (project, status). |
| `title` | TEXT | no | — | |
| `description` | TEXT | yes | NULL | |
| `verification_url` | TEXT | yes | NULL | Optional URL used by the validation workflow. |
| `status` | TEXT | no | `not_started` | One of `not_started`, `working`, `validating`, `remediating`, `complete`. |
| `owner` | TEXT | yes | NULL | Free-text assignee. |
| `created_at` | TEXT | no | — | ISO-8601 UTC. |
| `updated_at` | TEXT | no | — | ISO-8601 UTC; bumped on every partial update. |

Indexes:

| Index | Columns |
|---|---|
| `idx_tasks_project` | `(project_id)` |
| `idx_tasks_parent` | `(parent_id)` |
| `idx_tasks_status` | `(project_id, status)` |
| `idx_tasks_position` | `(project_id, status, position)` |
| `idx_tasks_owner` | `(owner)` |

**`depth` is deliberately not a column.** It is computed — in the embedded engine by walking `parent_id` per row, in hosted Postgres by a single in-memory pass over the already-fetched flat list. Persisting depth creates an update anomaly the moment a subtree is re-parented.

### 6.4.5 Ordering algorithm (gap numbering)

Positions are gap-numbered with a **gap constant of 1000**. Both backends must use the same constant or a migrated board reorders itself.

```
NEXT_POSITION(project, status) = MAX(position) in that column (or 0) + GAP
MIN_POSITION(project, status)  = MIN(position) in that column (or GAP)

REORDER(task, after_id, before_id):
    after_pos  = position of after_id  (0 if after_id is null)
    before_pos = position of before_id (null if before_id is null)

    if before_pos is null:  new_pos = after_pos + GAP        # append to end
    else:                   new_pos = (after_pos + before_pos) // 2

    if new_pos == after_pos or new_pos == before_pos:        # gap exhausted
        RENUMBER(project, status)                            # 1×GAP, 2×GAP, …
        return REORDER(task, after_id, before_id)            # retry once

    write new_pos and bump updated_at
```

`RENUMBER` reassigns every task in the column, ordered by current position, to `(index+1) × GAP`. Guard the recursion so a pathological state cannot loop.

**On status change**, if the caller did not supply an explicit position, assign `NEXT_POSITION` in the *target* column. Without this, a card dropped into a new column collides with whatever already occupies that position value.

### 6.4.6 `task_sessions`

Link table joining a board task to an agent session.

| Column | Type | Null | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `task_id` | TEXT | no | — | FK → `tasks(id)` ON DELETE CASCADE. |
| `session_id` | TEXT | no | — | Session identifier. **Not** a foreign key — sessions are files, not rows. |
| `created_at` | TEXT | no | — | |
| `session_type` | TEXT | no | `session` | `session` (user work) or `planner` (AI planning run). |

Primary key: `(task_id, session_id)`.

Required operation: `remap_session(old_id, new_id)` — updates every row's `session_id`. See §6.13.3 for why session ids change underneath you.

### 6.4.7 `task_issues`

| Column | Type | Null | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | TEXT | no | — | Primary key, UUID4. |
| `task_id` | TEXT | no | — | FK → `tasks(id)` ON DELETE CASCADE. |
| `description` | TEXT | no | — | |
| `session_id` | TEXT | yes | NULL | Session that logged the issue. |
| `resolved_at` | TEXT | yes | NULL | NULL = open. |
| `created_at` | TEXT | no | — | |

Index: `idx_issues_task(task_id)`.

### 6.4.8 `task_status_history`

Append-only audit trail. The substrate for every analytics view.

| Column | Type | Null | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | TEXT | no | — | Primary key, UUID4. |
| `task_id` | TEXT | no | — | FK → `tasks(id)` ON DELETE CASCADE. |
| `old_status` | TEXT | yes | NULL | NULL on task creation. |
| `new_status` | TEXT | no | — | |
| `changed_by` | TEXT | yes | NULL | Actor label. |
| `changed_at` | TEXT | no | — | ISO-8601 UTC. |
| `session_id` | TEXT | yes | NULL | Session that caused the transition. |

Indexes: `idx_status_hist_task(task_id)`, `idx_status_hist_time(changed_at)`.

Rows are written automatically in exactly two places: on task creation (`old_status` NULL), and inside the partial-update path **only when `status` actually changes**. Do not write a history row for a no-op update; it poisons cycle-time reports.

Populate `changed_by`. The reference implementation leaves it NULL on both automatic paths, which makes "who moved this card" unanswerable — the column exists but carries no information.

### 6.4.9 `task_tags`

| Column | Type | Null | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | TEXT | no | — | Primary key, UUID4 (Postgres: generated default). |
| `task_id` | TEXT | no | — | FK → `tasks(id)` ON DELETE CASCADE. |
| `tag` | TEXT | no | — | |
| `created_at` | TEXT | no | — | |

Constraint `UNIQUE(task_id, tag)`; indexes `idx_tags_task(task_id)`, `idx_tags_tag(tag)`.

> **Cautionary note — two definitions of one table.** In the reference implementation this table is declared *twice* and incompatibly: the migration SQL declares a bare two-column link table `(task_id, tag)` with a composite primary key, while the runtime upgrade code declares the surrogate-key form above. A fresh install therefore creates the wrong shape from SQL and immediately rewrites it in code (rename to temp → create new → `INSERT … SELECT` with generated ids → drop temp → recreate indexes). It works, but nobody reading the SQL can tell what the table actually is. **Ship exactly one definition of every table, in the migration files, and let code only ever consume it.**

### 6.4.10 Hosted-Postgres deltas

Same logical schema. Physical differences:

- Timestamp columns are `TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()` rather than TEXT.
- `is_terminal` / `is_regression` are native `BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE`.
- `task_tags.id` uses a server-side UUID default.
- **Row-level security is enabled on every table with no policies defined.** With RLS on and zero policies, the anonymous/public role gets zero access. The server uses a service-role key that bypasses RLS, so application behavior is unchanged. This is a pure security hardening: without it, anyone holding the project URL and the publishable key can read, modify and delete everything through the provider's public REST API.
- Two stored procedures are required: `get_ancestors(task_id_param)` (recursive CTE returning the parent chain) and `execute_readonly_sql(query, params)` (used by the analytics layer).

### 6.4.11 Dead schema to *not* build

The reference implementation's initial migration creates a project-level tag registry — `tags(tag, project_id, color, usage_count)`, primary key `(tag, project_id)`, index on `project_id`. **It is never read or written by any code path**, and it is absent from the hosted-Postgres bootstrap entirely. If you want tag colors or usage counts, design that table deliberately and wire it up. Otherwise omit it. Dead tables are not free: they appear in migrations, in backups, in every schema diff, and in the mental model of everyone who reads the schema.

---

## 6.5 Schema evolution: what each migration added, and how to build a migration runner that actually works

### 6.5.1 The evolution, so you can see the shape of the change

| # | What it introduced |
|---|---|
| 001 | The entire base schema: `schema_version`, `preferences` (seeded), `board_columns`, `tasks` + five indexes, `task_sessions`, `task_issues`, `task_status_history`, the (dead) `tags` table, and the first form of `task_tags`. Records version 1. |
| 002 | Upgrades `task_tags` from a bare link table to the surrogate-key form (`id`, `created_at`, `UNIQUE(task_id, tag)`), migrating existing rows. |
| 003 | Hosted-Postgres only: the `get_ancestors` recursive-CTE stored procedure. |
| 004 | Hosted-Postgres only: enable row-level security on all eight tables, no policies. |
| 005 | `ALTER TABLE task_sessions ADD COLUMN session_type TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'session'` — distinguishes user work sessions from AI-planner sessions. |
| 006 | `ALTER TABLE task_status_history ADD COLUMN session_id TEXT` — attributes a status transition to the session that caused it. |

Note the shape: two structural migrations, two additive column migrations, and two that apply only to the remote dialect. That mix is typical and it is exactly what breaks naive runners.

### 6.5.2 Build this runner

```
MIGRATE(connection):
    ensure schema_version table exists
    current = MAX(version) from schema_version, or 0
    for each file matching NNN_*.sql in the migrations directory, ordered by NNN:
        if NNN <= current: continue
        BEGIN TRANSACTION
            execute the file's statements
            INSERT INTO schema_version(version, applied_at) VALUES (NNN, now_utc())
        COMMIT                                  # version recorded in the same txn
        on any error:
            ROLLBACK
            abort startup with a message naming the failing file and the SQL error
```

Requirements, each of which the reference implementation violates in some way:

1. **Discover migrations by filename.** Do not hardcode a list of "apply this, then this". Adding migration 007 must require adding one file.
2. **Gate on the recorded version.** The recorded version must *decide* what runs.
3. **Record the version inside the same transaction as the DDL.** Otherwise a crash between the two leaves the database migrated and the ledger stale, and the next boot re-applies.
4. **Fail loudly.** A migration error must stop startup with the filename in the message, not surface later as a missing-column error in an unrelated feature.
5. **Run the same files against both dialects,** or generate both dialects from one source. See §6.5.4.
6. **Keep introspective idempotence as a belt-and-braces layer only.** Checking "does this column already exist" before adding it is a good safety net. It is a bad primary mechanism.

### 6.5.3 What went wrong in the reference implementation

Present these to your team as anti-patterns; every one is real.

- **The version ledger is a log, not a gate.** The runner reads `MAX(version)` but never compares it to a target. Only its *existence* matters: if any row exists, the runner skips the base schema and calls three hardcoded upgrade functions unconditionally; otherwise it executes the base SQL and then calls the same three. Adding migration 007 means editing the runner in two places. *Fix: gate on the version.*
- **Only one migration file is ever read from disk.** The base schema. Everything after it is Python code that introspects `PRAGMA table_info` and adds columns when missing. The `.sql` files for those migrations exist but are decorative. *Fix: the files are the migration.*
- **One migration file duplicates a block from another.** The "tags" migration's SQL is a copy of the `task_tags` block already present in the initial migration; the actual upgrade lives only in code. *Fix: one migration, one change, one place.*
- **No transaction wraps a migration.** A DDL failure leaves a half-migrated database and an unrecorded version. *Fix: transaction per migration.*
- **Two methods with the same name in one class.** The embedded backend defines `create_column` twice with different signatures; the later definition silently shadows the earlier one, making the first dead code that still reads as live. A linter catches this in one second. *Fix: enable a linter that flags redefinition, in CI, from day one.*

### 6.5.4 The dialect-divergence trap (read this twice)

**The correct design:** one set of migration definitions, applied to both backends, with dialect differences handled by a translation layer or by generating both dialects from a shared description. The remote schema version must be tracked and checked exactly like the local one.

**What went wrong:** the remote schema is created not from the migration files but from a hardcoded list of bootstrap statements inside the remote backend. That list was written when the schema was at version 1 and **was never updated**. It therefore lacks `task_sessions.session_type` (migration 005), `task_status_history.session_id` (006), the `idx_tasks_owner` index, and the `tags` table.

The failure is silent, and the way it is concealed is worse than the bug: the remote backend wraps writes and reads in try/except and, on failure, **retries without the missing column**. A user on the remote backend silently loses the ability to distinguish planner sessions from work sessions, and status transitions silently lose their session attribution. Nothing logs, nothing alerts, and every test passes because the local backend has the columns.

Rules that fall out:

1. Never let a schema difference be absorbed by a runtime `except` clause. Detect the version, and refuse to start with a clear message telling the user to run the pending migration.
2. Provision remote schemas from the same migration ledger you use locally, and store `schema_version` remotely too.
3. Write one integration test that asserts *column-for-column equality* between the two dialects' final schemas.

### 6.5.5 The unprovisioned stored procedure

The analytics layer requires an `execute_readonly_sql(query, params)` stored procedure on the remote backend. **It is not in the bootstrap statement list.** On a fresh remote install every analytics view fails with a "this feature requires a stored procedure; see the plan document" error, and the SQL to create it exists only in a docstring.

*Correct design:* every server-side object a feature depends on is created by the provisioning path, and provisioning is verified by a smoke test that calls each procedure once.

There is a related dead artifact: a stored procedure defined in the migration files (`get_project_status_history`) declares a return type of `SETOF status_history` — a table that does not exist under that name; the real table is `task_status_history`. It has evidently never been executed. *Correct design:* if a migration file contains a procedure, the provisioning path must run it and a test must call it.

### 6.5.6 The dialect-specific-SQL trap in analytics

The analytics endpoints use a raw-SQL escape hatch on the repository interface. Those queries are written in the **embedded engine's dialect** — `DATE(...)` scalar functions and `?` positional placeholders — and are then shipped verbatim to hosted Postgres through the stored procedure, which expects different placeholder syntax and does not have identical date functions.

Portability here was assumed, never tested. Either (a) write dialect-neutral SQL and test both backends in CI, or (b) give the repository interface real methods for each analytics query and let each backend implement them natively. Option (b) is better: it also removes the raw-SQL escape hatch, which is the only place in an otherwise fully abstracted data layer where a caller can hand-write SQL.

---

## 6.6 The repository pattern and backend selection

### 6.6.1 The abstraction

Define an abstract base class that specifies the **entire** data-access surface for the board, plus a set of plain data classes. Every other module in the system programs against these types and never touches SQL, HTTP, or a client library.

All methods are **synchronous**. The web tier runs a threading concurrency model with no event loop to await on; making the data layer async would force a bridge at every call site.

Data classes:

| Class | Fields |
|---|---|
| `Task` | `id`, `project_id`, `parent_id`, `title`, `description`, `verification_url`, `status` (enum), `position`, `depth` (computed, not persisted), `created_at`, `updated_at`, `owner` |
| `TaskSession` | `task_id`, `session_id`, `created_at`, `session_type` (default `session`) |
| `TaskIssue` | `id`, `task_id`, `description`, `session_id`, `resolved_at`, `created_at` |
| `TaskTag` | `id`, `task_id`, `tag`, `created_at` |
| `BoardColumn` | `id`, `project_id`, `name`, `status_key`, `position`, `color`, `sort_mode`, `sort_direction`, `is_terminal`, `is_regression` |
| `TaskStatus` (enum) | `not_started`, `working`, `validating`, `remediating`, `complete` |

Each data class exposes a `to_dict()` that produces JSON-safe output (the status enum becomes its string value).

Interface method groups:

| Group | Methods |
|---|---|
| Lifecycle | `initialize()`, `close()` |
| Tasks | `create_task`, `get_task`, `update_task(id, **partial_fields)`, `delete_task`, `get_children`, `get_ancestors`, `get_tasks_by_status` |
| Ordering | `reorder_task(id, after_id, before_id)`, `get_next_position`, `get_min_position` |
| Session links | `link_session(task_id, session_id, session_type)`, `unlink_session`, `get_task_sessions(task_id, session_type=None)`, `get_session_task`, `remap_session(old, new)` |
| Issues | `create_issue`, `resolve_issue`, `get_open_issues`, `get_all_issues` |
| Tags | `add_tag`, `remove_tag`, `get_task_tags`, `get_tasks_by_tag`, `get_all_tags` |
| Columns / board | `get_columns`, `upsert_columns`, `get_board` |
| Batch (performance) | `get_children_counts_batch(ids) → {id: (total, complete)}`, `get_session_counts_batch(ids) → {id: count}` |
| Migration support | `get_all_preferences`, `set_preference`, `get_all_columns_all_projects`, `get_all_tasks_ordered`, `get_all_task_sessions`, `get_all_task_tags`, `get_all_status_history`, `add_status_history`, `create_task_from_dict`, `create_column`, `clear_all_data` |
| Escape hatch (avoid) | `execute_sql(sql, params) → list[dict]` — see §6.5.6 |

`get_board(project_id)` returns `{columns: [BoardColumn…], tasks: {status_key: [Task…]}}` and **auto-creates the default columns** when a project has none. Every status key present in the data must appear in the tasks map even if no column declares it, or tasks silently vanish from the UI when a column is renamed.

### 6.6.2 Backend selection and the singleton

```
CREATE_REPOSITORY(backend=None):
    if a cached instance exists: return it
    acquire lock; re-check cache (double-checked locking)
    if backend is None:
        backend = application_config["kanban_backend"]  # default "sqlite"
    if backend == "sqlite":
        repo = EmbeddedRepository()                     # default path <agent-home>/gui_kanban.db
    elif backend == "supabase":
        url = config["supabase_url"] or env <APP>_DB_URL
        key = config["supabase_secret_key"] or env <APP>_DB_SECRET_KEY
        if either is missing: raise a descriptive configuration error
        repo = HostedPostgresRepository(url, key)
    else:
        raise unknown-backend error
    repo.initialize()
    cache and return repo

RESET_REPOSITORY():
    close the cached instance (swallowing close errors) and clear the cache
```

The instance is a **process-wide singleton**. `RESET_REPOSITORY` must be called after any backend switch or credential change, or the process keeps serving the old connection. Missing this call is the single most common cause of "I switched backends and nothing changed".

If the client library for the remote backend is not installed, raise an import error whose message names the package and the install command. Do not fall back silently to local storage — the user asked for the cloud, and a silent fallback writes their data to the wrong place.

### 6.6.3 Local backend implementation notes

- **One connection per thread**, held in thread-local storage. Never share a connection across threads.
- Enable **write-ahead logging** (concurrent readers alongside one writer) and **foreign-key enforcement** on every connection — foreign keys are off by default in most embedded engines and cascade deletes silently do nothing without it.
- Set a **connection busy timeout of 10 seconds** so a concurrent writer waits rather than failing instantly.
- `delete_task` must delete descendants explicitly via a recursive query *in addition to* relying on the cascade, because the parent self-reference cascade is not universally honored across engine versions.
- Ancestor lookup is a recursive CTE, one query.

---

## 6.7 The second backend: what genuinely differs, and the batch-fetch discipline

Build the second backend only if you actually need the shared-board story: two people, on different machines and possibly different operating systems, working one board.

### 6.7.1 The differences that matter

| Concern | Local embedded | Hosted Postgres |
|---|---|---|
| Latency per call | Sub-millisecond | **50–150 ms per call.** This dominates every design decision. |
| Concurrency model | Thread-local connections, WAL | Stateless HTTPS per call |
| Ancestors | Recursive CTE, one query | Stored procedure call |
| Analytics SQL | Direct execution | Stored procedure; raises "not implemented" if absent |
| Cascade delete | FK cascade + explicit recursive delete | **Manual**: breadth-first collect all descendant ids, delete link rows per id, then delete tasks child-first |
| Bulk delete | `DELETE FROM <table>` | The REST gateway refuses an unfiltered delete; use a match-all filter such as "id not equal to an impossible sentinel" (and the key column for the preferences table) |
| Depth | Per-row parent walk | **Computed once in memory** from the flat list |
| Auth | Filesystem permissions | Service-role secret key that bypasses row-level security |
| Security posture | N/A | RLS enabled, zero policies → public key can do nothing |
| Schema provisioning | Migration runner | Management-API call with a personal access token, plus a copy-pasteable SQL bundle |

### 6.7.2 The batch-fetch discipline — the rule that makes it usable

> **Never call a per-row repository method inside a loop.** Fetch everything once, compute in memory.

This is not a micro-optimization. Computing task depth by walking the parent chain one query at a time cost **60–80 extra HTTP round-trips for roughly 30 tasks** — several seconds of wall-clock latency on a board that renders instantly locally.

Concrete requirements for the board endpoint:

1. Fetch columns (1 call) and all tasks for the project (1 call). Nothing else per task.
2. Compute depth in memory from the flat list.
3. Compute recursive child counts and completion counts in memory from a parent→children index built from the same flat list, with memoization.
4. Fetch session counts for **all** task ids in one batched call, then aggregate recursively in memory.
5. Merge tags into the same board response so the client does not need a second request.
6. Cache the "columns have been ensured for this project" check in memory, keyed by project id, with an explicit invalidation function called after any column mutation. After the first request this costs zero calls.
7. On a task move, emit only the specific "task moved" event, not a general "task updated" event as well — the latter triggers a second full board refresh on the client.

### 6.7.3 Provisioning and the not-ready state

`initialize()` must smoke-test the remote schema by selecting one row from `schema_version`. On failure raise a **distinguished exception type** (a subclass of connection error) meaning "connected, but the tables do not exist yet", so the UI can show the setup SQL rather than a generic failure. A generic error here sends users into credential debugging when their credentials are fine.

Provision through the provider's management API using a personal access token, parsing the project reference out of the project URL, with explicit handling for HTTP 401 ("invalid access token, generate one at …") versus other 4xx/5xx (surface the response body, truncated). Also expose the full setup SQL as a string so a user without a management token can paste it into the provider's SQL editor.

---

## 6.8 Backend-to-backend migration

This is a **separate mechanism** from schema migration. Conflating the two is a classic error; name them differently in your codebase (`SchemaMigrator` vs `BackendTransfer`).

### 6.8.1 Export shape

A portable dictionary with six keys, ordered for referential integrity:

```
{
  "preferences":   [ {key, value, updated_at}, … ],
  "board_columns": [ {id, project_id, name, status_key, position, color,
                      sort_mode, sort_direction}, … ],
  "tasks":         [ {id, project_id, parent_id, title, description,
                      verification_url, status, position, owner,
                      created_at, updated_at, depth}, … ],   # depth informational
  "task_sessions": [ {task_id, session_id, created_at, session_type}, … ],
  "task_tags":     [ {id, task_id, tag, created_at}, … ],
  "status_history":[ {id, task_id, old_status, new_status, changed_by,
                      changed_at, session_id}, … ]
}
```

`tasks` **must be exported in topological order** — roots first, then each generation — via a recursive query that carries a depth counter and orders by `(depth ASC, position ASC)`. Import replays in that order so every `parent_id` resolves.

### 6.8.2 Import and the switch algorithm

```
IMPORT(target, data):
    preferences  → set_preference(key, value)
    board_columns→ create_column(dict)
    tasks        → create_task_from_dict(dict)   # preserves original ids, insert-or-ignore
    task_sessions→ link_session(task_id, session_id)
    task_tags    → add_tag(task_id, tag)
    status_history→ add_status_history(task_id, old, new, changed_by, changed_at, session_id)

SWITCH(current, target):
    data  = EXPORT(current); n = total record count
    target.initialize()                # creates schema if needed
    target.clear_all_data()            # clean slate, no stale rows
    IMPORT(target, data)
    verify = EXPORT(target); m = total record count
    if m != n: raise MigrationError("exported n, found m; source untouched")
    return success
    # THE SOURCE BACKEND IS NEVER DELETED — it remains as a live backup
```

Only after `SWITCH` returns success does the caller flip the configured backend, persist any credentials, reset the repository singleton, and invalidate the ensure-columns cache. Order matters: flipping config before verification strands the user on an empty backend.

### 6.8.3 Two flavors, and the preflight

Expose the operation with a `copy_data` flag:

- `copy_data = true` — the destructive export/wipe/import above. For pushing a local board to a fresh cloud project, or pulling a cloud board down.
- `copy_data = false` — verify the target is reachable and initialized, then flip the pointer. Both sides keep their data. This is the correct flavor when **joining** an existing shared board.

Provide a **preflight** endpoint that runs the export against both sides and returns, for each: `tasks`, `columns`, `preferences`, `total_records`, `is_empty`, and (for the remote) `reachable`. The UI branches on these so users never see a "this will replace your cloud data" warning when the cloud is empty — and, more importantly, never *miss* that warning when it is not. If the remote reports "schema not ready", the preflight must return that state distinctly so the caller can route to setup.

### 6.8.4 Verification is too weak — strengthen it

Comparing total record counts catches "half the rows didn't land". It does not catch "rows landed with wrong values", "timestamps were re-defaulted to now", or "the parent pointers were dropped". **Verify per-table counts and a content hash** (sort each table's rows by primary key, serialize canonically, hash). It costs one extra pass over data you already have in memory.

---

## 6.9 The full-text search index

### 6.9.1 Purpose and stance

Once a session scrolls out of the sidebar, the decisions, fixes and errors inside it become unfindable. A derived index over transcripts answers three questions:

1. "Where did we decide X?" — full-text search with relevance ranking.
2. "Which session touched file Y?" — a touched-file lookup table.
3. "Which sessions hit this error?" — because tool output is indexed too.

**The index is derived state and must be treated as disposable.** On any database error, or any schema-version mismatch, delete the file (and its write-ahead sidecars) and rebuild from transcripts. The transcripts are the source of truth.

Store it at `<agent-home>/gui_search_index.db`. Track schema with the engine's built-in user-version pragma, currently `1`. Resolve the path **lazily, through a function call**, never as a module constant — see §6.17.2.

### 6.9.2 Schema

`indexed_files` — incremental-indexing bookkeeping:

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `project` | TEXT | Encoded project directory name. |
| `session_id` | TEXT | Transcript filename stem. |
| `mtime` | REAL | Modification time at last index. |
| `size` | INTEGER | Byte size at last index. |

Primary key `(project, session_id)`. The `(mtime, size)` pair is the change signature.

`session_files` — the touched-file lookup:

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `project` | TEXT | |
| `session_id` | TEXT | |
| `file_path` | TEXT | Path exactly as recorded in the tool input. |
| `norm_path` | TEXT | Lowercased, forward-slashed form used for matching. |

Primary key `(project, session_id, norm_path)`.

"Touched" means **edited**, matching the daemon's tracked-file semantics: only file-writing tools count (`Edit`, `Write`, `MultiEdit`, `NotebookEdit`). Read-only access is deliberately not "touched" — otherwise every session that grepped the repository claims to have touched every file.

`messages` — a full-text virtual table:

| Column | Indexed? | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `content` | yes | Message or tool-output text. |
| `project` | no | Filter/display only. |
| `session_id` | no | |
| `role` | no | `user` or `assistant`. |
| `ts` | no | Original timestamp string. |
| `msg_idx` | no | Message index within the session, for deep-linking. |

Use a Unicode-aware tokenizer and relevance ranking.

### 6.9.3 Load-bearing behaviors

- **Cap indexed tool output at 4000 characters per block.** Build logs and test runs are megabytes; errors appear overwhelmingly at the head. Without the cap the index is dominated by noise and grows without bound.
- **Index incrementally.** Compare each transcript's `(mtime, size)` against `indexed_files`; re-parse only changed files; delete rows for transcripts that no longer exist. Delete-then-insert per changed session, inside one transaction.
- **Debounce per project** with a TTL of ~20 seconds, so search-as-you-type does not re-stat the whole project directory on every keystroke. Accept that results may lag disk reality by that long.
- **Index only in the web process, inside a search request.** Never in the session daemon, never on a per-turn path.
- **Filter deleted, utility and remapped sessions at query time, not index time.** Tombstoning a session does not change its transcript's mtime, so an index-time filter would keep serving a session the user just deleted. This is subtle and it is the kind of thing that reads as a performance mistake in review; annotate it.
- **Serialize writes with a lock; do not lock reads.** Write-ahead logging lets searches proceed during indexing.
- **Build the match expression defensively.** Convert raw user input into a safe query by quoting each whitespace-separated token as a phrase (doubling any embedded quote characters per the engine's string rules) and AND-joining them, with a trailing wildcard on the final token for prefix search. Raw input must never be parseable as query syntax.
- **Mark snippet hits with private delimiters**, not HTML. The client HTML-escapes the snippet *first* and only then converts the delimiters to markup — otherwise transcript content injects markup into your UI.

---

## 6.10 Transcript persistence: format, reading, and pagination

### 6.10.1 The format you must consume

One JSON object per line at `<agent-home>/projects/<encoded-working-dir>/<session-id>.jsonl`.

| `type` | Meaning and salient fields |
|---|---|
| `user`, `assistant` | Conversation turns. Carry `uuid`, `parentUuid`, `timestamp`, `isSidechain`, and `message.content`, which is **either a string or a list of blocks**. Assistant turns also carry `message.stop_reason`, `message.stop_sequence`, `message.id`. |
| `custom-title` | User-set title in `customTitle`. Last occurrence wins. |
| `ai-title` | Agent-generated title, written eagerly at session start. |
| `file-history-snapshot` | Rewind checkpoint: `messageId`, `snapshot.trackedFileBackups` (map of file path → `{backupFileName, …}`), `isSnapshotUpdate`, and an inner `snapshot.messageId`. |
| others | `progress`, `system`, `mode`, `last-prompt`, `summary` — ignore. |

Content block types inside a list: `text`, `thinking`, `redacted_thinking`, `tool_use` (with `name` and `input`), `tool_result` (whose `content` is itself either a string or a list of sub-blocks), and `image` (with `source.type = "base64"`, `source.media_type`, `source.data`).

**Two structural facts that will bite you:**

1. **Lines and API messages are not 1:1.** Consecutive lines sharing a `message.id` are grouped into one message when replayed. Any rewrite that adds or removes lines can therefore change the message structure.
2. **A `file-history-snapshot` appears *after* the message it describes.** Single-pass association always yields zero results.

### 6.10.2 The storage abstraction

Front all of this with an abstract interface so that no other module parses transcript internals. Required operations:

| Operation | Contract |
|---|---|
| `find_session_path(session_id, cwd)` | Locate the file. Returns nothing if absent. |
| `read_tracked_files(session_id, cwd)` | Returns `(tracked_files, file_versions, last_user_uuid, last_assistant_uuid)`. |
| `read_tail_uuids(session_id, cwd)` | Returns `(last_user_uuid, last_assistant_uuid)` from the tail only. |
| `write_snapshot(session_id, snapshot, cwd)` | Append one snapshot record. |
| `repair_incomplete_turn(session_id, cwd)` | Heal the transcript for replay. Returns whether anything changed. |
| `prepare_for_resume(session_id, cwd, evict_media, keep_recent_turns, dedup_recent)` | Combined repair + size management. Concrete, defaulting to plain repair, so a backend that does not support eviction still works. |
| `load_summary(session_id, cwd)` | Lightweight metadata for the session list. |
| `read_entries(session_id, since, cwd)` | Display entries from index `since` onward. |

**All parameters are strings** (session id, working directory), never filesystem path objects, so a future database-backed or API-backed store satisfies the same interface without leaking the file model.

### 6.10.3 Locating a transcript

```
FIND(session_id, cwd):
    if cwd given:
        p = <agent-home>/projects/ENCODE(cwd)/<session_id>.jsonl
        if p exists: return p                       # fast path
    for each directory d under <agent-home>/projects:
        skip d if its name begins with the sub-agent prefix
        if d/<session_id>.jsonl exists: return it   # fallback scan
    return nothing
```

Every caller must tolerate "nothing".

### 6.10.4 Reading, and the tolerant-parse rule

> Open text as UTF-8 with **replacement** error handling. Parse **per line** inside a try/except and skip failures. Wrap the whole read so a missing, locked, or corrupt file returns a documented empty value, never an exception.

Replacement decoding is not optional: transcripts can contain binary fragments or truncated multi-byte sequences if the writing process was killed mid-write.

Three readers share one parser:

**Summary** (sidebar). Full-file scan collecting: the last `custom-title`, the first and last message timestamps, the first user message's text, and a message count. Produces `id`, `custom_title`, `user_named`, `display_title`, `date`, `last_activity`, `last_activity_ts`, `effective_ts`, `sort_ts`, `file_bytes`, `size` (human-readable), `preview` (first 120 characters, ellipsized), `message_count`. On any failure return a fully-formed error-shaped dict with zeroed numerics — never a partial dict, or every consumer needs a null check.

**Full session** (chat render). Same scan, but flattens content blocks: text blocks joined with spaces; `tool_use` blocks collapsed to a bracketed list of tool names when there is no text; `tool_result` content pulled out of either its string or list form. Empty and thinking-only messages are dropped. Each emitted message carries `role`, `content`, `ts`, and an optional `type` of `tool` or `tool_result`. A user message containing only tool results is system plumbing and must be typed as such so the UI can style or hide it.

**Timeline** (fork/rewind picker). Adds `index`, `line_number`, `uuid`, `preview` (140 chars), and a `changes` object with `added`, `removed`, and up to five `files`. Line deltas are estimated from edit tool inputs: for an edit, count newlines in the old and new strings and take the positive difference each way; for a whole-file write, count newlines in the content as additions. Filter out user tool-result messages and system-generated user messages (those beginning with an angle bracket, or with known continuation/summary preambles).

**Tail read.** To obtain the most recent user and assistant `uuid`s, seek to `max(0, size − 65536)` and parse only that window. Transcripts reach tens of megabytes; a full scan per turn is not affordable. 64 KiB reliably contains several complete lines even with large tool results.

### 6.10.5 The snapshot association rules

1. Collect **all** snapshot records first, indexing each by both the outer `messageId` **and** the inner `snapshot.messageId` (they differ on update records). Then post-pass the message list marking `has_snapshot`.
2. A snapshot counts **only if at least one `trackedFileBackups` entry has a non-null `backupFileName`.** A null means the file was not actually backed up; offering "rewind" on it produces a failure at restore time, which is much worse than not offering it.

A fallback exists in the reference implementation that, when no explicit snapshot is found but edits occurred, looks for a backup directory whose modification time is within 60 seconds of the transcript's. **Do not copy this.** It is a heuristic that will mis-associate backups across concurrent sessions. If you need the fallback, record your own authoritative mapping when you write the backup.

### 6.10.6 Pagination

Pagination is **index-based, not byte-offset-based**: `read_entries(session_id, since=N)` parses and slices from message index N. This is O(file) per page, which is honest but not good.

If you are building fresh: maintain a sidecar index of `(message_index → byte_offset)` updated on append, and seek. The reference implementation does not, and large-session paging is correspondingly slow.

### 6.10.7 Appending

Two paths append to the foreign file: snapshot records, and `custom-title` records on rename. For titles, de-duplicate by scanning backwards through the last 8 KiB so repeated renames do not accumulate records.

Both are plain, unlocked appends. Single-line appends are effectively atomic on both major platforms, so this is *usually* safe — but see §6.13.4. It is the sharpest edge in the whole design.

---

## 6.11 Transcript rewriting: the resume-safety passes

### 6.11.1 Why rewriting is necessary at all

Resuming a session replays its transcript to the model API. Two classes of on-disk corruption make the API reject the **entire** request, which the user experiences as "the session is dead and I don't know why". Both must be healed before resume.

**Governing constraints, non-negotiable:**

- Run these passes **only on the resume/reconnect path**, never on the per-turn send path.
- **Gate on change**: if nothing needs fixing, do not rewrite. An unnecessary rewrite invalidates the provider's prompt cache and costs the user money and latency on the next turn.
- **Validate before persisting**: re-parse every produced line as JSON; if any line fails, abandon the write entirely and leave the original file untouched.
- **Write atomically**: temp file in the same directory, then atomic replace.

### 6.11.2 Pass 1 — complete an interrupted trailing turn

**Symptom:** the daemon is killed mid-response; the last conversational record is an assistant message with `stop_reason` null; resume immediately closes the stream with no useful error.

```
scan backwards from the last line:
    skip blank lines
    if the line does not parse: stop (do not risk mis-repairing)
    if type == "file-history-snapshot": continue   # snapshots can trail a real turn
    if type == "assistant" and message.stop_reason is null:
        set stop_reason = "end_turn", stop_sequence = null
        drop every block whose type is in {thinking, redacted_thinking, tool_use}
        append a short text block: "[session interrupted — resuming from last checkpoint]"
        mark changed
    stop after the first conversational line either way
```

Why those three block types must be dropped:

- An interrupted turn's `thinking` is partial and unsigned, and you are about to modify the message by appending the notice. The API forbids modifying thinking blocks of the latest assistant message.
- A `tool_use` block never produced its matching `tool_result`. A dangling tool use triggers a hard "tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks" rejection.

The appended text block is not cosmetic: an assistant message with an empty content list is a shape the CLI never emits, and the API rejects it.

### 6.11.3 Pass 2 — strip unreplayable thinking blocks

**Symptom:** on heavily-resumed sessions, resume fails with "thinking or redacted_thinking blocks in the latest assistant message cannot be modified. These blocks must remain as they were in the original response."

**Root cause:** the Agent CLI persists thinking blocks with their cryptographic `signature` intact but the `thinking` text field **emptied** on disk. The signature no longer matches the (now empty) text, and replay is rejected.

A block is unreplayable when it is a `thinking` block with blank text, or a `redacted_thinking` block with blank `data`. Intact blocks (non-empty text plus signature) are replayable and must be left untouched.

```
parse all lines; build uuid → parentUuid map
classify: for each assistant entry with a content list
    if EVERY block is unreplayable → mark its uuid for removal
rebuild:
    for each entry:
        if its uuid is marked for removal → drop the line
        if its parentUuid points at a removed uuid → relink by walking up
            the parent chain past removed entries to the nearest survivor
        if it is an assistant entry with SOME unreplayable blocks →
            rewrite with those blocks filtered out
```

> **This pass must scan the whole file, not the tail.** Verified on a real transcript of roughly 491,000 lines: the empty-thinking blocks span the entire back half of the file, not just the recent turns. A tail-only optimization here produces a "fix" that appears to work in testing and fails in production on exactly the large sessions that need it.

Deleting an entry rather than writing an empty content list is deliberate: it keeps the healed file within the set of shapes the CLI itself produces. Cap the parent-chain walk (100,000 hops is ample) so a corrupt cyclic chain cannot hang the process.

### 6.11.4 Combining the passes

Repair and size management (§6.12) must run in **one read and at most one conditional rewrite**. Structure it as: read lines → repair in memory → cheap eviction pre-scan → evict in memory if warranted → if nothing changed, return without writing → validate → atomic replace.

Eviction failure must never block resume: catch it, log it, and fall back to the still-valid repaired lines.

> **Inconsistency to avoid:** in the reference implementation the combined path writes atomically but the standalone repair path still does a plain truncate-and-rewrite. Make **every** transcript rewrite atomic. There is no reason for two policies.

---

## 6.12 Size management: lossless media eviction

### 6.12.1 The problem

Sessions that involve screenshots accumulate megabytes of inline base64 image data. Every resume re-feeds all of it: stale full-resolution images the model already looked at many turns ago, plus a much larger file for the CLI to read and parse. The cost is paid on every single turn of a long session.

### 6.12.2 The design

**Externalize old image bytes to content-addressed files and replace them in the replayed transcript with a short text placeholder.** This is lossless: every byte is preserved on disk and recoverable by hash. What changes is only what gets re-fed to the model.

Storage location: `<agent-home>/session-env/<session-id>/<app>-media/<sha256>.<ext>`.

- The per-session directory is created by the foreign tool; use a **subdirectory with your own prefix** so you can never collide with anything it owns.
- It lives under the user's home, outside any repository tree, so it can never be committed.
- The filename is the SHA-256 of the **decoded** bytes, so writing the same content twice is a no-op and de-duplication across the session is automatic.
- Derive the extension from the declared media type (`image/jpeg`→`jpg`, `image/png`→`png`, `image/gif`→`gif`, `image/webp`→`webp`, `image/bmp`→`bmp`, `image/svg+xml`→`svg`, `image/tiff`→`tiff`), otherwise take the subtype up to any `;` or `+`, otherwise `bin`. The hash is the real key; the extension is a convenience.
- Write the media file atomically (temp + replace) so a concurrent reader never sees a half-written image.

### 6.12.3 The recency floor

Recent images must stay inline. An active screenshot→fix→screenshot loop is exactly the case where the model needs to see the picture.

```
RECENT_FLOOR(lines, K):
    if K <= 0: return len(lines)              # keep nothing recent
    seen = 0
    for idx from last line down to 0:
        parse; skip non-"user" entries
        skip entries flagged as sidechain / sub-agent
        content is a genuine human turn if it is a string,
            or a list containing at least one non-tool_result block
        if not a human turn: continue          # tool plumbing, not a turn
        seen += 1
        if seen >= K: return idx               # this turn starts the recent window
    return 0                                   # fewer than K turns → everything recent
```

Anything at index ≥ floor is recent and untouched. Anything before it is evictable.

### 6.12.4 The pass

```
PREPARE_FOR_RESUME(session, evict=true, K=4, dedup_recent=true):
    lines = read all
    lines, changed, removed = REPAIR(lines)                # §6.11
    if evict and SCAN_HAS_EVICTABLE(lines, K, dedup_recent):
        try:
            lines, ev_changed = EVICT(lines, session, K, dedup_recent)
            changed = changed or ev_changed
        except: log and continue with the repaired lines
    if not changed: return false                            # no rewrite, no cache bust
    validate every line re-parses as JSON
    atomic replace
    return true

EVICT(lines, session, K, dedup_recent):
    floor = RECENT_FLOOR(lines, K)
    for idx, line in lines:
        obj = parse (pass through unchanged on failure)
        is_old = idx < floor
        if is_old:
            for each block in message.content:
                if block is a tool_result: evict inline images in its sub-list, in place
                elif block is an inline base64 image: replace it in place by index
        if obj has a non-externalized toolUseResult.file.base64 and (dedup_recent or is_old):
            externalize it and replace with a marker
        re-serialize only if this entry changed
```

The placeholder that replaces an image is a text block naming the relative path, the media type, the approximate original size in KB, and an instruction that the model can ask to re-read the source file if it needs to see it again. Keep the enclosing `tool_result`'s `tool_use_id` and every sibling block verbatim.

The auxiliary duplicate is worth handling separately: transcripts carry a byte-identical copy of image data in a `toolUseResult.file.base64` field that is CLI metadata and is **never replayed to the model**. Externalize it to the same content-addressed file and replace it with a marker object `{externalized: true, sha256, relpath, media_type}`. Because it is never replayed, de-duplicating it is safe even for recent images — hence the separate `dedup_recent` switch.

### 6.12.5 Invariants that make this safe

1. **No line is ever added or removed** — only mutated in place. This preserves `message.id` grouping, `tool_use`↔`tool_result` pairing, and the `uuid`/`parentUuid` chain *by construction*, rather than by careful reasoning.
2. **Per-image failure isolation.** An undecodable image stays inline and the pass continues.
3. **Idempotence.** A re-run finds only placeholders and markers, so the change gate returns false and nothing is written.
4. **A cheap pre-scan runs before any rewrite** — return as soon as one evictable image outside the floor (or one de-duplicable auxiliary copy) is found; if none, skip the whole rewrite.
5. **Config-gated.** A master switch disables the whole feature (reverting to pure repair), plus independent knobs for K (default 4) and auxiliary de-duplication.

---

## 6.13 Depending on another tool's private on-disk state

### 6.13.1 Inventory — know exactly what you touch

| Path under `<agent-home>` | What it is | How you use it | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| `projects/<encoded-cwd>/<sid>.jsonl` | The conversation | read, append, full rewrite, copy (fork), delete (orphan sweep) | **Highest** — concurrent foreign writer |
| `projects/<encoded-cwd>/` | Project directory | list, create, and (project-delete feature) recursive delete | Destructive |
| `file-history/<sid>/<backupFileName>` | The CLI's pre-edit file backups | read to restore files during rewind; also written by your own snapshot machinery | Shared write surface |
| `sessions/<pid>.json` | The CLI's PID→`{sessionId, cwd}` map | read-only, to map live processes to sessions | Undocumented, unversioned |
| `settings.json` | The CLI's settings | read; **whole-document replace** on save | Silent key loss |
| The CLI's global memory/instructions file | User's long-lived notes | read; **whole-document overwrite** on save | Data loss |
| `agents/`, `skills/`, `plugins/` | Extension catalogs | read-only scans; installs clone into `skills/<id>/` and uninstalls delete it | Very high (see §6.13.5) |
| `session-env/<sid>/` | CLI-created per-session directory | you add one prefixed subdirectory | Low, by design |

Never touch: the CLI's credential store, its global JSON config, its telemetry directory, its editor-integration directory, or its scratch/todo state. Enumerate the "never touch" list explicitly in your own documentation, because the temptation to reach into one of them for a shortcut arrives eventually.

### 6.13.2 The defensive-read pattern (encode this as a rule)

Every read of foreign state must:

- Open text as UTF-8 with replacement error handling.
- Parse per line inside try/except and continue on failure.
- Return a documented empty value on missing/locked/corrupt files.
- Use `.get()` with defaults for every field, and type-check before indexing — content may be a string *or* a list, a value may be a dict *or* a scalar.
- Prefer a bounded tail read to a full scan on any hot path.
- Never trust a "found" result without corroboration. Example: an entry in the CLI's PID registry is trusted only if the corresponding transcript actually exists in the recorded working directory; otherwise the PID goes on an orphan list instead of being treated as a live session.

### 6.13.3 Session identity is not stable — plan for remap on day one

The Agent SDK reassigns a session's identifier mid-flight: a client-generated temporary id becomes a server-assigned one. This ripples through **every** store:

- The temporary-id transcript remains on disk and would render as a duplicate "sleeping" session.
- The board's link table points at the old id.
- The user's chosen display name is filed under the old id.

Required machinery:

1. A per-project remap record `{old_id: {new_id, timestamp}}` so listings hide the stale file.
2. A repository `remap_session(old, new)` operation.
3. A name-store move that returns the moved title (or nothing).
4. A resolver that maps an old id to its canonical new id for any inbound request that still carries the old one.

Decide early whether identity is stable in *your* system. If it is, you skip all of this. If it is not, retrofitting it is expensive and every miss is a user-visible duplicate.

### 6.13.4 The risks, stated plainly

1. **No API contract.** Filenames, record types and field names can change in any release of the foreign tool. There is no version marker to check. Consider writing a probe that asserts your structural assumptions at startup and logs loudly when one fails.
2. **Concurrent writer, no lock.** Appends are line-atomic in practice; **full rewrites are not safe** against a concurrent append. This is why rewrites are confined to resume boundaries, when the session is not being written.
3. **You delete their files.** Startup sweeps unlink transcripts that look like orphan stubs, based purely on content heuristics (§6.14.3).
4. **Whole-document replacement of their configuration** discards any key your UI did not round-trip. Either merge, or do not expose the file for editing.
5. **Encoding coupling.** The directory-name encoding is reverse-engineered; a change breaks project detection *silently*.

### 6.13.5 The highest-risk surface: extension installs

Installing an extension by cloning a repository into a directory owned by another tool, and then running a setup command supplied by that repository, is remote code execution — even on localhost, even behind a loopback-only bind. If you build this, require an explicit user confirmation naming the source, disallow setup-command execution by default, and validate the destination path against the extension directory root before any recursive delete.

## 6.14 Complete on-disk layout, lifetimes, and cleanup

### 6.14.1 Home-directory state (authoritative)

```
<agent-home>/
├── projects/                                   [foreign-owned dir; you add sidecars]
│   ├── _project_names.json                     {encoded_project: display label}
│   └── <encoded-working-dir>/
│       ├── <session-id>.jsonl                  transcripts (foreign-owned)
│       ├── _session_names.json                 {session_id: user-set title}
│       ├── _session_names.json.backup-<UTC>    written before any maintenance scrub
│       ├── _deleted_sessions.json              tombstones {session_id: epoch}
│       ├── _utility_sessions.json              {session_id: epoch} hidden system sessions
│       ├── _remapped_sessions.json             {old_id: {new_id, ts}}
│       ├── _session_access.json                {session_id: epoch} last UI interaction
│       └── _trash/
│           ├── _trash_index.json               {sid: {deleted_at, name, protected_until?}}
│           └── <session-id>.jsonl              soft-deleted transcripts
├── _system/                                    working dir for internal utility sessions
├── file-history/<session-id>/                  pre-edit file backups (rewind)
├── session-env/<session-id>/<app>-media/       <sha256>.<ext> externalized image bytes
├── <app>-state/<parent-session-id>/inbox.json  inter-session report inbox
│                                               (+ inbox.json.broken-<epoch> quarantine)
├── sessions/<pid>.json                         foreign PID→session registry (read-only)
├── gui_kanban.db          (+ -wal, -shm)       the board database
├── gui_search_index.db    (+ -wal, -shm)       derived full-text index (disposable)
├── gui_active_sessions.json                    crash-recovery session registry
├── gui_message_queues.json                     persisted per-session message FIFOs
├── gui_permission_policy.json                  {policy, custom_rules}
├── gui_ui_prefs.json                           UI prefs incl. session_retention_days
├── gui_folder_tree[_<project>].json            sidebar folder tree, per project
├── gui_daemon.pid  /  gui_daemon_<port>.pid    daemon singleton lock
└── <foreign-owned files: settings, memory file, agents/, skills/, plugins/>

<home>/.<app>/
└── restore-points/<tag>-<ISO8601>/             operator snapshots + MANIFEST.json
```

**Sidecar naming rule:** every per-project bookkeeping file begins with `_`, and every session listing must skip files whose stem begins with `_`. Without this the bookkeeping files themselves appear as sessions named after their own filenames.

### 6.14.2 Repository-tree state (caches, logs, documents — all ignored by version control)

```
<repo-root>/
├── kanban_config.json          application config + remote credentials   [IGNORED]
├── confirmed_models.json       {model_id: display_name}                  [IGNORED]
├── backups/backup_<YYYY-MM-DD>_<HH-MM-SS>.json     manual board exports
├── compose-projects/<project>/ composed documents (layout below)
├── data/
│   ├── chrome-profile/         isolated browser profile for app-window launch mode
│   ├── previews/               <32-hex>.png and <32-hex>.thumb.jpg
│   ├── <assistant>-profile/    persistent browser-automation login context (lazy)
│   └── <assistant>-debug/      <tag>-<timestamp>.png / .html failure dumps (lazy)
├── logs/                       server, daemon, web, supervisor, browser-open logs
├── .cache/
│   ├── update_state.json       {last_check, cli_version, updated_last_check,
│   │                            daemon_restart_pending}
│   ├── speech-models/          speech model cache
│   └── speech-venv/            isolated virtual environment for the speech engine
├── docs/plans/                 working documents and specifications        [IGNORED]
└── tests/screenshots/          end-to-end failure artifacts (lazy)         [IGNORED]
```

Composed-document layout — one directory per project, deliberately **not** a table, because the artifacts are files the user may open in other tools:

```
compose-projects/<sanitized-name>[-<id-prefix> on collision]/
├── project.json          {id, name, created_at, root_session_id,
│                          shared_prompts_enabled, parent_project, position, pinned}
├── compose-context.json  {version, project_id, project_name, sections[], facts{},
│                          directives[], conflicts[], export_config{format, template,
│                          styles}, status{total_sections, complete, in_progress,
│                          drafting, reviewing}}
├── brief.md
├── sections/<sanitized-section-name>[-<id-prefix>]/
│   ├── section.json      {id, project_id, parent_id, name, status, order,
│   │                      artifact_type, session_id, changing, change_note,
│   │                      changing_set_by, summary, updated_at, ready_for_review, tags}
│   └── content/          working files
└── export/               final export output
```

Project lookup is a linear scan of `compose-projects/*/project.json` matching on id, with a name-sanitized path fallback. A background watcher polls each `compose-context.json` modification time on a 4-second interval and pushes changes over the realtime channel; a file caught mid-write is skipped and retried next cycle. Writes go through a per-project in-process lock plus temp-file-and-replace.

> **Correct design first:** pick **one** source of truth for section data. The reference implementation persists sections *both* as `section.json` files *and* inside `compose-context.json`, and every read consults only the latter. The per-section files are written and then never read — a divergence waiting to happen, and a trap for anyone who edits one by hand expecting it to matter.

Add a guard test asserting that the literal directory and filenames (`compose-projects`, `compose-context.json`) never change, because users have these directories on disk and a rename orphans them silently.

### 6.14.3 Lifetimes and cleanup

| State | Lifetime / collection policy |
|---|---|
| Transcripts | Permanent unless deleted by the user |
| Trash (`_trash/`) | Retention-bounded; pruned opportunistically on the next trash operation |
| Tombstones | 2 hours (7200 s) — **but only expire if the backing transcript is actually gone** |
| Utility-session marks | 24 hours (86400 s), lazily pruned on write |
| Remap records | 24 hours, or while the old transcript still exists |
| Session-access records | 90 days (7,776,000 s), or while the transcript exists |
| Internal utility transcripts | Deleted at startup when older than 24 hours |
| Title-only orphan transcripts | Swept at startup across all projects |
| Crash-recovery registry entries | Eligible for recovery only within 1 hour (3600 s) of last activity |
| Externalized media | Per session, **never pruned** |
| Search index | Disposable; deleted wholesale on corruption or version mismatch |
| Logs, preview images, automation debug dumps | **Never pruned — unbounded** |

**Both startup sweeps run at startup only, never from a per-request path.** This is a performance guardrail: the orphan sweep walks every project directory, and one product regression put an equivalent scan on the session-listing path.

The **title-only orphan sweep** deserves detail, because it deletes foreign files. The CLI eagerly writes a title record when a session starts. If the conversation never lands under that filename — the user closes the tab before typing, the CLI dies mid-write and recreates a file just after a delete, or the SDK remaps the session id — the result is a stub that renders in the sidebar as a bare-identifier empty chat. Classification rules, all of which are conservative on purpose:

- Skip any file larger than 100 KB without scanning (the largest observed real stub was 73 KB, because snapshot machinery can attach dozens of records before the first turn; real sessions with even one turn exceed the cap).
- Read all lines; **if any line fails to parse, return false** — you cannot be sure what it contains.
- Allow only title records and snapshot records. Any user, assistant, summary or tool record means it is a real session.
- **Require a title record to be present.** A snapshot-only file is left alone. This targets exactly one known leak; it is not a generic "delete anything without messages" sweeper.
- Skip the internal utility project (it has its own age-based sweep) and any directory whose name starts with the sub-agent prefix or an underscore.

**Fix the unbounded categories.** Logs, previews and debug dumps had grown to hundreds of megabytes on a real user machine. Give each an explicit retention policy from the start; retrofitting deletion into a directory a user has been accumulating for a year is a conversation nobody wants to have.
