# Part 9 — Compose (Multi-Agent Authoring) and the Agent Library

This chapter specifies two features that ship together but are architecturally independent, and can be built by two teams in parallel.

**Compose** is a multi-agent long-form authoring mode: a way to run N AI agents against one document without the document falling apart. **The Agent Library** (internally called *Workforce*) is a directory of reusable prompt-template agents — review, build, debug, audit specialists — that any session can load and delegate to. The only coupling between them is one persona agent in the library that is used to UX-review Compose changes.

Everything here is behavioral specification. Where an algorithm matters, it is written out step by step. Where a lesson was paid for in production breakage, the failure mode is stated alongside the rule.

---

## 9.1 The problem: N agents, one document

An LLM agent has one context window and one conversation. A long-form deliverable — a 40-page proposal, an annual report, a research paper, a pitch deck, a technical spec — exceeds what a single agent can hold coherently. Worse, such documents are *naturally parallel*: five sections could plausibly be drafted at the same time by five agents.

Naive parallelism produces incoherence, and it does so in three specific ways that you should hold in your head for the rest of this chapter:

1. **Fact divergence.** Section 3 invents a company name, a fiscal year end, or a product tier that section 1 already fixed. Nobody notices until assembly.
2. **Instruction leakage and instruction starvation.** A user looking at section 2 types "make the tone formal." Only section 2 changes. The document now has two voices. The inverse is equally bad: an instruction meant for one section is applied everywhere.
3. **Silent contradiction over time.** "Make it conversational" was said in week one. "Keep everything formal for the board" is said in week three. Both are still active. Neither is wrong. They cannot both be followed, and no human remembers the first one.

Compose exists to solve exactly this. The vocabulary, defined once, used throughout:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Composition** | One long-form deliverable. The unit of coherence. Owns a folder on disk. |
| **Section** | One independently-authored piece of the composition. Nestable. Owns a folder and an agent. |
| **Root orchestrator** | Exactly one agent per composition. Sees the whole tree, never one section's body. Owns structure, coherence, assembly, and conflict mediation. |
| **Section agent** | Exactly one agent per section (at most). Owns that section's content and nothing else. |
| **Directive** | A durable instruction. Scoped `global`, to one section, or to `root`. Carries a monotonic generation number. |
| **Fact** | A cross-cutting truth in a flat key/value store, visible to every agent. |
| **Conflict** | Two active directives that address the same topic with different instructions. |
| **Changing flag** | A per-section coordination primitive meaning "a mutation to this section is in flight; its current content is not the final word." |

**The product bet, stated plainly: Compose is not a document editor with AI assistance. It is an orchestration surface.** The artifact lives on disk as files written by agents. The UI never edits content — it edits *structure, status, and instructions*. That separation is what makes the whole thing buildable by a small team, and it is the first thing to defend when someone proposes adding a rich-text editor.

**Who it is for.** Users of an agent-session manager who already live in a multi-session workflow — dozens of concurrent sessions, a kanban board, a sidebar they glance at constantly. Compose is one top-level view mode among several. Crucially, the same product also serves **non-technical operators**: people who click a one-click "publish/update" button without reviewing a diff. That constrains everything downstream. No jargon in conflict resolution. No affordance that requires an explanation. No recoverable-only-by-a-developer state. The in-repo UX persona states the bar: *users do not read documentation; they expect to figure things out by clicking; if something needs explanation, it is probably designed wrong.*

**The end-to-end experience**, so you know what you are building toward:

1. The user enters the Compose view. A tab strip offers **Ad-hoc** (a live parent→child tree of lightweight subsessions spawned from any running session) and **Structured** (Compose proper). Ad-hoc is the default; Structured becomes visible once the current host project has at least one composition on disk, with a "+ New structured composition" affordance as the discovery entry point.
2. They create a composition from a name and optionally one of a handful of built-in templates (Business Proposal, Annual Report, Product Launch, Research Paper, Pitch Deck, Meeting Notes). **Creating a composition immediately auto-starts the root orchestrator session**, with the composition folder as its working directory.
3. They populate sections three ways: apply a template; describe the deliverable in prose and let an AI planner propose a nested section tree with per-section briefs; or add sections manually with an artifact-type picker (~48 types across 8 categories — report, financial-model, pitch-deck, flowchart, and so on).
4. "Launch All" starts one agent session per section that lacks one, seeds each with an initial prompt derived from its brief, then sends a coordination message to the root orchestrator summarizing the whole tree. Once every section has a session, the same button relabels to "Re-orchestrate."
5. Sections render as cards on a three-column status board (Drafting / Reviewing / Complete). Drilling into a card gives a two-pane detail view: metadata and output preview on the left, the section's live session on the right.
6. "Direct All" opens a textarea. The instruction is recorded as a global directive and handed to the root orchestrator, which distributes it with per-section context and flags affected sections. Contradictions surface as resolution cards.
7. Export to DOCX, PDF, a Markdown bundle, or a ZIP archive.

---

## 9.2 Data model and on-disk layout (and why files rather than a database)

### 9.2.1 Entities

**Composition**

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | UUID string | generated | Stable identity |
| `name` | string | required | Display name; seeds the folder name |
| `created_at` | ISO-8601 UTC | generated | |
| `root_session_id` | string \| null | null | The orchestrator's session id |
| `shared_prompts_enabled` | bool | **true** | Composition-level policy toggle (§9.6) |
| `parent_project` | string \| null | active host project | The host project this composition belongs to — the scoping key for everything |
| `position` | int | 0 | Sidebar sort order; gap-numbered as `index * 1000` on reorder |
| `pinned` | bool | false | Show in the sidebar even when its `parent_project` is not active |

**Section**

| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | UUID string | generated | |
| `project_id` | string | required | Owning composition |
| `parent_id` | string \| null | null | Nesting. **A flat list plus this pointer — never nested arrays** |
| `name` | string | required | Seeds the folder name |
| `status` | enum | `drafting` | `drafting` \| `reviewing` \| `complete` |
| `order` | int | append | Sort key |
| `artifact_type` | string \| null | null | One of ~48 keys |
| `session_id` | string \| null | null | The section agent's session |
| `changing` | bool | false | Mutation-in-flight flag (§9.8) |
| `change_note` | string \| null | null | Why it is changing |
| `changing_set_by` | string \| null | null | Who set it (`root` or a section id) — the authority token |
| `summary` | string \| null | null | Agent-written self-description. **The section's entire public surface** |
| `updated_at` | ISO-8601 \| null | null | Stamped on every context update |
| `ready_for_review` | bool | false | Agent-set; the UI renders it and never sets it |
| `tags` | string[] | [] | Free-form, lowercased |

Deserialization must be forgiving: legacy status values (`not_started`, `working`) migrate to `drafting` on read rather than raising.

**Directive**: `id`, `gen` (monotonic integer, assigned as `max(existing) + 1` at append time inside the lock — this is the recency signal), `scope` (`"global"` | a section id | `"root"`), `content`, `source` (`"user"` | `"root"` | a section id), `status` (`active` | `superseded`), `created_at`.

**Fact**: conceptually `key`, `value`, `source_section`, `discovered_at`. In the shipped implementation facts persist as a plain `{key: value}` map, which loses provenance. **A rebuild should persist the richer form** (§9.6.3).

**Conflict**: `id`, `project_id`, `directive_a_id`, `directive_b_id` (A = older, B = newer), `directive_a_content` and `directive_b_content` as **denormalized copies** so a conflict card renders without a join, `status` (`pending` | `resolved`), `recommendation` (human-readable explanation plus options, generated at detection time), `resolution`, `resolution_action` (`supersede` | `scope` | `keep_both`), `resolved_at`.

### 9.2.2 Relationships

```
host project (a path/name string)
  └─ 1:N  Composition                        [parent_project]
            ├─ 1:1  root orchestrator session [root_session_id]
            ├─ 1:N  Section  (tree via parent_id)
            │         └─ 0:1  section agent session [session_id]
            ├─ 1:N  Directive  (scope → global | section id | root)
            ├─ 1:N  Conflict   (→ two directives)
            └─ 1:N  Fact       (key/value map)
```

### 9.2.3 On-disk layout

```
compose-projects/                       (gitignored; storage root must be configurable)
  <sanitized-name>[-<id[:8]>]/
    project.json                        serialized composition
    compose-context.json                THE single source of truth for live state
    brief.md                            project brief, seeded with "# {name}"
    sections/
      <sanitized-section-name>[-<id[:8]>]/
        section.json                    serialized section (a cache/backup)
        brief.md                        written when a planner supplies a brief
        content/                        the agent's actual output files
    export/                             reserved for export output
```

Folder-name sanitization: lowercase, spaces → hyphens, strip anything that is not alphanumeric / hyphen / underscore, fall back to `unnamed`. On collision, append the first 8 characters of the UUID.

`compose-context.json` shape:

```
{ version: 1,
  project_id, project_name,
  sections:   [ <full section objects> ],
  facts:      { key: value },
  directives: [ <directive objects> ],
  conflicts:  [ <conflict objects> ],
  export_config: { format, template, styles },
  status: { total_sections, complete, in_progress, drafting, reviewing } }
```

`status` is **derived**, recomputed on every section mutation (`in_progress = drafting + reviewing`). Never trust it as input; always recompute.

### 9.2.4 Why files, not a database

This is the load-bearing architectural decision. Understand it before changing it.

1. **The agents are the primary writers.** Section agents are LLM sessions with filesystem tools whose working directory *is* the composition folder. A JSON file they can read and rewrite is a native interface. A database requires an API layer, a schema they must be taught, and a tool round-trip per operation. The root orchestrator's system prompt literally instructs it to read `compose-context.json` before every action — that instruction is only cheap because the file is right there.
2. **The context file doubles as shared agent memory.** Facts, directives, sibling statuses, conflicts — one file every agent can read. That is what makes coordination cheap enough to do on every turn.
3. **Output is files anyway.** Export is a filesystem walk. A database would hold metadata while the payload lived on disk regardless — two storage systems for one artifact.
4. **Human inspectability and portability.** A composition is a directory you can zip, copy, diff, or hand to someone.

The costs, and how you pay them:

- **Atomicity** — every write is temp-file plus atomic replace, using a rename primitive that *overwrites* (required for Windows), guarded by a per-composition in-process mutex keyed by composition id. Provide a read-and-lock helper returning `(context, lock)` for genuine read-modify-write cycles, and release the lock if the read fails.
- **Torn reads** — the file watcher tolerates JSON parse failures by recording the new mtime and skipping that cycle. A file caught mid-write is expected, not exceptional.
- **Lookup cost** — resolving `composition_id → directory` scans `compose-projects/*/project.json`. Fine at tens of compositions; keep an index if you expect hundreds.
- **Orphan recovery** — the lister repairs directories that have a `compose-context.json` but no `project.json` by reconstructing and persisting one, so a partially-written composition self-heals on the next scan.
- **Redundancy** — `section.json` inside each section folder duplicates the entry in `compose-context.json`. **The context file wins**; all reads go through it. Either drop the per-section copy or make the redundancy explicit and one-directional.

---

## 9.3 Orchestrator and section agents: who talks to whom

### 9.3.1 The two roles

**Root orchestrator** — one per composition, sees the whole composition and never one section's body. Four responsibilities, stated numerically in its system prompt:

1. **Structure.** Add, remove, reorder, merge, split sections. *Section agents never modify the tree.* Creating a section means scaffolding its folder, adding it to the context file, and writing an initial brief for the section agent.
2. **Coherence.** When sections contradict or drift, diagnose the gap. Fix *factual* errors in the context file directly. For *content* changes, set `changing: true` on the target section with a `change_note`, then send a specific directive to that section. **Never set `changing: false` on another agent's section.**
3. **Assembly and export.** Read all section source files, assemble in hierarchy order, apply export config, run the pipeline, deliver the file.
4. **Architectural intent.** When the tree changes structurally, or when a structural decision proves load-bearing for strategy, propose an update to an intent ledger and **present it to the user for approval before writing**. Never silently update it.

Two cross-cutting rules complete the role:

- **Conflict mediation** — present *both* directives with a recommendation and reasoning; never silently pick an interpretation; let the user resolve in one click or one sentence; after resolution, update the context file and signal affected sections via the changing flag.
- **Routing** — *if the user sends you a message that is clearly about a specific section, route the directive to that section. Interpret intent from content, not just from which card was selected.* This is an explicit acknowledgement that the UI's target selection is a hint, not a guarantee.

**Section agent** — one per section, owns exactly one section's content. Rules: do not modify other sections or the composition structure; if you receive a changing flag with a note, address it and clear the flag when done; if you discover facts that contradict other sections, *report* them and let root handle cross-section coherence.

### 9.3.2 The messaging topology

```
          user
        ↙      ↘
   root orchestrator  ←──(facts, reports)──  section agents
        │
        └──(directives + changing flags via compose-context.json)──→ section agents
```

- Root↔section is **not** a message channel. It is mediated entirely by the shared context file plus the changing flag. There is no direct agent-to-agent messaging primitive, and you should not add one.
- Sections never message each other. Coherence questions escalate to root.
- The only true message sends are user→root (Direct All, and the coordination message from Launch All) and user→any-agent (open that agent's session and type).

This is deliberate hub-and-spoke. **A rebuild that adds section↔section messaging reintroduces exactly the incoherence Compose exists to prevent**, because lateral instructions bypass the one component that has whole-document visibility.

### 9.3.3 The role token

A single opaque string encodes both role and addressing:

- `root:{composition_id}`
- `section:{composition_id}:{section_id}`

Parse by splitting on `:` with a maximum of two splits, so section ids containing colons survive. Unknown role prefixes and missing components raise.

This token is the *entire* contract between frontend and backend for agent identity. It travels on the session-start payload as `compose_task_id`. The server uses it to (a) build the correct system prompt and (b) link the resulting session id back to `composition.root_session_id` or `section.session_id`.

**Session-start performance shape (copy this).** Compose prompt resolution and cross-session-awareness injection are two independent operations that both mutate the system prompt. Run them **in parallel on a module-level thread pool of 2 workers with a 10-second timeout each**; when only one is needed, run it inline without touching the pool. Sequential execution costs up to 200 ms per compose session. The pool must be module-level — creating one per request costs more than it saves. Apply results in a fixed order: compose prompt first, awareness second. Perform the session-linking write **after** emitting the "session started" acknowledgement so the client never blocks on it.

Two further rules at this boundary:

- Sessions started from the Compose view **skip** the generic agent-catalog injection (§9.13); compose prompts are built entirely server-side.
- **A prompt-build failure must never block session creation.** The builder returns `{ok: true, system_prompt, agent_role}` or `{ok: false, error}`; every call site treats failure as non-fatal, starts the session anyway, and logs a warning. A user with a degraded prompt can still work; a user with no session cannot.

---

## 9.4 Input targeting, and why sending a message to the wrong agent is the worst possible UX failure

The **input target** is the answer to "when I type in the composer, who receives it?" In Compose that is either the root orchestrator or one specific section agent.

The in-repo UX standard states the stakes outright: *input target switching (root vs. section) must be obvious; sending a message to the wrong agent is the worst UX failure in Compose.* That is not hyperbole, and the reasoning generalizes to any multi-agent surface:

- **It is silent.** The wrong agent accepts the instruction and does something plausible. No error, no bounce, no undo.
- **It corrupts shared state.** A directive meant for section 2 delivered to root becomes a global directive that touches every section. The inverse — a global instruction delivered to one section — produces exactly the drift Compose exists to prevent, and it will not be noticed until export.
- **It is expensive to reverse.** Agent work is minutes of wall clock and real token spend. Unwinding means new directives, new changing flags, and a coherence pass.
- **It destroys trust in the mode.** Once a user believes "I do not know who I am talking to," they abandon orchestration and go back to one session — which means the entire feature was wasted.

**How the shipped implementation works, and where it is weak.** The target is a *consequence of navigation*, not a first-class control. Board view ⇒ root. Drilling into a section card ⇒ that section. Breadcrumb back or Escape ⇒ root. A thin bar shows "Talking to: {name}" plus a "Shared" badge when shared prompts are on.

Four weaknesses a rebuild must design out:

1. **The indicator is hidden exactly when it matters.** While the target points at a section (drill-down), the "Talking to:" bar is set to `display: none`. The default target is advertised; the non-default one is not.
2. **The target only affects starting a *new* session.** Once a session exists and is open, messages go to that session id directly and the target has no further influence. This is defensible as an implementation, but the user's mental model is "I am talking to X" while the system's model is "the next session I create will be bound to X." Unreconciled models produce misroutes.
3. **Stale tokens.** Deleting the section you are drilled into clears the selection but does not always recompute the token; the bar can render the literal string `unknown section` while still holding a dead section id.
4. **No session-death handling.** Nothing watches session state for section sessions. A dead section session keeps its `session_id`, so bulk launch skips it, and the only recovery is a manual unlink.

**Required rebuild rules:**

- Make the target an **explicit, always-visible, independently-settable control** — a persistent selector, not a navigation side effect. Navigation may *change* it; navigation must not be the only way to change it.
- **Validate the token against live state immediately before every send.** Resolve the composition and, if applicable, the section. If either is missing, refuse the send and say so in plain language. Never send on an unresolvable target.
- **Mirror the target in the composer chrome** — border color, placeholder text ("Message the Market Analysis agent…"), and the label — so the target is impossible to miss even in peripheral vision.
- **Recompute the target on every state change**, especially delete. A dead token that still renders a label is a live misroute waiting to happen.
- Derive the label and the token from **one** function, so they can never disagree.

---

## 9.5 Prompt assembly: the full algorithm

One function takes a role token and returns a system prompt plus the resolved role. Both prompt shapes follow the same macro-structure: **stable content first, volatile content last**, because prompt-prefix caching only pays off when the prefix does not move.

### 9.5.1 Root orchestrator prompt

Assemble in exactly this order:

1. **Identity line** naming the composition.
2. **Framing** — "You see the full composition, not one section. Users talk to you about the whole project: structure, coherence, conflicts, and export."
3. **Standing instruction** — before *every* action, read `compose-context.json` to understand all section statuses and summaries, all facts, all pending conflicts, all active changing flags.
4. **The four responsibilities** from §9.3.1, verbatim and numbered.
5. **Conflict resolution protocol.**
6. **Routing rule.**
7. **Post-update obligations** — update composition-level status; add cross-section facts and decisions; log conflict resolutions as new directives with explicit scope.
8. **`## Current State` — the live snapshot**, in this fixed internal order:
   - **Sections (N total)** — one line per section: `- [status] name [CHANGING] -- summary`. The `[CHANGING]` marker and the `-- summary` suffix are conditional. Empty → `(no sections yet)`.
   - **Facts** — `- key: value` per entry. Empty → `(no facts recorded)`.
   - **Pending Conflicts** — only `status == "pending"`, rendered `- CONFLICT [<id[:8]>]: "A" vs "B"`. Empty → `(no pending conflicts)`.
   - **Active Directives** — only `status == "active"`, rendered `- [gen N] (scope) content`. Empty → `(no active directives)`.

**Why this order.** Role and rules first because they are stable and cacheable. Live state last because it changes every turn. Within the state block the ordering is decreasing structural scope and increasing specificity: the tree, then the shared truths, then the things blocking progress, then the standing instructions. Every empty case gets an explicit parenthetical rather than being omitted, so the model never has to disambiguate "absent" from "none" — a small, real hallucination guard.

### 9.5.2 Section agent prompt

1. **Identity** — "You are a Compose section agent working on {section} within the project {composition}."
2. **Scope framing** — responsible for ONE section; root manages overall structure; you manage your section's content.
3. **`## Your Section`** — name, status, artifact type (defaulting to `text`).
4. **`## Your Responsibilities`** — write and refine content; follow root directives; report facts that might affect other sections; update your own status and summary as you progress.
5. **`## Rules`** — do not modify other sections or the structure; if you receive a changing flag with a note, address it and clear the flag when done; if you discover contradicting facts, report them.
6. **`## Project Context`**, built in this exact order:
   - **Sibling awareness** — "Other sections in this composition:" then `- [status] name` for every section except self. If none: `(this is the only section)`.
   - **Parent awareness** — if `parent_id` resolves: "You are a SUBSECTION of "{parent}" [{status}]. Coordinate with your parent section and stay within its scope."
   - **Child awareness** — if children exist: "You have N subsection(s) that handle parts of your content:" then `- [status] name -- summary` per child, closed with "Coordinate with these subsections. **Do not duplicate their work.**"
   - **Facts** — "Known facts:" then `- key: value`.
7. **`## Section Directives`** — active directives whose scope is *this section id* **or** `"global"`, labeled `- [gen N] (global|this section) content`. Empty → `(no directives)`.

**Why this order and this content:**

- **Siblings by name and status only, never content.** This is the central context-economy decision. A section agent needs to know "Market Analysis exists and is complete" so it does not re-derive market sizing; it does not need the 4,000 words. Names plus statuses cost O(sections) tokens instead of O(document).
- **Parent/child before facts.** Hierarchy determines scope, and scope determines what the agent should even attempt. Getting scope right first prevents the most expensive failure — writing content that belongs to a sibling.
- **"Do not duplicate their work" is stated explicitly** because duplication is the single most likely parallel-agent failure. State the anti-goal; do not assume it is implied.
- **Facts before directives.** Facts are what is true; directives are what to do. Truth then instruction.
- **Directive filtering is a union, not a hierarchy.** A section sees its own directives plus globals, and never another section's. This is the isolation guarantee that stops a per-section instruction from leaking laterally.
- **Generation numbers are shown.** The agent can order instructions by recency without parsing timestamps, which is what makes "the later one supersedes" legible to a model.

### 9.5.3 Two implementation details worth copying

- Build the section prompt from **one** read of the context file, locating the section inside the already-parsed structure, rather than calling a lookup helper that reads the file again. At three to four context reads per session start, this is measurable.
- Emit the empty-state parentheticals unconditionally. Never let a section header vanish because its list was empty.

---

## 9.6 Shared context and context-window management

### 9.6.1 The mutation surface

All context mutations go through a small API, and every one of them takes the per-composition lock, reads, mutates, **recomputes derived status**, and atomically writes:

- add / update / remove / reorder sections
- merge facts (shallow dict update: new keys win, existing keys are overwritten, nothing is deleted)
- update section status / summary / changing / change_note as a **partial** update, where `None` means "leave this field alone" so a caller can set exactly one field
- append directive (assigning `gen = max(existing) + 1` **inside** the lock)
- set / clear changing
- add / update conflict

Locks are per-composition mutexes in a module-level map guarded by a meta-lock.

### 9.6.2 How context propagates without blowing up context windows

The economy is achieved by **projection, not summarization**. Seven mechanisms:

1. **Root gets breadth; sections get names.** Root's snapshot is the whole tree plus all facts, conflicts, and directives — but each section contributes exactly one line. A section's snapshot is its siblings' names and statuses only.
2. **Agents write their own summaries.** Each section maintains a one-line `summary`. That line is the section's entire public surface to every other agent, so cross-section awareness costs O(number of sections), independent of document length.
3. **Facts are a flat key/value store, not prose.** "Company name is X", "fiscal year ends March 31." This is the mechanism that prevents section 3 from inventing a name section 1 already fixed, and it costs a handful of tokens.
4. **Directives are filtered by scope at prompt-build time.** The full directive log — which grows without bound — never reaches a section agent.
5. **Superseded directives are filtered out.** Only active directives enter any prompt, so conflict resolution actively *shrinks* prompt size. Nice incentive alignment: cleaning up is rewarded.
6. **Conflicts go to root only.** Sections never see the conflict list; mediation is not their job.
7. **Content never crosses.** No agent ever receives another section's body text. If a section needs a sibling's content it reads the file itself — it has filesystem access and the composition folder as its working directory. A deliberate **pull** model rather than push.

### 9.6.3 The shared-prompts toggle, and a general rule about policy scope

`shared_prompts_enabled` is a boolean **on the composition**, default true, exposed as a single toggle in a gear popover next to the composition name, with a "Shared" badge on the target bar as the ambient indicator. Semantics: when on, user prompts are logged and shared across all section agents.

Per-prompt and per-session toggles were designed, offered, and **explicitly rejected by users as "annoying."** The reasoning is worth internalizing:

- A **per-prompt** toggle taxes every message with a decision the user cannot make well in the moment — they do not yet know whether this instruction will turn out to be global. It converts a background policy into foreground friction on the highest-frequency action in the product.
- A **per-session** toggle multiplies state by the number of sections and creates an invisible matrix. Eight sections means eight independent booleans, no single place that shows them, and no way to reason about "why did section 5 not get that."
- A **composition-level** toggle is one boolean with one visible indicator, set once, when the user decides what kind of document this is.

Generalized: **scope a consistency policy to the unit that consistency is defined over.** A per-item override on a consistency policy is self-defeating.

### 9.6.4 Gaps you must close

The shipped implementation has no pruning. Directives, facts, and conflicts accumulate forever, and all of them flow into the root prompt, which therefore grows monotonically over the life of a composition. Build these from day one:

- **Fact supersession with provenance.** A fact set twice keeps the latest value *and* records who set it and when. Overwriting silently loses the prior value and its source.
- **Directive compaction** after N resolutions, and **conflict archival** after resolution.
- **Explicit budgets with visible truncation.** Cap sections, facts, and directives entering a prompt, and when you truncate, say so in the prompt ("showing 40 of 120 sections") rather than overflowing silently.

---

## 9.7 Directive conflict detection and resolution

### 9.7.1 What a conflict is

Two **active** directives that address the same topic but give different instructions. "Make the tone conversational" from week one versus "keep everything formal for the board" from week three. Neither is wrong; they cannot both be followed; nobody remembers the first.

### 9.7.2 Detection algorithm

Detection runs **synchronously whenever a new directive is appended**. The shipped algorithm is intentionally crude and intentionally biased toward recall:

1. Load all directives; keep the active ones; skip self-comparison.
2. For each existing active directive, test topical overlap against the new one:
   - Tokenize both to lowercase word sets.
   - Subtract a stop list of roughly 50 words (articles, auxiliaries, common prepositions, plus `all`, `use`, `just`, `only`).
   - If either side is empty after subtraction → no conflict.
   - Compute `|A ∩ B| / min(|A|, |B|)`. If that ratio **exceeds 0.30**, treat them as addressing the same topic.
3. Every topical match becomes a conflict record with a generated recommendation. **Nothing is auto-resolved.**

Two keyword lists exist in the code and are **deliberately unused in classification**: "global signal" phrases (`actually`, `across the board`, `everywhere`, `all sections`, `globally`, `override`, `always`, `never`, `for everything`, `in all cases`) and "contextual signal" phrases (`for this section`, `just here`, `only in`, `only for`, `in this part`, `this chapter`, `this section only`, `just this`, `locally`). An earlier version used them to auto-classify and auto-resolve. **That was removed on purpose**, and the removal is the most transferable lesson in this chapter:

> **The system detects; the user decides.** A heuristic good enough to *flag* is not good enough to silently pick a winner, because picking wrong on a directive is invisible until the document is finished.

Keep the lists for generating better *recommendations*. Do not let them decide.

Consequences you must accept or improve:

- Recall is high, precision is low. `min()` in the denominator means a short directive sharing two meaningful words with a long one trips the threshold.
- Detection is O(active directives) per new directive, so total work grows quadratically with log length.
- It is **purely lexical**. "Use British spelling" and "use American spelling" share almost no words and will **not** be detected. That is the failure mode that matters most, and it is the one to target with embeddings or an LLM classifier.

### 9.7.3 Surfacing

Four surfaces, all fed from one conflict list:

1. **Header pill** — warning triangle with a count, non-interactive.
2. **Board banner** — prepended above the columns: "⚠ N directive conflict(s) need your attention" plus a Review button.
3. **Resolution modal** — one card per conflict showing Directive A and Directive B with relative timestamps, the recommendation, and the action buttons.
4. **Inline chat cards** — pushed into the live session log via a socket event, supporting one-click resolution *and* free-form natural-language resolution whose intent is mapped by regex: "keep both / both … valid / intentionally different / intentional" → `keep_both`; "scope / separate / each section / their own" → `scope`; everything else → `supersede`. Resolved cards swap their action row for a badge ("Superseded" / "Scoped separately" / "Kept both").

Additionally, the sidebar row for a composition shows a distinct status dot when any conflict is pending, and that dot **takes precedence over every other status state** — a conflicted composition is visible without opening it.

**Unify the action vocabulary across surfaces.** In the shipped version the modal offers `supersede` and `keep_both` while the chat surface also offers `scope`. Two vocabularies for one decision is a bug.

### 9.7.4 Resolution semantics

Server-side, under the composition lock:

- **`supersede`** — mark directive A as `superseded`. If A had a non-global scope, collect that section id as *affected*.
- **`scope`** — split the two directives into disjoint scopes. **In the shipped version this is a no-op and must be finished.** Specify it as: prompt for the scope assignment, rewrite each directive's scope accordingly, keep both active.
- **`keep_both`** — no-op on the directives.

Then, for every action: mark the conflict resolved with the action, a timestamp, and a note recording the user's choice; and **append a new synthetic directive** (id `resolution-{conflict_id[:8]}`, global scope, source `root`, content "Conflict resolved ({action}): {directive_b_content}"). Writing the resolution back as a directive is the mechanism by which the decision becomes durable and visible in every agent's next prompt.

Finally — **outside the context lock** — set `changing: true` on every affected section with the note "Directive conflict resolved ({action}). Review your content." This must be outside the lock because the changing-flag call re-acquires the same lock; doing it inside deadlocks. **Never lock twice.**

---

## 9.8 The change watcher and the "in flux" signal

### 9.8.1 The changing flag

`changing: true` on a section means **"a mutation to this section is in flight; its current content is not the final word."** It is a coordination primitive, not a status: a section can be `complete` *and* `changing` at the same time. Three fields carry it: `changing`, `change_note` (why), `changing_set_by` (who — `"root"` or a section id).

**The authority protocol is the whole point:**

- **Anyone with a reason can set it.** Root sets it on any section when issuing a content-affecting directive; conflict resolution sets it on affected sections.
- **Only the section itself can clear it.** The clear operation validates the clearing party against `changing_set_by`; a mismatch raises, and the HTTP layer returns **403**.
- The root's system prompt reinforces the same rule in prose.

Why the asymmetry matters: it makes "work is outstanding" a claim only the worker can retract. Without it, the orchestrator can mark a section clean while its agent is mid-edit, and the coherence guarantee evaporates. **Close the hole in the shipped guard**: if `changing_set_by` is empty (a legacy record), anyone can clear. Treat an empty setter as "owner only."

The flag is **read-only in the UI**. No control anywhere sets or clears it — only agents do. The UX standard classifies it as ambient: *users should not have to think about it, but they should see that something is in flux.*

### 9.8.2 The watcher

A single background daemon thread, started once at application startup, polling every **4.0 seconds**:

1. Iterate every directory under the compose storage root.
2. For each with a `compose-context.json`, stat it for mtime.
3. Compare against a remembered mtime map keyed by absolute path.
4. On change, read and parse. **On parse or OS error, record the new mtime and skip this cycle** — a file caught mid-write is normal, and the next poll will catch it.
5. On successful parse, emit within an application context:
   - `compose_context_updated` with `{composition_id, context}` — the entire context object.
   - `compose_changing` with `{composition_id, section_id, changing: true, change_note}` for **every** currently flagged section.
6. Record the mtime regardless of outcome.

Design notes and traps:

- **First sighting never emits.** A path absent from the mtime map is recorded silently, so a freshly created composition does not fire on first observation. Preserve this.
- **`compose_changing` re-fires every poll while any flag is set.** It is a *level* signal, not an edge. Clients must be idempotent; dedupe or document it.
- **The watcher is the only path that sees direct agent writes.** When an agent edits the context file with a file tool, no API route fires. Removing the watcher silently breaks live progress display for the entire parallel-agent workflow — which is the feature.
- **Polling, not a filesystem-notification library.** Deliberate: no external dependency, and 4 s is well inside human tolerance for a background progress indicator.
- Broadcast is global rather than room-scoped. Fine at single-user scale; scope by composition when you have concurrent users.

### 9.8.3 Surfacing

A changing dot next to the card title, tooltipped with the change note (falling back to "Change in progress"); a "● changing" marker in the drill-down metadata row in the warning color; and a real-time handler that patches the affected section in local state and re-renders only the affected surface.

---

## 9.9 Export and assembly

### 9.9.1 Formats

| Format | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `markdown` | `text/markdown; charset=utf-8` | Single concatenated document |
| `zip` | `application/zip` | Per-section folders plus a generated `master.md` at the archive root |
| `docx` | Word MIME | Requires a DOCX library; 404 with an installation hint when absent |
| `pdf` | `application/pdf` | DOCX→PDF conversion; **400 with "Try DOCX format instead"** when no converter is available |

The download filename derives from the composition name: spaces → hyphens, lowercased, truncated to 40 characters, plus extension, delivered as an attachment.

### 9.9.2 Assembly order — and the fix you must make

The shipped exporter sorts sections by `(order, name)` — a stable composite, because the insert-at-top path can produce duplicate `order` values by using `min(order) - 1`. But **it is a flat sort, not a tree walk**: a subsection is placed by its own `order`, not adjacent to its parent. Markdown export compensates by emitting `#` for root sections and `##` for anything with a parent, but ordering can still interleave, and grandchildren render at the same level as children.

**Specify a depth-first traversal of the tree with depth-aware heading levels.** This is one of the few places where the shipped behavior is simply wrong rather than a deliberate tradeoff.

Per section, the walker reads `sections/{folder}/content/*.md` in sorted filename order. In Markdown export a section with no content directory or no `.md` files is skipped entirely — no heading is emitted.

### 9.9.3 Per-format post-processing

**Markdown** — heading per section by depth, each file's stripped content, a blank-line separator, parts joined by double newlines. A fully empty composition yields the literal `# (No content yet)`.

**ZIP** — deflate-compressed; each file stored at `{section-folder}/{filename}`, flat, with no nesting reconstruction, so two sections whose names sanitize identically collide (fix by using the stored folder path). The combined document is added as `master.md`. Return nothing if zero files were added.

**DOCX** — the elaborate path, and worth matching because it is what makes exports feel like a product rather than a dump:

- 1-inch margins; default body style at 11 pt with 1.15 line spacing.
- **Title page**: centered composition name at 28 pt bold in near-black, centered formatted date at 12 pt gray, then a page break.
- **Per section**: Heading 1 with the section name; the section `summary`, if any, as italic 10 pt gray intro text; then content; then a page break after every section **except the last**.
- **Markdown→DOCX conversion** is line-oriented: fenced code blocks collected until the closing fence and rendered as a single monospace 9 pt gray run with tight spacing; `####`/`###`/`##` mapped to heading levels 4/3/2; `-` and `*` to a bullet list style; `N.` to a numbered list style; blank lines skipped; everything else a normal paragraph.
- **Inline formatting** is a single regex alternation over bold, italic, and inline code, emitting one run per matched span and plain runs for the gaps.
- **Page numbers** in a centered footer, built from raw field-code elements, wrapped so that failure degrades to no page numbers rather than no document.
- Empty sections and empty compositions get an italic gray `[No content yet]` placeholder — unlike Markdown, DOCX always emits the heading.

**PDF** — generate DOCX, write to a temp file, try a direct converter, fall back to a headless office suite with a 60-second timeout, and if both fail return nothing (surfaced as HTTP 400 with actionable text). Clean up temp files in a `finally`.

### 9.9.4 Known gaps to close

- `export_config` (format, template, styles) is persisted and named in the orchestrator's responsibilities but **never read by the exporter**. Wire it or delete the field; a persisted setting that does nothing is a lie to the user.
- The `export/` directory is scaffolded and never written to — all exports stream to the browser.
- **Do not resolve content paths by re-sanitizing a mutable name.** Renaming a section orphans its content folder from export, because the folder keeps the old sanitized name. **Store the folder path on the section record.**

---

## 9.10 Complete HTTP API

All routes sit under an `/api/compose` prefix. Errors are `{ok: false, error}`; successes are `{ok: true, ...}` except where noted.

### Board

| Method | Path | Query | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | `/board` | `project_id` (optional), `project` (optional host-project filter) | **Bare object or JSON `null`** — deliberately no `ok` envelope. `{project, sections[], status{}, conflicts[], sibling_projects[]}` |

Selection logic: if `project_id` is given, load exactly that; otherwise list all, filter by `parent_project == project`, and take the most recently created. **Return `null` when nothing matches** — that null is the signal the client uses to trigger its stale-selection fallback (§9.12).

`sibling_projects` is: all compositions sharing the effective host project (each with a status summary and a `has_conflicts` boolean), plus **all pinned compositions from any other host project**, deduped by id. With no host filter, only the selected composition is returned as its own sibling.

### Composition CRUD

| Method | Path | Body | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| POST | `/projects` | `{name, parent_project?}` | 201. Scaffolds folders **and auto-starts the root orchestrator** (non-blocking; a start failure is logged, not returned). Emits `compose_board_refresh` |
| GET | `/projects` | — | `?project=` filters by host project **or pinned** |
| GET | `/projects/<pid>` | — | `{project, sections[], context{}}`; 404 when unknown |
| PUT | `/projects/<pid>` | any of `name`, `shared_prompts_enabled`, `root_session_id`, `position`, `pinned` | Emits `compose_board_refresh` |
| POST | `/projects/reorder` | `{order: [ids]}` | Assigns `position = index * 1000` |
| POST | `/projects/<pid>/clone` | `{name?}` (default "Copy of {source}") | 201 |
| DELETE | `/projects/<pid>` | — | Recursive folder removal. Emits `compose_board_refresh` with `deleted: true` |

**Clone must remap in two passes.** Assign new ids in pass one so pass two can rewrite forward-referencing `parent_id` links. Remap directive scopes and sources that reference section ids, conflict directive references, and clear every `session_id`. A clone inherits neither pinned state nor a running session.

### Section CRUD

| Method | Path | Body / Query | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| POST | `/projects/<pid>/sections` | `{name, parent_id?, artifact_type?, insert_position?}` | `insert_position: "top"` → `min(order) - 1`; else `max(order) + 1`. 201. Emits `compose_task_created` |
| PUT | `/projects/<pid>/sections/<sid>` | any of `name`, `status`, `artifact_type`, `session_id`, `parent_id`, `summary`, `ready_for_review`, `tags` | Emits `compose_task_updated`, plus `compose_task_moved` when status changed |
| DELETE | `/projects/<pid>/sections/<sid>` | `?cascade=true` | Deletes descendants deepest-first. Returns `{deleted_count, deleted_sections[]}`. Emits `compose_board_refresh` |
| GET | `/projects/<pid>/sections/<sid>/children` | — | Recursive descendants `[{id, name, status}]` plus `count`, for the cascade confirmation |
| POST | `/projects/<pid>/sections/reorder` | `{order: [ids]}` | Rewrites `order` by index; unlisted sections appended |
| GET | `/projects/<pid>/sections/<sid>/preview` | — | Reads the section's `content/`, whitelisting `.md .csv .yaml .yml .json .html .mmd .puml .txt`, **capping each file at 50 KB** |
| POST | `/projects/<pid>/sections/<sid>/launch` | — | Builds the section prompt, starts a session, links it. **409 if already linked** |
| POST | `/projects/<pid>/sections/add-and-link` | `{name, session_id, parent_id?, order?, artifact_type?}` | Atomic create-and-link. **409 if that session is already linked to another section in this composition.** On context-write failure, delete the scaffolded folder so no orphan remains |

### Orchestration

| Method | Path | Body and behavior |
|---|---|---|
| POST | `/projects/<pid>/launch-all` | `{orchestrate_only?}` — launch every unlinked section with an initial prompt derived from its summary (or a generic "begin drafting" fallback), then send the root a coordination message listing every section with type and truncated summary. Returns `{succeeded, failed, launched[], root_message}` |
| POST | `/projects/<pid>/direct-all` | `{message}` — record a global user directive, then send root a wrapped instruction telling it to review, add per-section context, ensure all agents receive it, and **set the changing flag on each section that needs to act**. 400 if no root session is running |
| POST | `/projects/<pid>/planner/accept` | `{sections: [{name, artifact_type?, brief?, subsections: [...]}], parent_id?}` — recursively create the tree, writing each brief to both `section.summary` and the section folder's `brief.md`. Returns `{created_count, sections[]}` |

### Context, directives, conflicts, flags, tags

| Method | Path | Body |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/projects/<pid>/context` | — |
| PUT | `/projects/<pid>/context/facts` | `{facts: {k: v}}` (shallow merge) |
| PUT | `/projects/<pid>/sections/<sid>/status` | `{status?, summary?, changing?, change_note?}` — partial; omitted fields untouched |
| POST | `/projects/<pid>/directives` | `{content, scope?, source?}` — append, run detection, emit `compose_directive_logged` with a conflict payload `{id, classification, existing_id, existing_text, recommendation}`. 201 |
| POST | `/projects/<pid>/directives/resolve` | `{conflict_id, action}`, action ∈ `supersede｜scope｜keep_both`. Emits `compose_directive_conflict_resolved` |
| PUT | `/projects/<pid>/sections/<sid>/changing` | `{changing: true, change_note?, set_by?}` or `{changing: false, cleared_by}`. **403 on authority violation.** Emits `compose_changing` |
| POST | `/projects/<pid>/sections/<sid>/tags` | `{tag}` (lowercased, trimmed, deduped) |
| DELETE | `/projects/<pid>/sections/<sid>/tags/<tag>` | — |

### Export

| Method | Path | Body |
|---|---|---|
| POST | `/projects/<pid>/export` | `{format}` → binary or text with `Content-Disposition`. 404 when there is no content; 400 for an unsupported format or an unavailable PDF converter |

### Socket events (server → client)

| Event | Payload | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| `compose_board_refresh` | `{project_id, deleted?}` | composition create/update/delete, section delete, section reorder, plan accept |
| `compose_task_created` | `{project_id, section}` | section create, add-and-link |
| `compose_task_updated` | `{project_id, section}` | section update, tag change, section launch |
| `compose_task_moved` | `{project_id, section_id, old_status, new_status}` | status transition |
| `compose_changing` | `{project_id, section_id, changing, change_note?}` | flag API **and** the watcher |
| `compose_directive_logged` | `{project_id, directive, conflicts[]}` | directive create, direct-all |
| `compose_directive_conflict_resolved` | `{project_id, conflict_id, action}` | resolve |
| `compose_context_updated` | `{project_id, context}` | **watcher only** |

Client → server: the standard `start_session` payload plus `compose_task_id`, and the standard `send_message`. **Pick one field name for message text across all modules** — the shipped code sends `text` from one place and `message` from another for the same event, which is a bug waiting to be discovered by whoever adds the third caller.

## 9.11 Frontend interaction specification

### 9.11.1 Static DOM skeleton

These elements must exist in the page template *before* any rendering code runs:

| Element | Role |
|---|---|
| `compose-sidebar` | Composition list, tag filters, actions, recent history. Fully rewritten each render |
| `compose-board` | The whole compose main panel. **Never clear this element's contents** (§9.12, Fix 4) |
| tab strip (`adhoc` / `structured` / `new-structured` buttons) | Mode selection |
| ad-hoc body | Ad-hoc subsession tree |
| `compose-root-header` | Root orchestrator bar. Toggled between hidden and flex |
| `compose-input-target` | The "Talking to:" bar. Toggled between hidden and flex |
| `compose-sections-board` | **The only dynamic content area** — cards, drill-down, empty states, skeletons |

Everything else (menus, popovers, overlays, toasts, the planner slideout) is created on demand and appended to the document body.

### 9.11.2 Boot algorithm

1. Load persisted per-column sort modes.
2. Capture a **monotonic init epoch**; after every `await`, abort if a newer init has started.
3. Restore the selected composition id from `activeComposition:{hostProject}` if not already set.
4. Build the board query: `?project_id=&project=` when a composition is selected (**always include the host-project filter so the sidebar stays rooted in the active host project even while viewing a cross-project pinned composition**); `?project=` alone otherwise; no query at all when there is no host project.
5. Fetch the board. Populate the sidebar from the response's `sibling_projects` — there is no separate list fetch.
6. Apply tab state. If the effective tab is Ad-hoc, or there are zero compositions, render the sidebar, attach shortcuts, and stop.
7. If the response is `null` or has no composition → **stale-selection fallback** (§9.12, Fix 2).
8. Otherwise adopt composition, sections, and pending conflicts; persist the selection; then either restore a drill-down from the URL hash, or show the header and target bar, render cards, and set the target token to `root:{id}`.

### 9.11.3 Persistence keys

| Key | Value |
|---|---|
| `activeComposition:{hostProject}` | Selected composition id, **scoped per host project** |
| `composeColumnSorts` | `{columnKey: sortMode}` |
| `compose.activeTab` | `adhoc` \| `structured` (default `adhoc`) |

Host-app keys (active project, active session, view mode) are read but not owned. No sessionStorage.

### 9.11.4 Root header bar

Left: composition name; clicking opens the root session. (If no root session exists this is currently a silent no-op — **replace that with an explicit "Start orchestrator" affordance**.)

Center: a status line — `"N sections"` plus conditional `", n complete"`, `", n reviewing"`, `", n drafting"` — over a stacked segment progress bar (zero-count segments omitted) and a `"{complete}/{total} complete"` caption. The whole wrapper is removed when there are no sections.

Right, in order: **gear** (settings popover with inline name edit saved on blur/Enter, and the Shared Prompts toggle with an explanatory hint) · **Plan with AI** · **Launch All / Re-orchestrate** (visible only when sections exist and no launch is in flight; the label depends on whether any section lacks a session) · **Direct All** · **Export** · **+ Add Section** · **conflict count pill** (only when conflicts are pending).

### 9.11.5 Board and cards

Three columns keyed `drafting` (teal), `reviewing` (amber), `complete` (green). Each column header carries a color bar, name, live count, and a sort control highlighted when the mode is not `manual`. **Only root sections appear on the board**; children are represented on their parent's card and inside the parent's drill-down.

Card contents in render order: selection checkbox · drag handle · artifact-category icon · title · **changing dot** (tooltip = change note) · **session dot** (running/idle; absent when unlinked) · overflow menu · status pill · artifact type label · relative updated-at · **"Ready for review" badge** (only when flagged and status ≠ complete) · tag pills (hash-colored, click to filter) · summary paragraph · subsection roll-up (`"{done}/{total} subsections"`, direct children only).

Per-column sort modes, persisted: `manual` (server order), `alpha-asc`, `alpha-desc`, `updated-new`, `updated-old`.

An empty board renders a hero: "What would you like to create?", a prose textarea (Ctrl/Cmd+Enter submits), a "Plan with AI" button, and two links — "Start from a template" and "Add a section manually."

### 9.11.6 Drill-down detail view

Breadcrumb (Board › [parent] › current). Left pane: clickable status badge with dropdown; click-to-edit title; artifact icon, type, and the "● changing" marker; summary or a placeholder; tags with add/remove; a collapsible **Output** preview (Markdown rendered, CSV as a table, everything else preformatted; empty → "No output yet — the agent hasn't started writing."); a "Related Sections" list derived from shared keywords; a Subsections panel with a completion bar and an inline add row. Right pane: if a session is linked, a row showing running/idle with rename, unlink, and click-to-open; if not, three chooser cards — **Spawn session**, **Link existing session**, **Plan subsections with AI**.

### 9.11.7 Lifecycle controls

| Operation | Mechanics |
|---|---|
| Create section | Modal with Top/Bottom insert toggle, name field, grouped artifact-type select. **Optimistic ghost card with spinner** in the drafting column, removed on failure |
| Rename | Card context menu, or inline edit in the drill-down (blur/Enter saves, Escape reverts) |
| Delete | Query children first. With children → cascade modal listing them and warning about irreversibility. Without → inline in-card confirm that stashes prior markup for Cancel. Optimistic removal; failure re-inits |
| Link existing session | Modal listing all sessions minus already-linked ones, each with a running/idle dot, filtered client-side |
| Unlink | Confirm, then clear `session_id`. The session itself survives |
| Set status | Drag between columns (**optimistic with revert on failure**), card menu, drill-down dropdown, bulk action |
| Ready-for-review / changing | **Read-only. Agents only.** |
| Tags | Inline input with a commit-once latch so Enter-then-blur cannot double-fire |

### 9.11.8 Sidebar

Sections in order: **Compositions** (search box shown only above three items; bulk bar when items are selected; the list; "+ New Composition"), **Tags**, **Actions**, **Recent** (last five actions with relative times).

Each row: multi-select checkbox · pen icon · name · pin dot · status badge. **Status dot precedence, first match wins: conflicts → no sections → all complete → any in progress → idle.** Badge text is `{complete}/{total}`, and a completion-fraction change pulses the badge briefly.

Right-click menu: Rename · Duplicate · Pin/Unpin · Delete. Positioned at the cursor, then clamped to the viewport on the next frame.

**Delete has a 5-second undo window.** Hide the row immediately, show a stacked undo toast, and fire the DELETE on timeout. Undo restores the selection including the persisted key. **Navigating away flushes pending deletes rather than abandoning them.**

**Drag-reorder** is delegated HTML5 drag/drop, and is **disabled entirely while the search filter is active** — the filtered DOM is a subset, and reordering it would post an incomplete order list. Cross-project pinned items are not valid drop targets and are excluded from the posted order, then re-appended locally.

### 9.11.9 AI planner

A hidden utility session (excluded from the session list) started with a system prompt that: demands JSON only; forbids refusal, explanation, and questions; gives the exact output shape `{sections: [{name, artifact_type, brief, subsections: []}]}`; enumerates every legal artifact type; requires a 1–3 sentence brief per section; and instructs the model to break content into independently-writeable units with 1–3 nesting levels. Existing sections are appended as context with "avoid duplicating them"; when planning subsections, a scope note names the parent.

A slideout streams progress: a 1-second tick counts name-key occurrences in the accumulated text and shows "Building plan… N sections so far (Ss)". On idle, parse the accumulated text with **three fallbacks in order**: a fenced JSON block → the whole text as JSON → brace-balanced extraction with string and escape awareness. Success renders a collapsible tree with an "Add N sections to Board" button; failure shows an error plus the first 2 KB of raw text. A refine textarea sends follow-ups to the same session.

### 9.11.10 Real-time behavior — and the required improvement

In the shipped version, four events (`compose_task_created`, `compose_task_updated`, `compose_task_moved`, `compose_board_refresh`) each trigger a **full board refetch and full re-render, undebounced**. Two do targeted work: `compose_changing` patches one section, and `compose_context_updated` replaces sections and conflicts wholesale from the pushed context, falling back to board view if the drilled-into section vanished.

**Do not copy the full-refetch pattern.** Under parallel agents it is a refresh storm, and every re-render destroys transient UI: open menus, inline edits, pending delete confirms. Debounce socket-driven refreshes (a few hundred milliseconds is enough) and prefer targeted patches.

### 9.11.11 Keyboard, routing, and cross-module contract

Global shortcuts, active only in the Compose view and suppressed inside form fields or when a modifier is held: `n` new · `r` refresh · `Escape` with priority order (close help → clear selection → clear focus → back to board) · `↑`/`↓` move focus through visible compositions (Shift extends selection) · `Enter` switch to focused · `Space` toggle selection · `Delete` schedule an undoable delete with focus advancing first · `?` shortcut help.

Routing uses `#compose` and `#compose/section/{id}`. **The composition id is never in the URL** — which is precisely why the stale-selection fallback matters. The back/forward handler renders detail versus board using a non-history-pushing variant so Back does not create duplicate entries.

The module exports: init, a reset that **increments the init epoch to cancel in-flight loads and flushes pending deletes**, a session-grouping function the sidebar uses to render root and section sessions under a composition header, an in-view session opener, the socket handlers, and the tab switcher.

Two frontend rules that are easy to get wrong and expensive to debug:

- **Do not use HTML escaping as JavaScript-string escaping.** Interpolating names and ids into inline handler attributes breaks on an apostrophe. Use event delegation with data attributes.
- **Shift-range selection must operate on the visible list**, not the underlying one, or it silently selects filtered-out items.
