## 9.12 Multi-project scoping: four bugs that made this feature unusable, and the rules that fixed them

Compose lives inside a host application with its own "active project." A composition belongs to exactly one host project via `parent_project`, except when pinned. Four bugs made the feature unusable across multiple host projects. All four fixes are load-bearing; reverting any one re-breaks Compose.

### Fix 1 — Filter every composition-list read by the host project

**Symptom.** Right-click a session → "Add to Composition" showed every composition from every host project, including ones the user had not opened in weeks.

**Root cause.** That one call site omitted the `?project=` query parameter, and the list endpoint returns *all* compositions when unfiltered. The endpoint was not wrong; the caller was.

**Rule.** Every composition-list read from every UI surface passes the host-project filter. Server-side, that filter is `parent_project == filter OR pinned` — pinning is the sanctioned cross-scope escape hatch, so the predicate must not be "simplified" to plain equality. Audit call sites, not just endpoints: one unfiltered fetch is enough to make the feature look broken.

### Fix 2 — A persisted pointer to a deletable entity needs a self-healing fallback

**Symptom.** The Compose view rendered completely empty even though valid compositions existed. Reloading did not help. It stayed broken forever.

**Root cause.** The selected composition id is persisted per host project. When that composition is deleted — or its folder removed out of band — the board endpoint returns `null` for that id. The boot routine treated `null` as "nothing exists" and rendered the empty state. Permanently, because the stale id was re-read from storage on every subsequent load.

**Rule.** Inside the "no data" guard, add a retry: if a saved id was in play, clear it **in memory and in storage**, refetch with **only** the host-project filter, and if that succeeds, adopt the recovered composition, persist the new selection, and render. Swallow any throw in the retry and fall through to the empty state.

Three sub-rules generalize:

- **(a)** The board endpoint must return an explicit `null` for an unknown id. Do not "helpfully" fall back server-side — the client needs the null to learn that its persisted state is stale.
- **(b)** The client must clear both the in-memory id and the persisted key before retrying, or the next load repeats the failure.
- **(c)** The retry drops the id and keeps the scope filter. Never the reverse.

Pin this with backend tests: a nonexistent id returns null; a scope-only query finds the most recent match; a scope-only query does not leak other projects' compositions; and the retry response still includes sibling data so the sidebar renders.

### Fix 3 — Never clean up test data by name pattern when the code under test generates names

**Symptom.** 52 orphan compositions leaked into real user data from the test suite.

**Root cause.** The cleanup fixture deleted directories whose names started with a `test-` prefix. But cloning produces names like `copy-of-test-clone-src-…`, and collision handling appends UUID fragments. Neither matched the prefix, so the leftovers survived every run and accumulated.

**Rule.** Snapshot the set of directory names before each test and remove anything new afterwards. Never match on a generated name. And note the deeper cause: those tests wrote to the **real** data directory. **Make the storage root configurable and point it at a temp directory per test run** — the snapshot fixture is a mitigation, not the fix.

### Fix 4 — Never clear a container whose children are contract, not content

**Symptom.** Switching host projects while in the Compose view blanked the panel permanently, even though the API returned valid data. Only a full page reload recovered it.

**Root cause.** The teardown path set the compose *container's* innerHTML to empty. That container holds three statically-defined children the boot routine looks up by id — the root header, the input-target bar, and the sections board. Destroying them made every lookup return null, and the boot routine then wrote into null **without throwing**. Silent, total, unrecoverable.

**Rule.** Clear **only** the dynamic region (the sections board), never the parent. State the structural principle explicitly in the code and in your project rules: *a container whose children other code resolves by id is a contract, not content.*

Two structural defenses, in order of preference:

1. Keep the dynamic region in its own dedicated element and clear only that. (Already true here — the bug was clearing the wrong node.)
2. Make id lookups **fail loudly**: assert on null and throw, rather than letting writes into null succeed silently. A visible crash on the first render is infinitely cheaper than a blank panel with a healthy-looking network tab.

A rebuild using a component framework gets this class of bug for free, which is the single strongest argument for using one.

---

## 9.13 The Agent Library ("Workforce"): concept and runtime loading

### 9.13.1 What it is

A directory of Markdown files, each defining a **reusable prompt-template agent** — a named body of instructions with a defined invocation contract and output format. These are *not* framework subagents with their own tool permissions. They are prompt bodies loaded into a parent session's context so the parent knows **when** to delegate and **what to write in the kickoff prompt**.

The architecture that makes the authoring rules necessary: the subagent runs in an isolated context window, returns a summary, and **that summary is the only artifact the parent ever sees.** Every rule in §9.14 exists to defend that lossy boundary.

Invocation is by natural-language phrase — the user types "build team", "plan team", "execute pipeline" — or by slash command.

### 9.13.2 Frontmatter schema

Flat YAML between `---` fences. The parser is deliberately naive: split the file on the fences into three parts, then parse one `key: value` per line using the first colon as the separator. Coercions: `[a, b, c]` → list of strings with quotes stripped; `true`/`false` → boolean; `null` or empty → null; otherwise a string with surrounding quotes stripped; skip lines beginning with `#`. **No nested YAML, no multi-line values, no block scalars.** A naive parser is a feature: agent files are hand-edited by both humans and LLMs, and a strict parser turns a stray indent into a broken catalog.

| Key | Type | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | kebab-case | yes | Falls back to the filename stem |
| `name` | string | yes | Falls back to `id`; must match the H1 |
| `department` | string | yes | Grouping label; a flat string, not a folder |
| `source` | string | yes | Provenance and tier signal; also the uninstall key for installed packs |
| `version` | semver | yes | |
| `depends_on` | list of ids | yes (may be empty) | Read by the pipeline agent to construct its workflow |
| `type` | string | yes | `prompt-template`; the special value `workforce-map` diverts the file into a hierarchy slot |

Optional and loader-supported: `tags`, `active` (default true — a de-facto enable switch), `allowed-tools`, `preamble-tier`. **Do not add `model`, `color`, or a top-level `tools:` field expecting them to be honored** — the mechanism has no such concept, which is exactly why Rule 7 (tool limits in prose) exists.

The loader returns per file: `{id, name, department, tags, active, version, allowed_tools, source, systemPrompt}`, where `systemPrompt` is the entire stripped body after the frontmatter. Response envelope `{ok, assets[], map, source}`.

**Department hierarchy lives in a separate map file** marked `type: workforce-map`, whose body is a two-level indented list of `- {id}: {label}`. The loader diverts that file out of the asset list into a dedicated map slot; the client parses indentation to build parent/child links. **Absent that file the tree silently flattens** and every asset becomes a root — which looks like data loss to the user. Detect and warn.

### 9.13.3 Runtime loading: from disk to system prompt

```
agent-library/*.md
  → GET /api/workforce/assets        (parse frontmatter; body → systemPrompt)
  → client merges the flat asset list + hierarchy map into a department tree
  → catalog cache invalidated
  → POST /api/agents/write-catalog {agents: [{id, label, systemPrompt}]}
  → server writes ONE Markdown catalog file to the OS temp dir, per host project
  → the session system prompt receives a SINGLE LINE pointing at that file path
  → the agent reads that file before spawning anything
```

**Why the indirection.** Inlining every agent prompt into the system prompt cost roughly **8,000 tokens per session** and made the process argument enormous. A one-line pointer costs nothing. The file is written atomically, cached per host project by absolute path, skipped if it already exists (unless forced), and invalidated on host-project switch and whenever disk assets reload.

The catalog file is **not** a raw dump. It opens with instructions to the model:

- how many specialists exist;
- **"These agents are defined HERE in this file — do NOT look for them on disk or in any agents directory. This is the authoritative and complete list."**;
- use the delegation tool, and **copy the agent's full system prompt into the delegation call's prompt parameter so the subprocess adopts that role**;
- when the user asks what agents are available, list them from this file and do not search the filesystem.

Then an index of `- **{label}** ({id})` lines, a separator, then the full definitions.

Without that preamble, models reliably go hunting on disk for agent definitions that do not exist there, and either report "no agents found" or invent ones. The preamble is load-bearing.

**Local project assets** fold into the same catalog: scan for any directory named `skills/` or `agents/` anywhere in the project tree up to 4 levels deep (skipping version-control, dependency, cache, virtualenv, and build directories), read `.md` files up to 2 levels inside each match, and never recurse into a matched directory looking for nested ones. Cache per project; invalidate on the newest mtime among discovered directories. Label them distinctly in the catalog.

**Compose sessions skip the catalog entirely** — their prompts are built server-side from the role token.

### 9.13.4 Invocation flow

Slash commands are intercepted client-side before anything is sent: `/invoke {id}` and `/as {id}` select an asset directly; a bare `/invoke`, `/team`, or `/departments` opens a picker modal listing Local Skills, Local Agents, and Departments (a collapsible tree; branch nodes with their own prompt get a "Use" button, leaves are directly clickable), with a search box. Store items in an index-keyed registry rather than serializing them into click handlers.

Selecting an asset sets a pending-invoke object and applies a visual treatment to the composer — a gradient plus a floating "Invoke {name}" label with an × to cancel. On submit, the pending invoke **wraps the user's message**:

```
[[invoke::{name}::path={path}]]
{full system prompt}
[[/invoke]]

{user text}
```

A short notice is prepended to the session system prompt telling the model that a library skill was invoked and that the instructions are inside the tags. When rendering the transcript, detect the block and replace it with a compact pill showing only the agent name, so the user sees "Design Review" rather than a wall of prompt text.

So: **invocation injects a prompt; it does not spawn a subagent.** The agent's body becomes an instruction block inside the user's turn. Chaining is single-slot — selecting a second asset replaces the first.

The management surface offers a Departments tree with per-node counts and inline edit/delete, an Available catalog, and a Discovery tab that scans the user's configuration directories for existing agent or skill definitions and offers one-click import (marking already-imported ids). Community "skill packs" install by cloning a repository, walking it for Markdown, and rewriting each file as a library asset with a generated id and a `source` tag; uninstall removes every asset carrying that tag plus the cloned directory.

Endpoints: `GET /api/workforce/assets`, `GET /api/workforce/discover`, `POST /api/workforce/write-asset` (id sanitized to alphanumerics, hyphen, underscore; catalog cache invalidated on write), `POST /api/workforce/delete-asset`, `POST /api/workforce/install-pack`, `POST /api/workforce/uninstall-pack`, `POST /api/workforce/uninstall-builtin`, `GET /api/invoke/discover?depth=`, `POST /api/agents/write-catalog`, plus a persisted folder-tree endpoint holding the user's arrangement.

### 9.13.5 Loader traps to design out

1. **Merging vs. replacing.** Loading disk assets currently *replaces* the entire default department tree rather than merging into it. With eleven files on disk and no map file, a rich default collapses to eleven flat roots. Merge, or make the replacement explicit and reversible.
2. **Non-agent Markdown parses as an agent.** The authoring-standard file has no frontmatter, so the loader ingests it as an asset whose id is the filename and whose prompt is the entire standard. **Require frontmatter, or maintain an explicit exclusion list.**
3. **`depends_on` accuracy decays.** Several agents declare dependencies on ids that exist only as conceptual role lanes, not as files. Decide whether the field means "files that must exist" or "lanes," and validate accordingly — a real orchestrator reads it.
4. **Two modules defining the same function names, one unloaded, is a live hazard.** A dead duplicate of the invocation module will silently shadow the live one the day someone adds it to the page. Delete dead code rather than keeping it "for reference."
5. **A generator that overwrites unconditionally will eventually destroy hand-authored work.** If you ship a bootstrap generator that emits agent files, give it a dry-run, a diff, and a force flag — and generate from data, not by regex-scraping source text, which breaks the first time a `const` becomes a `let`.

---

## 9.14 The agent authoring standard (complete, reproduced as a spec)

This section is normative. It is the standard that every agent file in the library must satisfy, and it should be enforced in CI rather than in prose.

### 9.14.1 Why the standard exists: four canonical failure modes

Every rule below targets one of these:

1. **Vague descriptions** → the parent writes a vague kickoff prompt → the subagent burns context re-deriving what it should have been told.
2. **No defined output format** → the subagent has no stopping point → it runs long and returns shapeless prose the parent cannot parse.
3. **No obstacle reporting** → workarounds and environment quirks die in the subagent's context → the next stage rediscovers them at full cost.
4. **Result summarization** → diagnostic detail compresses into "tests failed" → the parent must rerun the work just to debug it.

The standard asserts its own authority: it must be read before any agent file is created or edited, and **any divergence must be documented in-file with a "Why this agent diverges" note. Silent violation is prohibited.**

### 9.14.2 Required structure, in order

Every agent file must contain these sections, in this order:

```
---
id: <kebab-case-id>
name: <Human Name>
department: <department>
source: <provenance>
version: <semver>
depends_on: [<other-agent-ids>]
type: prompt-template
---

# <Human Name>

Reusable prompt template. Invoke by typing: **<lowercase invocation phrase>**

**Unique value**: <one sentence — the failure class this agent catches that no other agent catches>

## Invocation Contract

The caller MUST include in the kickoff prompt:
- <concrete input 1>
- <concrete input 2>
- <concrete input 3 …>

If any of these are missing and cannot be inferred reliably from conversation
context, request them before starting.

## The Prompt

<the actual instructions to the subagent — what to do, how to think, what not to touch>

## Standing Criteria          (or a named variant: "Standing Review Criteria", etc.)

<the non-negotiable checks this agent always performs>

## Fix Policy                 (or "Escalate when" — whichever fits)

<when to auto-fix vs. when to escalate>

## Output Format

Return one combined report in this numbered structure:

1. <section>
2. <section>
…
N-1. **What was not validated or could not be fully verified** — blind spots, skipped areas, env limits.
N.   **Obstacles encountered** — setup issues, workarounds discovered, commands that needed
     special flags or configuration, dependencies or imports that caused problems, env quirks.
     Report anything the next stage would otherwise have to rediscover.
```

Additionally: **a confidence rating (HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW with a one-sentence rationale) is required for any agent that produces a judgment about whether work is shippable.**

### 9.14.3 The ten rules

**Rule 1 — Unique value statement, one sentence.**
The body opens with a `**Unique value**:` line naming the specific failure class this agent catches. The test: if you cannot complete the sentence "No other agent catches X," the agent does not earn a slot — merge it into an existing agent or delete it. Good: "Catches integration failures, workflow breakage, concurrency issues, and performance regressions through broad validation." Bad: "Helps with testing."
*Failure mode prevented:* catalog bloat. Every entry is injected into the parent's context and pays rent in tokens on every session; an agent with no distinct value is a permanent tax with no return, and it makes the parent's delegation decision harder by adding a near-duplicate option.

**Rule 2 — Invocation Contract, mandatory, near the top.**
List exactly what the caller must include in the kickoff prompt. It must be **3–6 bullets** (fewer is too vague, more goes unread), name **concrete inputs** rather than abstract qualities ("the spec path" beats "context about the spec"), and end with the fixed fallback sentence: *"If any of these are missing and cannot be inferred reliably from conversation context, request them before starting."* The contract must not duplicate The Prompt — **the contract is what to pass in; The Prompt is what to do with it.** Anti-patterns: "the caller should provide enough context" and "include any relevant files."
*Failure mode prevented:* failure mode 1. This is the single biggest lever on parent behavior, because the catalog injects the agent body into the parent's context and the contract is re-read every time the parent decides to delegate.

**Rule 3 — Output Format is a numbered list, with two fixed final sections.**
The last two numbered items, in this order, at the end of every agent's output format:
- **What was not validated or could not be fully verified** — blind spots and non-completion.
- **Obstacles encountered** — setup issues, workarounds, commands that needed special flags, dependency or import problems, environment quirks.

These are different concerns and **must not be collapsed**: the first is *scope coverage*, the second is *practical hacks the next stage needs*.
*Failure mode prevented:* failure modes 2 and 3. Numbered sections create explicit stopping points — the agent knows it is done when every section is filled — and the fixed final sections make the two most-commonly-dropped categories structurally impossible to omit.

**Rule 4 — Raw output discipline for any agent that runs tests, queries, or external commands.**
1. **Failures or errors → verbatim.** Full stack trace, full assertion message, full stderr. Do not paraphrase. Do not truncate to "the relevant part." If it is long, include it anyway — the parent can scan; it cannot reconstruct what was hidden.
2. **Successes → summarize freely.** One-line counts are fine.
3. **Flaky results → include at least one failing run's raw output AND note the flake.** Never silently retry until green.
4. **Document non-default commands** (custom flags, filters, env vars) in Obstacles so the next stage can reproduce.

*Failure mode prevented:* failure mode 4, described in the standard as "the single worst subagent failure mode — the parent cannot debug what is hidden." A summarized failure forces a full rerun, which costs more than the entire subagent invocation saved.

**Rule 5 — Claim a frame, not expertise.**
"You are a Python expert" adds nothing; the model already has the knowledge. What an agent adds is a **distinct lens that changes the questions asked** — for example, "you evaluate every change from the perspective of someone who uses this product eight hours a day." Multiple *named internal roles within one agent* are fine and encouraged; those are role frames, not subagents.
*Failure mode prevented:* subagent proliferation with zero informational gain. An "expert" subagent costs a context window and returns what the parent would have produced anyway.

**Rule 6 — No blind pipelines: artifacts on disk.**
Sequential multi-stage pipelines lose information at every handoff, because the summary returned to the parent strips exactly the detail the next stage needs. Mandatory mitigation: each stage writes its **full** findings to a numbered file under a run directory (`plans/runs/{YYYY-MM-DD-HHMM}-{slug}/`, with `00-request.md`, `01-<stage>.md`, …), and the next stage **reads the prior artifact in full**, not the in-context summary. That directory is gitignored, so writing is free. The final report references artifacts by path so the user can inspect any stage without rerunning.
*Failure mode prevented:* information loss between stages — described in the standard as the number-one failure mode of multi-stage pipelines. Numbers are stage *identities*, so a skipped stage leaves a gap rather than renumbering.

**Rule 7 — Tool restrictions are encoded in prose.**
The mechanism has no `tools:` field, so any restriction must be written into The Prompt: "Do not modify code files. Read and analyze only." / "Write to the plans directory only." / "Fix problems that are clear, low-risk, and unambiguous; for anything requiring judgment or with broader risk, escalate." State it **once**, near the top of The Prompt or in the Fix Policy — repeating it in three places is noise.
*Failure mode prevented:* an agent that quietly edits code during what the caller believed was a read-only audit. Prose is the only enforcement channel available; if you do not write it, there is no restriction.

**Rule 8 — Versioning and `depends_on`.**
Bump `version:` on every substantive change: patch for wording, minor for added section/rule/scope, major for a changed output format, removed required behavior, or anything breaking for callers. `depends_on` lists the agent ids this one invokes or builds on, and **must be kept accurate because the orchestrator agent reads it to construct its workflow.**
*Failure mode prevented:* silent contract drift. When an output format changes and consumers are not updated, downstream agents parse for sections that no longer exist and report nothing rather than reporting an error.

**Rule 9 — Standing criteria live in the agent, not the kickoff prompt.**
Recurring checklists — project-rule compliance, performance-marker preservation, public-repo safety, lifecycle-state coverage — belong in a `## Standing Criteria` section in the agent body. They must be **non-negotiable**; anything optional belongs in The Prompt or the Fix Policy instead.
*Failure mode prevented:* reliance on caller memory. The catalog injects the body, so standing criteria are always in context; requiring the caller to restate them guarantees they will eventually be forgotten, and the check silently stops happening.

**Rule 10 — One agent, one failure class.**
Every agent removes a distinct class of failure the others cannot. If two agents repeatedly catch the same issues, one is redundant — merge, narrow, or delete the weaker one. Enforce this at the orchestrator's unique-value registry: **adding an agent requires being able to add a "catches X that nothing else catches" line to that list.**
*Failure mode prevented:* an unmaintainable roster where nobody can predict which agent to invoke, and where two agents both half-cover a gap that neither owns.

### 9.14.4 Editing checklist

1. Read the standard first.
2. Read the target agent file **in full — do not edit blind.**
3. Bump `version:` per Rule 8.
4. Preserve the agent's distinct frame (Rule 5) and unique value (Rule 10).
5. If the output format changed, update every consumer listed in `depends_on`.
6. **After saving, re-read the file** to confirm the edit landed and the structure is intact.

### 9.14.5 Creation checklist

1. Read the standard first.
2. State the unique value in one sentence. **If you cannot, stop** — the agent does not earn a slot.
3. Use the required-sections template. Every section is required unless you have a documented divergence.
4. Add the agent to the orchestrator's unique-value list and routing rules.
5. **Test by invoking on a real task and reading the output.** If the output is shapeless or runs too long, the format is wrong — fix the format, not the invocation.

### 9.14.6 Scope boundaries

The standard is **not** the agent list (the runtime catalog is authoritative), **not** the loader specification, and **not** guidance for one-off mid-session delegations that never go through the catalog. Keeping these separate is what stops the standard from rotting into stale documentation.

### 9.14.7 Enforce it in CI

Prose standards decay. Validate mechanically: required sections present and in order; contract bullet count within 3–6; the fallback sentence present; the output format numbered; the final two sections present, in order, and not merged; a confidence rating present for judgment-producing agents; semver bumped relative to the previous commit; `depends_on` ids resolvable; frontmatter present on every file the loader will ingest.

---

## 9.15 Our agent roster and each agent's unique value

Treat this as a **recommended starting roster**. Ten agents, each owning one failure class, plus one orchestrator that routes between them. Every "team" is a cast of **named internal role frames executed by one agent in one context** — no agent spawns real subagents, and that is deliberate (Rule 5).

| Agent | Unique value — the failure class it owns | Contract highlights | Output shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Plan Team** | Catches spec gaps, ambiguity, and architectural risk **before any code is written**. The only team that operates before implementation | Draft spec path or text; the original request verbatim; prior decisions and ruled-out options; constraints; **whether it may add scope for coherence or must stay strictly inside the request** | 7 numbered sections including a dedicated **Lifecycle states covered**. Internal roles run in sequence: Spec Analyst → Product Strategist → Architect → Implementation Auditor → Integration Reviewer → Expert User. Fixes are written *into the spec*, not merely reported |
| **Build Team** | Catches implementation errors, step-by-step correctness, and spec-to-code drift. **No other team builds with integrated review gates** | Spec path or inline spec; explicit out-of-scope items; partial implementation to extend vs. replace; performance-critical paths; desired step granularity | 7 sections including **Strategic conflicts surfaced** and **Top 3 suggested enhancements — plain English only, do NOT implement them**. Runs a review gate after every step, a full-solution review, a re-review after fixes, a rules-compliance gate, a cleanup pass, and a regression pass |
| **Review Team** | Catches code quality, security, documentation, and project-rule violations in completed code. The only deep code-level review | Scope (file list, git range, or PR); the spec the code should satisfy; explicit out-of-scope areas; **whether to auto-fix or only report**; performance-critical constraints | 7 sections. Five role lanes coordinate into one shared picture — explicitly "not four independent reports" |
| **Test Team** | Catches integration failures, workflow breakage, concurrency issues, and performance regressions. **The only team that tests the system as a user would experience it** | One-sentence description of the change; changed files or git range; workflow paths to exercise end to end; risk areas flagged upstream; whether to run the suite and which markers | 8 sections: item 1 is the **exact command strings**, item 2 is **Failures (raw output)** verbatim, item 8 is a confidence rating. Owns the canonical raw-output-discipline block, plus the rule: **if a failure is not trivially fixable, do not diagnose — escalate, because speculation here pollutes the record** |
| **Debug Team** | Catches unknown-cause failures through root-cause analysis. **The only team that reasons backward from symptom to cause** | Symptom in user-facing language; exact repro steps *or an explicit note that repro is unknown*; logs/traces/screenshots; recent related changes; suspected blast radius; **raw test output if a test failure triggered it** | 10 sections separating **Root cause ("not the trigger, the cause")** from Fix, and distinguishing files *modified* from files merely *verified*. Roles: Triage Lead → Root Cause Analyst + Context Investigator → Fix Engineer → Regression Guard |
| **Hotfix Team** | Catches production-blocking failures and applies minimum safe containment. **The only team optimized for speed over thoroughness** | Symptom plus proposed severity (may be reclassified); exact user-facing impact; whether the cause is known — **if unknown, prefer Debug unless minutes truly matter**; captured evidence; **known-good rollback options, because containment may be a revert** | 10 sections with a P0/P1/P2 severity taxonomy. Root cause may legitimately read "containment only — root cause deferred," in which case **a follow-up ticket is mandatory**. Verification steps must be written so they can be repeated |
| **Refactor Team** | Catches structural decay, duplication, and maintainability drag **without changing external behavior**. The only team whose primary mission is internal quality | Target scope (files, modules, or a named smell); explicit goals; **explicit non-goals**; performance-critical paths, which are no-touch unless preservation is provable; the validation step that proves behavior unchanged | 10 sections including a **before/after assessment with a concrete metric — "not vibes, measurable"** — and a Risks section for things that might subtly differ with tests still green (timing, ordering, log output, error text). Hard rule: existing tests must pass **without semantic modification** |
| **Final Audit** | Catches intent mismatch, whole-system coherence failures, blast-radius damage, and behavioral drift that pass every other stage. **The only team that audits the finished result as a whole against the original goal** | **The original request verbatim, not paraphrased**; changed files or git range; pointers to prior pipeline artifacts; the spec; **prior teams' confidence levels and escalations so the audit can probe what was deferred** | 9 sections ending in a confidence rating with explicit definitions and the guard **"do not assign HIGH unless there is no meaningful unresolved risk."** Framed negatively for clarity: *"this is not a re-review."* Fixes only clear, low-risk, unambiguous problems |
| **Expert User (persona)** | The only persona agent: evaluates a change purely as a daily power user. Defined by negation — **not** code quality, **not** bugs, **not** edge cases, **not** spec coverage. One question: does this work the way a real user would expect? | The change in one sentence; affected files or UI areas; screenshots or flows if visual; **whether it is backend-only, in which case it PASSes quickly**; existing patterns to match or deliberately diverge from | A fenced report template rather than a numbered list: PASS/FAIL verdict · Workflow Assessment · a **Consistency Check table** (Element / Expected from rest of app / Actual / Match) · Discoverability · Findings with Severity, What (no code references), Scenario, User impact, and a one-sentence fix · Quick Hits · What Was Not Validated · Obstacles Encountered. Findings are BLOCKING or NON-BLOCKING |
| **Execute Pipeline** (orchestrator) | Full end-to-end orchestration from idea to shipped without intermediate prompts. Holds the unique-value registry for everyone else | The original request **verbatim**; constraints and out-of-scope items; pointers to prior context; the work type if known, otherwise it classifies in step 1 | 11 sections ending in a confidence rating, with obstacles **aggregated so the next pipeline run benefits**. Carries the operating-tempo block, the non-negotiable standards list, the unique-value registry, the artifact-discipline spec, and the routing rules |

**Routing.** Only the pipeline agent is a true orchestrator; Build is a secondary one via its review gates; everything else is a leaf. Four routes, chosen **before any team runs**, with an explicit warning not to default to the feature route:

- **(a) New feature or major change** → Plan → Build → Review → Test → Final Audit
- **(b) Bug with unknown cause** → Debug → Build → Review → Test → Final Audit
- **(c) Production issue where speed matters** → Hotfix → Review → targeted test validation → Final Audit
- **(d) Internal cleanup, no behavior change** → Refactor → Review → Test → Final Audit

Classification guidance: a known cause with a small bounded patch makes route (b) overkill — use (a) with a minimal spec, or (c) if production is broken *right now*. Symptoms with no known why → (b). A broken user-facing workflow where minutes matter → (c). "Clean up / refactor / consolidate / extract" → (d). **Ambiguous → ask the user, because picking the wrong route burns more time than asking.**

Forward edges are Plan → Build → Review → Test → Audit, with three declared back edges (Review→Build, Review→Plan, Test→Plan/Build) and one escalation edge (Test→Debug).

**Why this particular set.** Each entry maps to a distinct moment in the lifecycle where a *different* kind of thing goes wrong: before code exists (Plan), while writing it (Build), in the code itself (Review), in the assembled system (Test), when the cause is unknown (Debug), when the clock is the constraint (Hotfix), when the code works but the structure is rotting (Refactor), when everything passed but the result is not what was asked for (Final Audit), and when it is technically correct but feels wrong to use (Expert User). If you cannot place a proposed eleventh agent at a moment none of these own, do not add it.

---

## 9.16 Consequential decisions

| Decision | What we chose | Why | What breaks if you choose differently |
|---|---|---|---|
| Storage substrate | Files on disk, one folder per composition, one JSON context file | Agents are the primary writers and already have filesystem tools; the context file doubles as shared agent memory; output is files anyway | With a database, every agent read becomes an API round-trip you must teach the model; coordination stops being cheap and agents stop reading state before acting |
| Agent topology | Hub-and-spoke: root ↔ context file ↔ sections; no lateral messaging | One component must hold whole-document visibility for coherence to be enforceable | Mesh messaging reintroduces exactly the drift the feature exists to prevent, and no component can detect it |
| Cross-section awareness | Names, statuses, and one agent-written summary line per section | Cost is O(sections), independent of document length | Pushing content across sections makes prompt size O(document); at eight sections you are re-sending the whole document eight times per turn |
| Conflict handling | Detect and present; **never auto-resolve** | A heuristic good enough to flag is not good enough to pick a winner, and picking wrong is invisible until the document is finished | Auto-resolution silently rewrites the user's intent, and the damage surfaces only at export when it is most expensive to fix |
| Conflict detection method | Lexical token overlap, ratio over `min(|A|,|B|)`, threshold 0.30 | Zero dependencies, instant, biased to recall — good enough to exercise the plumbing | Semantic contradictions with no shared vocabulary ("British" vs "American" spelling) are never detected; plan the embedding/classifier upgrade from day one |
| Changing-flag authority | Anyone may set; **only the owning section may clear** (403 otherwise) | "Work is outstanding" must be a claim only the worker can retract | The orchestrator marks a section clean mid-edit and the coherence guarantee evaporates silently |
| Shared-prompts control | One boolean per composition | Scope a consistency policy to the unit consistency is defined over | Per-prompt toggles tax every message with a decision the user cannot make yet; per-session toggles create an invisible N-boolean matrix nobody can reason about |
| Live update transport | 4-second mtime poll on the context file, broadcast over websocket | Agents write the file directly, so no API route fires; the watcher is the only observer of agent-driven change | Remove it and live progress silently dies for the entire parallel-agent workflow — the feature's whole point |
| Auto-start side effects | Creating a composition auto-starts the orchestrator, **non-blocking**, failure logged and swallowed | An optional side effect must never fail a primary create | A failed session start leaves the user with no composition and an error, instead of a composition they can launch manually |
| Prompt-build failure policy | Non-fatal; session starts without the compose prompt, with a warning | A degraded session is workable; no session is not | Coupling them means one transient file-read error blocks all work in that composition |
| Agent library delivery | One catalog file in temp per host project, referenced by a single line in the system prompt | Inlining cost ~8k tokens per session and bloated the process argument | Inline injection taxes every session; without the "do not look on disk" preamble, models hunt for files that do not exist and report no agents |
| Agent definition format | Markdown with naive flat frontmatter | Files are hand-edited by humans *and* LLMs; a strict parser turns a stray indent into a broken catalog | Strict YAML produces silent whole-catalog failures from cosmetic edits |
| Authoring standard enforcement | Documented now, **CI-validated in the rebuild** | Prose standards decay; the structure is what makes subagent output parseable | Formats drift agent by agent, and consumers that parse by section heading silently return nothing |

---

## 9.17 Non-negotiable rules

1. **Never clear a container whose children are contract, not content.** Clear only the dedicated dynamic region, and assert loudly on null id lookups.
   *Failure mode if violated:* the whole panel goes permanently blank while the API returns valid data, and writes into null succeed silently — unrecoverable without a page reload.
2. **Every composition-list read passes the host-project filter, and the server predicate is `scope == filter OR pinned`.**
   *Failure mode if violated:* pickers show every composition from every project, or pinned cross-project compositions vanish from the sidebar.
3. **Return an explicit `null` for an unknown id; never fall back server-side.**
   *Failure mode if violated:* the client cannot tell that its persisted pointer is stale, so it keeps re-selecting a dead id forever.
4. **Any persisted pointer to a deletable entity has a self-healing fallback**: clear it in memory *and* storage, retry with the broader scope filter, adopt what comes back.
   *Failure mode if violated:* one deletion permanently bricks the view for that host project.
5. **Only the owning section may clear its changing flag; return 403 otherwise, and treat an empty setter as owner-only.**
   *Failure mode if violated:* the orchestrator marks a section clean mid-edit and the coherence guarantee silently evaporates.
6. **Never auto-resolve a directive conflict.** Detect, present both sides with a recommendation, let the user decide in one click or one sentence.
   *Failure mode if violated:* the system silently discards half the user's intent, and the loss is invisible until the document is finished.
7. **Never push another section's content into an agent's prompt.** Project to name, status, and a one-line summary; let agents pull files if they need more.
   *Failure mode if violated:* prompt size becomes O(document × sections) and long compositions stop being affordable — or possible.
8. **Assemble prompts stable-first, volatile-last, and emit explicit empty markers** for every section of the live-state block.
   *Failure mode if violated:* prefix caching never hits, and the model must disambiguate "absent" from "none," which it does by inventing content.
9. **Make the input target explicit, always visible, and validated immediately before every send.** Recompute it on every state change, especially delete.
   *Failure mode if violated:* silent misroutes — the wrong agent does plausible work, shared state is corrupted, and trust in orchestration is gone.
10. **Never let an optional side effect fail a primary create; never let a prompt-build failure block session start.**
    *Failure mode if violated:* a transient error destroys the user's primary action instead of degrading one optional feature.
11. **Never acquire the same lock twice.** Set changing flags after conflict resolution *outside* the context lock.
    *Failure mode if violated:* deadlock on the composition that just had a conflict resolved — the exact moment the user is watching.
12. **Atomic write everywhere**, temp file plus overwrite-capable rename, under a per-composition mutex; tolerate torn reads in the watcher by recording the mtime and skipping the cycle.
    *Failure mode if violated:* a half-written context file destroys the composition's entire coordination state.
13. **Never resolve content paths by re-sanitizing a mutable name.** Store the folder path on the record.
    *Failure mode if violated:* renaming a section orphans its content, and the section silently disappears from every export.
14. **Never clean test data by name pattern when the code under test generates names; isolate the storage root per test run.**
    *Failure mode if violated:* generated artifacts leak into real user data (this cost us 52 orphan compositions).
15. **Debounce socket-driven refreshes and prefer targeted patches over full re-render.**
    *Failure mode if violated:* under parallel agents, every mutation triggers a refresh storm that destroys open menus, inline edits, and pending confirmations.
16. **Every optimistic UI operation has a revert path.**
    *Failure mode if violated:* the UI and the server diverge silently, and the user trusts the wrong one.
17. **Every agent file satisfies the authoring standard, validated in CI**, including the two fixed final output sections and a bumped semver.
    *Failure mode if violated:* subagent reports become shapeless, obstacles and blind spots go unreported, and consumers parsing by section heading silently return nothing.
18. **Diagnostic failures are reported verbatim; only successes may be summarized.**
    *Failure mode if violated:* the parent cannot debug what is hidden and must rerun the entire subagent invocation, erasing the savings that justified delegating.
19. **Multi-stage pipelines write full findings to numbered artifacts on disk, and each stage reads the prior artifact in full.**
    *Failure mode if violated:* every handoff loses exactly the detail the next stage needs, and the final report is confidently wrong.
20. **The agent catalog is a file reference plus a "this is the authoritative list, do not search disk" preamble.**
    *Failure mode if violated:* ~8k tokens per session of pure overhead, or models hunting the filesystem and reporting that no agents exist.

---

## 9.18 Implementation prompts

Paste these to a coding agent in order. Each assumes the previous ones are complete.

```
PROMPT 9.1 — Storage, scoping, and the role token

Build the Compose persistence foundation before any UI or prompt work.

1. Implement a configurable storage root (env var or config key, defaulting to
   compose-projects/ under the app data dir). No test may ever write to the
   production root.
2. Implement the composition folder layout: project.json, compose-context.json,
   brief.md, sections/<folder>/{section.json, brief.md, content/}, export/.
   Sanitize folder names (lowercase, spaces to hyphens, strip non
   [a-z0-9-_], fall back to "unnamed"), appending the first 8 chars of the UUID
   on collision. Store the resolved folder path on the section record — never
   recompute it from the name.
3. Implement atomic writes: temp file plus an overwrite-capable rename, guarded
   by a per-composition mutex held in a module-level map behind a meta-lock.
   Provide a read-and-lock helper returning (context, lock) that releases the
   lock if the read fails.
4. Implement forgiving deserialization: unknown fields ignored, missing fields
   defaulted, legacy statuses not_started/working migrated to drafting.
5. Implement the scoping model: parent_project on every composition, a list
   filter meaning (parent_project == filter OR pinned), and an explicit null
   return for an unknown id.
6. Implement the role token: encode/decode for "root:{cid}" and
   "section:{cid}:{sid}", parsing with a maximum of two splits so section ids
   containing colons survive. Raise on unknown role prefixes or missing parts.
7. Implement orphan self-heal: a directory with compose-context.json but no
   project.json gets a reconstructed project.json persisted on scan.

Acceptance criteria:
- A test suite runs entirely against a temp storage root, verified by asserting
  the production root is untouched.
- Concurrent writes from 10 threads to one composition never produce a corrupt
  or truncated context file.
- A composition whose folder is renamed on disk still exports its content,
  because paths come from the record.
- Round-trip tests cover legacy status migration and unknown-field tolerance.
- Token tests cover both shapes, colon-containing section ids, and every
  malformed input class.
```

```
PROMPT 9.2 — Context file API, CRUD, and the board endpoint

Build the data and API skeleton on top of PROMPT 9.1.

1. Implement the context-file mutation API. Every function takes the
   per-composition lock, reads, mutates, RECOMPUTES the derived status block
   (total, complete, in_progress = drafting + reviewing, drafting, reviewing),
   and writes atomically:
   add/update/remove/reorder sections; merge facts; partial section status
   update where a null field means "leave alone"; append directive assigning
   gen = max(existing)+1 INSIDE the lock; set/clear changing; add/update
   conflict.
2. Implement composition CRUD, including clone with a TWO-PASS id remap: pass
   one assigns new ids, pass two rewrites parent_id links, directive scopes and
   sources, and conflict directive references. Clones clear every session_id and
   do not inherit pinned state.
3. Implement section CRUD: insert_position "top" -> min(order)-1 else
   max(order)+1; cascade delete deepest-first returning deleted_count and the
   deleted list; a descendants query for the confirmation dialog; add-and-link
   returning 409 when the session is already linked, and deleting the scaffolded
   folder if the context write fails.
4. Implement GET /api/compose/board exactly as specified: bare object or JSON
   null with no ok envelope; select by id if given, else most recent within the
   host-project filter; sibling_projects = all compositions sharing the host
   project (each with a status summary and has_conflicts) plus all pinned
   compositions from any other host project, deduped by id.
5. Emit the socket events listed in the API table on the specified triggers.

Acceptance criteria:
- Board returns null for an unknown id and never falls back server-side.
- A host-project-filtered board never leaks another project's compositions, and
  always includes pinned cross-project compositions.
- Cascade delete of a 3-level tree removes exactly the descendants, deepest
  first, and leaves no orphan folders.
- Clone of a composition with nested sections, directives scoped to section ids,
  and one conflict produces a fully self-consistent copy with no id from the
  source surviving.
- Derived status is recomputed, never read from input.

```
PROMPT 9.3 — Prompt builders and agent lifecycle

Implement server-side prompt assembly and session wiring.

1. Build the root orchestrator prompt in exactly this order: identity; framing;
   the standing "read compose-context.json before EVERY action" instruction; the
   four numbered responsibilities (structure, coherence, assembly/export,
   architectural intent with user approval); the conflict-mediation protocol;
   the routing rule ("interpret intent from content, not just from which card
   was selected"); post-update obligations; then "## Current State" containing
   Sections, Facts, Pending Conflicts (pending only), Active Directives (active
   only) in that order.
2. Build the section prompt in exactly this order: identity; scope framing;
   Your Section; Your Responsibilities; Rules; Project Context (siblings by name
   and status only, then parent, then children with the literal sentence "Do not
   duplicate their work.", then facts); Section Directives filtered to this
   section id OR global.
3. Emit an explicit parenthetical for every empty list: (no sections yet),
   (no facts recorded), (no pending conflicts), (no active directives),
   (no directives), (this is the only section).
4. Show directive generation numbers in the rendered lines.
5. Build the section prompt from ONE context read; do not call a lookup helper
   that re-reads the file.
6. Return {ok: true, system_prompt, agent_role} or {ok: false, error}. Every
   call site must start the session anyway on failure and log a warning.
7. On session start with a role token: run compose prompt resolution and
   cross-session-awareness injection in parallel on a MODULE-LEVEL 2-worker
   pool with a 10s timeout each; run inline when only one is needed; apply
   compose prompt first and awareness second; link the session id back to the
   composition or section AFTER emitting the start acknowledgement. Skip the
   generic agent-catalog injection for compose sessions.
8. Implement per-section launch (409 if already linked) and launch-all (launch
   every unlinked section with a prompt derived from its summary, then send the
   root a coordination message listing every section with type and truncated
   summary; return succeeded/failed/launched/root_message).

Acceptance criteria:
- Golden-file tests pin both prompt orders, including every empty-state marker.
- A section prompt never contains another section's body text, and contains
  exactly its own directives plus globals.
- Deleting the context file mid-start still starts the session, with a warning
  logged and no compose prompt.
- A profiling test shows parallel prompt resolution is measurably faster than a
  sequential baseline, and that the pool is created once per process.

```
PROMPT 9.4 — Frontend shell, boot routine, and the input target

Build the Compose UI shell. Read the scoping rules before writing teardown code.

1. Define the static DOM skeleton in the page template: sidebar, board container
   with THREE static children (root header, input-target bar, sections board),
   and the tab strip. Add a comment on the container stating that its children
   are contract, not content.
2. Teardown clears ONLY the sections board. Never the container. Every id lookup
   asserts non-null and throws on failure.
3. Implement the boot routine: load sort modes; capture a monotonic init epoch
   and abort after every await if a newer init started; restore the selected
   composition id from a per-host-project key; build the query always including
   the host-project filter when one exists; fetch the board; populate the
   sidebar from sibling_projects.
4. Implement the STALE-SELECTION FALLBACK: when the response is null or has no
   composition and a saved id was in play, clear the id in memory AND storage,
   refetch with only the host-project filter, adopt the recovered composition,
   persist the new selection, and render. Swallow throws and fall through to the
   empty state.
5. Implement the input target as a FIRST-CLASS, ALWAYS-VISIBLE, independently
   settable control. Navigation may change it; navigation is not the only way to
   change it. Derive the label and the token from one function. Validate the
   token against live state immediately before every send and refuse
   unresolvable targets with a plain-language message. Mirror the target in the
   composer chrome (border color and placeholder). Recompute on every state
   change, especially delete.
6. Implement the sidebar: list with status-dot precedence (conflicts > no
   sections > all complete > any in progress > idle), search shown above three
   items, pin, right-click menu, drag-reorder DISABLED while a filter is active,
   and 5-second undo-delete that FLUSHES on navigation.
7. Implement the board: three columns, cards with all specified elements,
   per-column sort modes persisted, drag-to-status optimistic WITH revert on
   failure, and the empty-board hero.

Acceptance criteria:
- Switching host projects while in compose view and switching back renders a
  populated board every time. A test asserts the three static children still
  exist after teardown.
- Deleting the currently selected composition, then reloading, recovers to
  another composition in the same host project without user action.
- The target indicator is visible in every state including section drill-down,
  and a send against a deleted section is refused, not silently misrouted.
- Rapidly switching compositions five times leaves exactly one render in flight
  (epoch guard verified by test).
```

Implement coordination.

   sections and conflicts wholesale and falls back to board view if the
   drilled-into section vanished. DEBOUNCE the four refresh-triggering events
   (200-400ms) and prefer targeted patches over full refetch.

Acceptance criteria:
- Clearing another section's flag returns 403; clearing your own succeeds.
- Writing a context file directly on disk (simulating an agent) produces a UI
  update within 5 seconds with no API call involved.
- A file truncated mid-write produces no crash, no event, and is picked up on
  the next poll.
- Creating a composition emits no watcher event on first observation.
- Ten rapid section updates produce at most two board re-renders, and an open
  context menu survives them.

Implement the conflict lifecycle and all four export formats.

   semantic implementation can replace it without touching callers.
2. Implement resolution with ALL THREE actions under the composition lock:
   supersede (mark A superseded; collect its section scope as affected); scope
   (prompt for scope assignment, rewrite both directives' scopes disjointly,
   keep both active — this branch must actually work); keep_both (no-op). Then
   for every action mark the conflict resolved with action, timestamp and note,
   and append a synthetic global directive recording the resolution. THEN,

   DOCX gets the title page, per-section heading plus italic summary intro, page

5. Either wire export_config (format, template, styles) end to end or delete the
   field. Do not persist a setting that does nothing.

Acceptance criteria:
- Two directives sharing >30% of their meaningful tokens produce a pending
  conflict; nothing is ever auto-resolved.
- Resolving a conflict appends a synthetic directive, flags affected sections,
  and does not deadlock (a test asserts completion under a timeout).
- A 3-level composition exports with sections in depth-first order and heading
  levels matching depth, in markdown, zip and docx.
- Renaming a section then exporting still includes its content.
- Missing DOCX or PDF dependencies produce the specified status codes with
