# Part 10 — Surrounding Tools

---

## 10.1 What this part covers, and an honest gap report

The preceding parts of this specification described the core of the product: a local web application that
supervises long-running AI coding agent sessions on a developer's own machine. This part describes
everything that surrounds that core — the features that make the agent's work reachable, visible,
publishable, searchable, speakable, and usable from a phone.

Concretely, Part 10 covers:

- **File handling** — how files get *into* an agent session and how artifacts the agent *produces* get back out.
- **Git integration** — a cached status poller and a one-click commit-and-push button.
- **The one-click Update flow** — the safety-critical publishing path used by people who never read a diff.
- **Live preview** — how an agent shows a rendered UI to a user who is not sitting at the machine.
- **Search** — full-text search across every session transcript in a project.
- **Voice input** — dictation into the prompt box, and the browser constraint it imposes on the whole product.
- **Mobile and remote access** — reaching the app from a phone without exposing it to the internet.
- **Bridges and analysis endpoints** — a third-party-chat relay and a set of zero-cost session analyzers.

### The honest gap report: there is no file browser

Read this before you plan anything else in this part.

The reference product **never built a conventional file-browser panel.** There is no project file tree, no
file viewer, no syntax highlighting of repository files, no in-app editor, no working-tree diff viewer, no
`@`-mention file picker, no multi-select, no token budgeting for attached files, and no list virtualization.
A panel that *looks* like a workspace in the reference implementation is actually an agent-management card
grid whose data model is a client-side folder tree, not a filesystem.

What exists instead is a much smaller set of surfaces, each solving one narrow problem well:

| Surface | Problem it solves |
|---|---|
| Drag-and-drop landing zone | Get a file from the user's desktop onto the machine and tell the agent it is there |
| Folder picker modal | Choose a destination directory, one level at a time |
| Output shelf | Surface files the agent *created* as clickable cards inline in the conversation |
| Code-block extraction drawer | Pull every fenced code block out of a transcript, dedupe, name, copy, zip |
| Session comparison | Two-column diff of transcript code blocks between two sessions |
| Find-in-transcript | Browser-style Ctrl/Cmd+F over the rendered conversation |
| Embed mode | Run the whole app as a pinned single-project panel inside a host application |

**Our recommendation to a fresh team: build the real file browser, and scope it deliberately as v2 work.**

The absence was not a decision; it was an accumulation. The product got by without one because the agent has
shell access and can read anything itself, and because the drop-and-tell-the-agent trick (§10.2) removed the
immediate pressure. But the cost showed up constantly in user behavior: people asked the agent "what's in
the config file" instead of looking, they could not review a change before publishing it, and the one-click
publish button (§10.4) shipped without any way for a non-technical user to *see* what they were about to
publish. That last one is the strongest argument. If you are going to ship a button that commits and pushes
everything, a read-only working-tree diff viewer is not a nice-to-have; it is the only thing that makes the
button honest.

Do not inherit our absence by default. Decide.

---

## 10.2 File handling: drop, attach, embed, extract, and the output shelf

### 10.2.1 The filesystem sandbox

Every file endpoint shares exactly one containment rule: **resolve the requested path to an absolute,
symlink-free canonical form, then require that it lie under the current user's home directory.** Violations
return HTTP 403. Resolution must happen *before* the comparison — otherwise a symlink inside the home
directory pointing outside it escapes the sandbox.

This is a deliberately wide boundary. Everything under the user's home directory is reachable: read metadata,
copy, upload into, open with the system handler. It is defensible only because the application binds to the
loopback interface and the realistic threat model is accidental self-harm, not remote intrusion (see §10.8.4).
State this in your own security documentation rather than implying a tighter boundary than you have.

### 10.2.2 The file API contract

| Endpoint | Method | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `/api/file-info` | GET | `path` | `{name, size, exists}` | `size` is pre-humanized server-side (`B`/`KB`/`MB`) so no client duplicates the formatting |
| `/api/open-file` | POST | `{path}` | `{ok}` | Opens with the OS default handler |
| `/api/download-to-downloads` | POST | `{path}` | `{ok, filename, dest}` | Copies into the user's Downloads folder with dedup |
| `/api/copy-file-to` | POST | `{source, target_dir}` | `{ok, filename, path}` | Both ends sandbox-checked |
| `/api/file-drop` | POST | multipart `file`, form `target_dir` | `{ok, path, filename}` | Filename sanitized, then dedup |
| `/api/browse-dir` | GET | `path` | `{path, dirs[]}` | Directories only, one level, dot-directories filtered, permission errors swallowed to an empty list |
| `/api/default-save-dir` | GET | — | `{path}` | Downloads folder, falling back to home |
| `/api/project-path` | GET | — | `{path}` | Active project's filesystem path |

**The dedup naming rule is an invariant used by three endpoints:** on a name collision, insert ` (n)` before
the file extension and increment `n` until a free name is found. This is the convention every desktop OS uses,
which means it needs no explanation, and it is what makes dropping the same file twice non-destructive.

**Portability bug to avoid.** The reference implementation's `open-file` endpoint calls the Windows-only
shell-open function with no platform branch, so "Open" returns HTTP 500 on macOS and Linux. Branch on platform
from day one: Windows shell-open, macOS `open`, Linux `xdg-open`.

### 10.2.3 Drag-and-drop, exactly

1. Bind `dragenter` at the document level. React only when the drag payload's type list includes files —
   this filters out text and element drags within the app.
2. **Use a drag counter, not a boolean.** Increment on `dragenter`, decrement on `dragleave`, hide the drop
   overlay only at zero. This is the fix for the classic flicker bug: moving the cursor over a child element
   fires `dragleave` on the parent, and a boolean flag would hide the overlay mid-drag.
3. On `drop`, push every dropped file into a **queue** and process one at a time. Ten dropped files must
   produce ten sequential destination prompts, not ten racing modals.
4. Open the folder picker defaulted to the Downloads folder. Build the breadcrumb by splitting on *both*
   path separators and special-casing a Windows drive-letter first segment (`C:` must render and navigate as
   `C:/`).
5. On confirm, POST multipart to `/api/file-drop`.
6. **Then — the important part — if a live session is running, emit an ordinary chat message on the user's
   behalf: `"[file dropped] <name> is now at <absolute path>"`.**

Step 6 is the whole design. **There is no attachment protocol.** The agent learns about the file through
the normal conversation channel and reads it with its normal file tools. This is dramatically cheaper than
building an attachment pipeline, and it composes with everything downstream — no special-casing in the
transcript renderer, no MIME negotiation, no token budgeting, no upload lifecycle. Copy this.

The picker should also be reusable headlessly: a "choose a folder" mode with a completion callback, so other
features (the output shelf's Save-to, for instance) reuse the same dialog rather than growing their own.

### 10.2.4 The output shelf

The agent produces files. The user needs to open them without hunting through the filesystem. The output
shelf watches the conversation stream and materializes clickable file cards inline, under the messages that
produced them.

**Detection is three-strategy and deliberately sloppy-tolerant:**

1. **Tool-name strategy.** For transcript entries recording a call to a file-writing tool (`write`, `edit`,
   `multiedit`, `notebook-edit`), the entry's description field carries the path. Strip a trailing
   `(write N chars)` suffix and a leading `file_path:` prefix.
2. **Shell strategy.** For shell tool calls, regex-scan the command text for paths.
3. **Text strategy.** For any tool *result* or assistant prose, regex-scan for absolute paths ending in a
   known extension.

Strategy 3 is not redundant. It is the only one that catches a file written by a Python script that the agent
ran through the shell — the tool call was "run this script," and nothing in it names the output. Without
strategy 3, generated spreadsheets and reports are invisible.

**Allowlist gate.** Only these extensions produce a card: spreadsheets, documents, presentations, PDF, common
image formats, SVG, CSV, JSON, ZIP, HTML, and plain text. Source-code extensions are *deliberately excluded*.
A card for every `.py` file the agent edits is noise that buries the one `.xlsx` the user actually wants.

**Card contract:** a family-colored icon, the basename, an asynchronously fetched size (via `/api/file-info`),
an **Open** button, and a **Save to…** button that opens the folder picker and then copies. If the picker
module is not loaded, Save-to falls back to the Downloads-folder copy.

**Invariants:** a set of already-carded paths dedupes across re-renders during streaming; both the set and the
shelf DOM are cleared on session switch.

This feature has the highest value-per-line in the entire part. Build it early.

### 10.2.5 Code extraction and export

`GET /api/extract-code/<session_id>` parses a session transcript, extracts every fenced code block from user
and assistant text, and returns per block: `language`, `content`, `msg_index`, `role`, `inferred_filename`,
`is_shell`, `duplicate_of`.

- **Filename inference.** First try two patterns over the *surrounding* message text: a quoted `name.ext`,
  and a `save as | create | file | write to | named <name.ext>` phrase. Reject matches of three characters or
  fewer, and reject anything without a dot. Otherwise fall back to a language → default-filename table
  covering roughly 35 languages.
- **Near-duplicate detection.** Pairwise sequence-similarity comparison within the same language; a ratio
  above 0.85 marks the later block as a duplicate of the earlier index. This exists because agents restate a
  whole file after a small edit, and without it a 40-turn session yields 30 near-identical copies of the same
  module.
- **Unique-name assignment.** Collisions get `_2`, `_3` inserted before the extension.
- **Export** (`GET /api/export-project/<session_id>`) builds an in-memory ZIP of the *non-duplicate* blocks
  plus a generated README listing file → language → originating message number.

### 10.2.6 Session comparison

`GET /api/compare/<id1>/<id2>` compares **transcript code blocks, not files.** Key both sessions' blocks by
inferred filename, falling back to language, falling back to `"unknown"`; first block wins per key. Union the
key sets and classify each key as `added`, `removed`, `same` (similarity above 0.98), or `changed`. Return
both sessions' metadata, a `code_diff[]` array carrying `content1`/`content2`, and aggregate statistics.
Render side-by-side with content truncated per cell.

Be honest about what this is: an approximate diff of what two conversations *talked about*, not a diff of what
they *did*. It is a narrow-use-case feature. Treat it as optional.

### 10.2.7 Embed mode

Query parameters (`?embed=1&project=<encoded-or-path>&view=sessions&chrome=1`) turn the whole app into a
sessions-only panel pinned to a single project, suitable for hosting inside another application's iframe.

**The load-bearing insight is that both naive implementations break the user's other window.** Browser local
storage is shared across every tab on the origin, so writing the pinned project there repoints the user's real
window. And a server-side "set active project" call mutates global state for every connected client. Neither
is acceptable for an embed.

The solution is to **shim local storage inside the embedded document**: reads of the active-project key return
the pinned project, reads of the per-project view key return the pinned view, and writes to the active-project
key, the view-mode key, and per-project view keys are silently dropped. Every existing caller — a dozen or
more — keeps working unmodified. Nothing else in the app needs to know it is embedded.

Three details that fail *silently* if you get them wrong:

- Define the overrides as **own properties of the storage instance** via a property definition, not as a
  prototype patch and not as plain assignment. A prototype patch no-ops against polyfills and test doubles
  that put the methods on the instance, and you lose the isolation guarantee with no error anywhere. Plain
  assignment is worse: the storage object has a named-property setter, so assigning to `getItem` can store an
  *item* under the key `"getItem"` while leaving the method intact.
- The client-side project-path encoder must match the server's encoder **exactly** — separators, colons, and
  also the non-obvious rules: underscores and dots become dashes too. A mismatch means the pinned project
  never resolves to a directory and the panel is silently empty. This was a real bug that required a
  follow-up fix.
- **Wrap, do not replace,** the view-mode setter: the real implementation must still render; the wrapper only
  coerces every requested mode to the pinned one. Poll for the app to finish booting (100 ms interval, capped
  at ~40 attempts) rather than assuming load order.
- Stub out any navigation entry point you cannot fully hide, so the embed **fails closed** rather than
  leaving a half-hidden UI that can wander to another project.

---

## 10.3 Git integration

### 10.3.1 Scope: this is a self-update button, not a git client

In the reference product, **every git write operation targets the application's own repository**, not the
user's active project. The single project-aware endpoint is read-only. This makes the feature a
*self-update / self-publish* mechanism for a tool that its users also develop.

**Recommendation: build it project-scoped from day one.** The self-scoped design was a consequence of the
product being its own dogfood, and it surprises users who expect the Publish button to publish *their* work.
Everything else in this section transfers unchanged; only the target repository differs.

### 10.3.2 Operations exposed

| Endpoint | Method | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `/api/git-status` | GET | cached `{has_git, ready, ahead, behind, uncommitted, branch, default_branch, on_default}` |
| `/api/git-sync` | POST `{action, confirm_branch}` | `{ok, messages[], git_status, scan?, needs_branch_confirm?, branch?, default_branch?}` |
| `/api/git-scan` | GET | full security-scan result |
| `/api/git-scan-stream` | GET (SSE) | `{type:"progress", current, total, file}` … terminal `{type:"done", …}` |
| `/api/project-git-status` | GET | `{is_git, branch, dirty_count, recent_commits[{hash,message}], project_path}` |

`action` is one of `pull`, `push`, `both`. There is deliberately **no branch switching, no stash UI, no blame,
no per-file revert, no log browser, and no commit-message input.** The whole point is that a non-technical
user has three states — behind, ahead, both — and one button per state.

### 10.3.3 Status caching and the throttle rules

**Never compute git status inline on a request.** Keep a module-level cache dictionary refreshed by a
background thread.

- Fire one refresh thread at application startup.
- Every `/api/git-status` hit calls a `refresh_if_idle` function that is **triple-gated**:
  1. suppressed entirely while inside a post-sync cooldown window,
  2. skipped if the last refresh was less than the minimum interval ago (**45 seconds**),
  3. skipped if the fetch lock is already held.
- **Stamp the last-refresh time eagerly, before spawning the thread.** Otherwise a burst of concurrent polls
  all pass the check and stampede.
- **Re-check the cooldown inside the thread, under the lock** — a double-check, because a sync can set the
  cooldown between the outer check and the thread actually starting.

Commands used, all as `git -C <dir> …` subprocesses with explicit timeouts (fetch 15 s, pull 30 s, everything
else 5 s) and the platform flag that suppresses console-window creation on Windows:

- current branch: `symbolic-ref --short -q HEAD`
- default branch: `symbolic-ref --short -q refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`
- `fetch --quiet`
- ahead/behind in one call: `rev-list --left-right --count HEAD...@{upstream}`
- dirty state: `status --porcelain` (as a boolean here; as a line count for the project endpoint)
- recent commits: `log --oneline -5`

Without the console-suppression flag, a detached background launch flashes command-prompt windows across the
user's screen every 45 seconds. Users report this as a virus.

### 10.3.4 Two rules that came from real bugs

**The fail-open rule.** Default-branch detection returns an empty string when it cannot determine the answer.
Callers must treat empty as *do not gate*: `on_default = (not default_branch) or (branch == default_branch)`.
Uncertainty must never block a normal sync or produce a spurious warning. A repository without an
`origin/HEAD` reference is common and entirely normal.

**The post-push trust rule.** After a successful commit-and-push, set the cache to `ahead=0, behind=0,
uncommitted=false` **without re-running the dirty check.** The reason: a concurrent agent session — which has
shell access and is very likely editing files right now — can dirty the tree between the commit and the
verification read. When that happens the Publish button never goes away, and the user presses it repeatedly,
producing a chain of empty commits. Only the pull-only path and the error path re-read actual state. Follow
this with a **10-second cooldown** that suppresses background refresh so the trusted state is not immediately
overwritten by an in-flight poll.

---

## 10.4 The one-click Update flow (commit + push for non-technical users)

This is the most safety-critical feature in Part 10, and it deserves to be treated that way.

**The threat model, stated plainly.** A non-technical user presses a button labeled "Publish App Update."
They do not read a diff. They may not know what a diff is. The button stages *everything* in the working
tree — including files an autonomous agent wrote in the last ten minutes without the user reading them — and
pushes to a repository that may be public. Every failure of this feature is a permanent, irreversible
disclosure. Git history does not forget, and neither do the automated scrapers that index public repository
pushes within minutes.

Design accordingly.

### 10.4.1 The three button states

Header buttons are mutually exclusive and driven entirely by the cached status:

- `behind > 0` → **Update App** (down-arrow badge)
- `ahead > 0 || uncommitted` → **Publish App Update** (up-arrow badge)
- both conditions → a single **Sync App** button (double-arrow badge), with the other two hidden

One state, one button, one verb. No git vocabulary anywhere in the UI.

### 10.4.2 The publish path, step by step

**Step 1 — Nothing-to-do check.** If there is no push work, show a modal: *"Nothing to publish — your app is
already up to date on remote."* Single OK button. Do not silently no-op; a button that does nothing when
pressed reads as broken.

**Step 2 — Branch guard, fired FIRST, before any other option is shown.** If the cached status says the
working copy is not on the default branch, show a modal whose copy is deliberately non-technical:

> You are on branch **X**, not **main**. Syncing now publishes your work to **X** — **not** your main app.
> Most of the time you want to be on **main**.

Buttons: **Cancel** (primary — the default action is to back out) and *Sync to "X" anyway*. This preserves a
fork/branch workflow for people who want it while stopping a non-technical user from silently publishing to a
feature branch and then wondering why nothing changed.

**Step 3 — Test gate.** Offer four choices: *Fast Tests + Publish* (primary), *Full Tests + Publish*,
*Skip & Publish*, *Cancel*. Tests stream over server-sent events with live output rendered in the modal.

- On pass: *"N tests passed — proceeding to publish…"* then auto-continue after ~1.2 seconds.
- On fail: **"Publish Blocked — Tests Failed"**, with the failing lines rendered in a scrollable
  fixed-width block, and buttons *Publish Anyway* / **Cancel (primary)**.
- On a test-runner error (not a test failure): *"Could not run tests. Publish anyway?"*

**Step 4 — Streaming security scan.** Before touching git at all, the client opens a server-sent-event stream
on the scan endpoint and renders a progress bar with `current/total` and **the name of the file currently
being scanned**. Showing the filename matters: a bare spinner on a 2,000-file repository reads as a hang.

- If the scan finds problems: buttons *Fix with AI* (primary) and *Close* (see §10.4.4).
- If the *stream itself* errors: fall through and continue. The server runs its own scan anyway (§10.4.3), so
  a broken progress UI must never be the thing that blocks a publish, and must never be the thing that
  *allows* an unscanned one.

**Step 5 — Server-side sync**, with an indeterminate progress animation (a sine-wave pulse between roughly
20 % and 80 %) while it runs.

**Step 6 — Result modal** listing the server's plain-English messages.

### 10.4.3 Server-side sync internals — the safety checks that must exist

1. **Re-check the branch guard server-side.** The client's polled status can be stale by up to 45 seconds. If
   the working copy is off the default branch and the request did not carry an explicit confirmation flag,
   short-circuit with `needs_branch_confirm: true` **before touching git at all** — return the branch name and
   the default branch so the client can render the modal. Enforce on both sides. The client guard is UX; the
   server guard is the actual control.

2. **Pull path** (for `pull` and `both`): `stash --include-untracked` → `pull --rebase -X theirs` → on
   failure, `rebase --abort` then plain `pull -X theirs` → `stash pop`. Conflict resolution is automatic and
   **biased to theirs** (remote wins). Detect "already up to date" by substring and report it as *"&lt;App&gt; is
   already up to date."* rather than "Pulled latest updates," which would be a lie.

   Automatic conflict resolution is a deliberate trade: this user cannot resolve a conflict, so a conflict
   *must not* be surfaced. Biasing to remote is the safe direction for a self-update button — the user's local
   edits that lose are, at worst, recoverable from the stash; a half-merged application is not recoverable at
   all.

3. **Push path — scan, stage, scan AGAIN, commit, push.**

   - Run the full security scan. If it fails, return with `ok: false`, the scan payload, and messages naming
     the block.
   - Check dirty state. If clean, skip straight to push.
   - `add -A`.
   - **Run the scan a second time.** `add -A` can stage files the first scan never saw — files an agent
     created between the two moments, or files that were previously ignored and are no longer. This is not
     paranoia; the window is real and it is seconds wide on an active machine.
   - **If the second scan trips, run `reset HEAD` to unstage everything** and return the block. Leaving files
     staged means the next commit anyone makes — including one an agent makes from the shell — silently
     includes them. Unstaging is what makes the block actually a block.
   - Commit with an auto-generated message: `"Update <AppName> YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM"`. The user never types one.
   - Push. No rebase-and-retry on rejection, and **no force-push option anywhere in the UI.**

4. **Commit-failure special case.** If the commit's standard error contains the missing-identity phrases
   (`Author identity unknown`, `Please tell me who you are`), append paste-ready `git config --global
   user.name` / `user.email` commands to the response message. This is the single most common first-run
   failure and the raw git error is incomprehensible to the target user.

### 10.4.4 Failure UX

Everything the user sees is plain English. Never surface raw git output except as the tail of a sentence that
already explains what happened.

| Condition | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Not a git repository | `{ok: false, messages: ["<App> has no git repo."]}` |
| Off default branch | Short-circuit before any git operation; "Wrong Branch?" modal; **Cancel is primary** |
| Merge conflict on pull | Auto-resolved biased to remote; rebase failure retried as a merge; second failure returns "Could not pull: …" and **aborts before the push stage** |
| Rejected push | Raw standard error surfaced as "Could not push: …". No auto-retry, no force option |
| Missing git identity | Detected by substring; paste-ready fix appended |
| Nothing to commit | Skipped silently (the dirty check gates the commit) |
| Network/fetch failure in the background poller | Swallowed; the cache keeps its last-known values |
| Client-side fetch throws | Generic "Could not complete. Try again." |
| Security scan blocks | Blocked-file list and redacted findings; primary action is *Fix with AI* |

**Minimize / mini-indicator.** The progress modal carries a minimize button, shown only while in flight (that
is, only when there are no action buttons). Minimizing swaps to a floating pill with a spinner and the current
step label. On completion while minimized, the pill turns done or error, reveals a close button, and flashes
for ~1.5 seconds. Clicking the pill while still working restores the modal; clicking it when finished dismisses
it. This is a small feature that converts a blocking modal into a background job, and on a slow repository it
is the difference between "I can keep working" and "I have to sit here."

### 10.4.5 The secret-leak risk, and the deterministic pre-push scanner

**The risk this button creates is specific:** a user who has never opened a terminal presses a button that
stages everything and publishes it to the internet. The files in that working tree were substantially written
by an autonomous agent. Nothing in the flow shows the user what is in them.

The mitigation is a **regex-only, no-AI, pre-push scanner**. This is the single most transferable idea in
Part 10, and it must ship **in the same release as the button** — never after.

**Scope: it scans the entire repository, not the diff.** Union of tracked files and untracked-but-not-ignored
files. The rationale is exact: what matters is what will *exist* in the published repository, not what changed
in this commit. A secret committed three months ago and never touched since is still published on every push.

**Five verdict paths, evaluated in order per file:**

1. **Skip list.** The scanner's own source file (its patterns match themselves), plus any deliberately exempt
   paths.
2. **Per-file finding suppressions** — pairs of (path pattern, finding-type-or-none). A null finding type
   skips the file entirely.
3. **Forbidden filenames → blocked.** Environment files, credential JSON, service-account JSON, token files,
   SSH private keys of every algorithm, `*_rsa`, PEM/PKCS12/PFX/P8, keystores, `.htpasswd`, package-manager
   credential files, Terraform state, and the application's own configuration file.
4. **Private-document detection**, by extension *and* by filename pattern regardless of extension:
   office documents, PDF, CSV/TSV, email exports, accounting formats, and filename patterns covering
   invoices, receipts, contracts, NDAs, tax forms, payroll, financial statements, medical/HIPAA, identity
   documents, confidentiality markers, customer lists, salary data, board minutes, legal memos, proposals,
   purchase orders, term sheets, resumes, and offer letters. Plus a binary-extension blocklist and a
   **"larger than 500 KB → too large to scan, review manually"** block.
5. **Content scan** — roughly 40 compiled patterns across cloud provider keys, platform tokens, AI provider
   keys, SaaS webhooks and tokens, payment keys, database connection strings, generic
   `api_key=`/`secret=`/`token=`/`bearer`/`password=` assignments, private key headers, JWTs, suspicious
   base64 blobs, hardcoded home-directory paths, internal IPs and hostnames, confidentiality markers, and
   personal-identifier patterns (national ID, credit card, tax ID, phone, date of birth, bank/routing,
   salary, MAC address, UUID).

**Output contract:** `{ok, findings[≤50], blocked_files[≤20], summary, files_scanned}`. Each finding carries
`{file, line, type, desc, match}` where **`match` is redacted** — first 6 characters followed by a redaction
marker, or 4 characters for short matches. A security report that prints the secret is worse than no report:
it creates a second copy in a log, a screenshot, or a support ticket.

Cap findings at 50 and blocked files at 20 so a single over-broad pattern cannot produce a megabyte response
that hangs the browser.

**Two false-positive fixes you will otherwise rediscover the hard way:**

- **A value-matching character class must exclude newlines.** A password pattern written as
  `[^"']{8,}` matches across line breaks, because a negated class includes `\n`. On a line like
  `body: 'password=' + encode(pw),` the pattern slurps subsequent lines of code until the next quote and
  reports a multi-line blob as a hardcoded password. Anchor to `[^"'\r\n]{8,}`. A real password literal never
  spans newlines, so this costs exactly zero detection.
- **Environment-variable secret patterns need a negative lookahead** excluding quoted pure-lowercase
  snake_case values. A line like `_CONFIG_KEY = "mobile_command_enabled"` is a dictionary-key constant, not a
  credential. Real credentials always contain digits, mixed case, or special characters.

And a discipline point: **once you fix a root cause, remove the suppressions it required.** The reference
implementation removed a password-assignment suppression from a pre-login unlock module on purpose, because
that file is precisely where a real hardcoded password would be most dangerous.

**"Fix with AI" — make the block actionable.** When a scan blocks a publish, the primary button spawns a
**new agent session** pre-loaded with a structured prompt containing: the scan summary, every blocked file
with its reason, every finding with `file:line` and the redacted match, and six numbered instructions —
move real secrets to environment variables or a gitignored config file; add genuine false positives to the
scanner's skip list; `git rm --cached` forbidden files; re-run the scan endpoint; verify the response is
`{"ok": true}` — closing with an explicit statement that this is a public repository. The client optimistically
inserts the session, switches to the sessions view, starts it, and opens the live panel.

This closes the loop. **A safety gate that only blocks trains users to bypass it. A safety gate that dispatches
the fix gets used.**

### 10.4.6 What the scanner does not protect against — say this out loud

- **It is a courtesy gate, not an enforcement boundary.** Nothing prevents an agent session, which has shell
  access, from running `git push` directly. If you need enforcement, use a pre-push git hook or server-side
  push protection.
- **Blanket-skipping all markdown files, documentation directories, and prompt/agent directories means those
  files are entirely unscanned** — and prose files are exactly where people paste an API key they copied out
  of a terminal. The reference implementation skips them because its own agent-definition prose is
  pattern-dense enough to false-positive constantly. That is a real cost, and it is the wrong trade. Scan
  prose too and invest in the suppression list instead.
- **Never hardcode owner personal information into a scanner that ships in a public repository.** The
  reference implementation embeds the repository owner's numeric user ID, first name, and surname as regex
  patterns with descriptions like "Owner name found in file" — which publishes to the internet exactly the
  personal information those patterns exist to protect. Load owner-PII patterns from a **gitignored
  configuration file**, never from tracked source. This is an anti-pattern, and it is called out here
  specifically so you do not copy it.

## 10.5 Live preview

### 10.5.1 The problem

The agent runs on a development machine. The user is on a phone, connected over an encrypted tunnel. The
phone **cannot reach the machine's loopback address**, and the agent has no way to "show" a screen. Three
mechanisms solve this.

### 10.5.2 Server-side headless render

`POST /api/preview/render` with `{url, name, width, height, wait_ms}` → `{ok, id, src, file, bytes, name,
type: "image"}`.

- Accept only `http:`, `https:`, and `data:` URLs.
- Clamp: width 200–2000 (default 1024), height 200–4000 (default 1400), wait 0–20000 ms (**default 3000**).
- **The blueprint must discover the browser binary itself and must NOT import the application's launcher
  module.** Importing the launcher executes module-level boot code and starts servers. Duplicate the small
  finder helper and leave a comment saying why. This is a real architectural rule: *a route module must be
  importable with zero side effects.*
- Headless flags that matter: new-headless mode, GPU disabled, scrollbars hidden, first-run and
  default-browser checks disabled, **a virtual time budget equal to the wait**, run-all-compositor-stages-
  before-draw, forced device scale factor of 1, an opaque white default background color, the screenshot
  output path, and an explicit window size.
  - **The virtual time budget is the single-page-app fix.** Without it, headless capture fires at the load
    event and misses everything a client-rendered application paints afterward — producing the documented
    "app chrome, empty inside" screenshot.
  - The opaque background color gives a white base so a transparent or late-painting body is not a blank
    frame.
- 45-second subprocess timeout → HTTP 504. Non-zero exit, missing output file, or zero-byte output → HTTP 500
  with truncated standard error.
- **Return the absolute file path on purpose**, so the agent can open the PNG and *visually verify it* before
  telling the user about it.

`GET /api/preview/asset/<id>` serves the image. The id must match a strict 32-hex-character pattern and is
resolved only inside a dedicated previews directory — an opaque, directory-scoped identifier rather than a
path parameter.

### 10.5.3 Thumbnails

`GET /api/preview/thumb/<id>` serves a downscaled JPEG for gallery tiles: width 480 (roughly twice the widest
tile so it stays sharp on a high-density phone screen), quality 78, high-quality resampling. Page captures up
to 4000 px tall are **cropped to a maximum 1.4 aspect ratio, keeping the top** — a whole scroll squeezed into
a 110 px tile is unreadable mush, and the top is what identifies the page. Regenerate when the thumbnail is
missing or older than its source. Serve thumbnails with a long cache lifetime (content is immutable per id)
and full-size assets with none.

**The image library must be an optional dependency.** If it is not installed, the thumbnail endpoint
**degrades to serving the full-size PNG rather than returning 500.** A heavy thumbnail is infinitely more
useful than a broken tile.

### 10.5.4 Reverse proxy

`GET /api/preview/proxy?u=<url>` is a best-effort proxy so a live iframe can load a localhost development
server through the tunnel origin. Fetch server-side with a distinctive user agent and a 15-second timeout; on
HTML responses, rewrite `src`, `href`, `action`, and `poster` attribute values to absolute URLs routed back
through the proxy, skipping `data:`, `mailto:`, fragment, and `javascript:` values. Failure returns 502 with a
plain-text message naming the URL.

Explicitly best-effort: JavaScript-injected URLs are out of scope, and the documentation should tell the user
to use render-to-screenshot when reliability matters.

**Security note you must carry into your own build:** this is an unauthenticated open proxy with no host
allowlist — a textbook server-side-request-forgery shape. It is defensible *only* because the application
binds to loopback and is reachable solely over an authenticated tunnel. **If you expose the application any
wider, an allowlist is mandatory.**

### 10.5.5 The marker protocol (agent → UI)

The agent emits, on its own line, a marker containing a JSON payload:

`[[VN-PREVIEW {"type":"browser","name":"Settings screen","src":"http://localhost:5173/settings"}]]`

or the same payload wrapped in a distinctive Unicode bracket pair. Accept both wrappers; use a non-greedy
match for the JSON payload. `type` is `"browser"` (rendered as an iframe) or `"image"` (rendered as an image).

Client behavior:

- An extraction function takes `(session_id, text)`, strips every marker, upserts each into a per-session
  store, and returns `{clean, found}`. **It must be idempotent** — it is called on every re-render during
  streaming. Achieve this by making the id a hash of `type|src|name`, so the same marker never creates a
  duplicate entry.
- Collapse the blank lines left behind by stripping (three or more newlines → two).
- Cards render inline under the assistant message; remove and rebuild the card block on each pass.
- A toolbar navigation button aggregates the session's previews with a count badge and a "has new" state
  cleared when the gallery opens.
- One bottom sheet serves two modes (grid and single). Snap points at 0 %, 46 %, and 72 % vertical offset;
  drag-to-resize from the whole header *except* the action buttons so taps still work; flick past 88 % to
  dismiss; tap the grabber to cycle snaps. Fullscreen strips the header and frame cap but is disabled in grid
  mode. Escape exits fullscreen first, then closes.
- Gallery sort: **last-opened descending, falling back to generation order descending.** Opening a preview
  bumps it.
- A refresh control must **cache-bust with an incrementing query parameter**, or re-rendering a screenshot
  silently shows the old image.
- Live iframes are sandboxed (scripts, forms, same-origin, popups) with a no-referrer policy, and any
  loopback-address source is automatically rewritten through the proxy.

### 10.5.6 The mobile preamble — environment-conditional prompt injection

When a turn is detected as originating from a phone over the tunnel, the server **prepends a delimited
preamble to the outgoing user message.** The preamble tells the agent: the user cannot see this screen; do not
describe visual results in prose; emit preview markers; here is the exact command to call the render endpoint;
**always open the returned file path and look at the image before emitting a marker** — if it is blank or
still loading, re-render with a larger wait (6000–10000 ms); and name previews distinctly, because the gallery
caption is the only differentiator.

**Detection must NOT be source-IP based.** The tunnel proxies the phone through the local machine, so the
remote address is loopback and lies. Use, in order: an explicit remote flag in the socket payload; the
identity header the tunnel proxy injects; or a Host header ending in the tunnel's DNS suffix. **Any failure
means "not mobile"** — the feature stays off rather than misfiring on a local turn. Mirror the same test
client-side from the hostname.

This pattern — an environment-conditional system-prompt injection that changes the agent's *output modality*,
paired with a client-side marker renderer — is reusable far beyond mobile. It is the cleanest way to teach an
agent a new output channel without changing its tools.

## 10.6 Search

Two deliberately separate features:

| | Deep search | Find |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Every session transcript in the project | The currently rendered chat DOM |
| Backend | SQLite full-text index | None |
| Entry point | Sidebar button → modal | Ctrl/Cmd+F → find bar |

Find-in-transcript is ~70 lines and immediately useful. Build it in v1. Deep search is v2.

### 10.6.1 What is searchable, and the three questions

Full message content of every user and assistant message, **including tool-result output** — so "which session
hit this error" works — plus a lookup table of files each session touched. Session titles are *not* in the
server index; they are folded in client-side.

The index is designed to answer exactly three questions: *where did we decide X* (ranked full-text), *which
session touched file Y* (lookup table), and *which sessions hit this error* (tool-result indexing).

### 10.6.2 Storage and schema

Database in the user's agent-CLI state directory, **outside the repository** so nothing can ever be committed.
Compute the path **lazily on every call**, not at import time — this gives test isolation for free when tests
monkeypatch the home directory, and it lets the module be imported before home-directory redirection happens.
Use write-ahead logging so searches read while an indexing pass writes. Stamp a schema version; on mismatch,
rebuild rather than guess.

- `indexed_files(project, session_id, mtime, size)` — bookkeeping, primary key `(project, session_id)`
- `session_files(project, session_id, file_path, norm_path)` — normalized path is lowercased with forward
  slashes for matching; primary key includes it
- `messages` — full-text virtual table with `content` indexed and `project`, `session_id`, `role`, `ts`,
  `msg_idx` unindexed; Unicode tokenizer

### 10.6.3 Index build and update

- **Incremental and debounced.** Compare each on-disk transcript's `(mtime, size)` against the bookkeeping
  table and re-parse only changed files; delete rows for transcripts that vanished. A **per-project TTL of
  20 seconds** short-circuits repeats so search-as-you-type never re-stats the directory on every keystroke.
- **Run the indexer only inside a search request, in the web-server process** — never in the session daemon,
  never on a per-turn hot path.
- A single lock serializes **writes only**; reads take no lock.
- **Cap indexed tool-result text at ~4000 characters per block.** Build logs and test runs reach megabytes,
  and errors appear overwhelmingly early.
- **"Touched" means edited** — only write-class tools register a file. Read and grep deliberately do not
  count, matching the session daemon's own tracked-files semantics.
- Files with underscore-prefixed stems are metadata, never transcripts.
- Parsing must mirror the main transcript loader exactly — same content shapes, same tolerance for blank and
  truncated lines, because the agent CLI may be mid-write.

### 10.6.4 The disposability doctrine

**The index is disposable derived state; the transcripts are the source of truth.** Build three recovery
layers from the start; retrofitting them is painful.

1. On a database error during an indexing pass: delete the database and its write-ahead and shared-memory
   sidecar files, rebuild.
2. On a database error at **query** time: delete, force a reindex, retry **once.** This exists for the one
   case the ensure pass cannot see — damage localized to full-text index pages that a no-change ensure pass
   (which only reads the bookkeeping table) never touches. Without this layer, every search returns 500 until
   some transcript's mtime happens to change.
3. On corrupt-file detection while connecting, **close the connection before re-raising.** On Windows an open
   handle blocks the file deletion the rebuild needs.

Invalid-query errors are re-raised untouched — that is a 400, not a corruption problem.

### 10.6.5 Query syntax and sanitization

User-facing syntax: plain words search content; a `file:<fragment>` token filters to sessions that *edited* a
matching path. **Only the first `file:` token is used** — the server does a single contains-match, so joining
several fragments would produce a filter that can never match.

**Full-text injection defense:** convert each whitespace-delimited token into a quoted phrase, doubling any
embedded double-quotes per the engine's escaping rules, so user input can never be parsed as query syntax.
AND-join the tokens. **Suffix only the last token with a wildcard** so search-as-you-type matches partial
words. An empty result after tokenization raises a 400. Map any residual operational error from the engine to
a 400 as well.

The file filter uses a `LIKE` with an explicit escape character, escaping `%`, `_`, and the escape character
itself in the user fragment.

### 10.6.6 Ranking and result shaping

- Order by the engine's BM25 ranking function.
- **Over-fetch `max(200, limit * 10)` messages** before grouping by session, or one chatty session consumes
  the entire result page and the user sees three results when twenty matched.
- Up to **3 snippets per session**, generated by the engine's snippet function with distinctive
  non-HTML hit markers and a context window of ~12 tokens.
- File-only queries (no text) order by transcript recency using the indexed mtime.
- Combined text-and-file queries **intersect**.
- **Filter deleted, utility, and remapped sessions at QUERY time, not index time.** Deletion is a tombstone
  that does not change the transcript's mtime, so an index-time filter keeps serving a session the user just
  deleted.
- Response: `{project, query, file, sessions:[{session_id, rank, snippets:[{role,ts,text}], files:[…]}],
  stats:{sessions_indexed, messages_indexed, took_ms}}`.

### 10.6.7 Client behavior

- 350 ms debounce; Enter searches immediately.
- **Sequence guard** — stamp each request and drop stale responses.
- **Project guard** — if the active project changed while a request was in flight, discard the response.
  Rendering the previous project's sessions would deep-link the user into the wrong project.
- **Defensive JSON parsing** — a crash or a proxy returning an HTML 500 must report as a failed search, not
  fall into the network-error branch and tell the user they are offline.
- **Title merge** — since titles are not server-indexed, mark content-result sessions whose title also
  matches (so the title highlights), and *append* title-only matches the content search missed. Skip this
  entirely when a `file:` filter is active: that is an explicit "edited this file" query and title-only
  additions would violate it.
- **Cross-site-scripting discipline, two different correct techniques.** Snippets: HTML-escape **first**,
  then substitute the hit markers for `<mark>` tags — raw transcript content can never inject markup. Titles:
  split on the **raw** string, then escape each part — so escaping never breaks the match offsets. Getting
  the order backwards in either case is a live XSS hole fed by arbitrary agent output.
- On the first search, status text should warn that indexing may take a moment.
- Escape inside the modal must call `stopPropagation()`, or every other overlay's Escape handler fires too.
- A result click must call the plain session-select function, **not** the click handler used by the sidebar —
  the latter triggers inline rename when the clicked id is already active.

### 10.6.8 Endpoint

`GET /api/search?q=&file=&project=&limit=` — `q` requires at least 2 characters unless `file` is given;
`limit` is clamped to 1–100 with a default of 20.

**Validate the project name against `/`, `\`, and `..`.** The indexer would otherwise happily walk into and
*persist* a foreign directory's transcripts into the search database. And when a project is passed explicitly,
**do not fall back to the active project** — searching a different project than the one requested is silently
wrong, and silent wrongness in a search box destroys trust in the whole feature.

---

## 10.7 Voice input

### 10.7.1 Two engines, one button

Resolve the voice mode in this order: **local engine → browser engine → none.**

- **Local speech engine** — a separately installable package running a local speech model, capturing via the
  browser's media recorder. Works in **every** browser. Wins whenever it reports ready.
- **Browser speech recognition API** — the built-in Web Speech recognition interface. **Chromium-only.**
- **none** — the microphone button silently becomes a Send button.

The microphone button is dynamic: inject a sibling **Send** button on its right (shown only when there is text
and no recording in progress) and a **Cancel (✕)** button on its left (shown only while recording). Icon,
title, and class swap through one shared update function on every state change.

### 10.7.2 The browser-native path

Configure continuous recognition with interim results.

- **Preserve existing textarea content; voice appends to it.** Never clobber what the user typed.
- Paint interim results straight into the textarea, raw and on purpose — post-processing runs once on the
  finalized transcript, not on every interim tick.
- **7-second silence timer**, reset on every result, then an intentional stop. Chosen to leave room to pause
  and think mid-message before auto-send fires.
- **Auto-restart loop**: if the browser kills recognition unexpectedly (not silence, not a manual stop),
  restart, up to 5 times; reset the counter on any result.
- **The onstart guard.** Auto-restart may engage *only* after the engine's start event proves microphone
  permission was granted and audio is flowing. Without this guard, a first-time permission prompt that ends
  recognition before it ever ran trips the restart loop and traps the UI in listen mode until the prompt is
  answered — which the user cannot see, because the prompt is behind the modal they are staring at.
- Error handling: network, aborted, and audio-capture errors are transient and fall through to the end
  handler; no-speech is silent; anything else raises a toast.
- On end: if the user pressed ✕, clear the textarea. Otherwise run the transcript through the processor chain
  and commit.

### 10.7.3 The transcript processor seam

Register an ordered chain of functions `(text, context) -> string | Promise<string>` where the context carries
the textarea, the submit callback, and the source engine. **Ship the chain empty** — it is a pure identity
pass on day one.

Its entire purpose is to create a *seam*. Before the seam exists, assigning the final transcript directly to
the textarea means recognition output, displayed text, and submitted payload are the same value with nowhere
to intervene. Every future feature — vocabulary correction, punctuation repair, command interception, profanity
handling, translation — needs that seam, and retrofitting it later means touching every commit path.

Contract: a non-string return is ignored, and **a thrown exception is caught and the prior text preserved.** A
broken processor must never destroy the user's dictated message. Include a synchronous fast path when zero
processors are registered so behavior is byte-for-byte identical to the pre-seam implementation.

### 10.7.4 The local-engine path

**Capture:** request an audio stream, feed a media recorder, and request a chunk every 400 ms.

**Streaming transcription via local agreement.** Keep exactly one transcription request in flight and re-chain
the instant it returns. Each partial re-transcribes the audio so far with a fast, greedy decode. Compute the
common prefix of the previous and current word arrays; words that two consecutive partials agree on become
**committed and never rewrite again.** Only the unstable tail keeps updating. This is what eliminates the
jumpy, rewriting-itself caption that makes streaming transcription feel broken.

**Live caption UI:** a floating pill anchored above the input, **anchored to the textarea's *bottom* so it
grows upward** rather than off the top of the screen. Committed words render solid; the settling tail shimmers.
Reconcile per word so only changed words re-render, and **glow only true retroactive corrections**, not
freshly appended words. Use an animated placeholder with the same shimmer so the panel reads as alive even
when partials are empty — without it, "no live text yet" is indistinguishable from "the capture is dead."
Leave the textarea itself untouched until the final transcript lands.

**Adaptive throttle:** run partials at full speed and back off only if one actually comes back slow (add
300 ms on a response over 1200 ms, subtract 200 ms otherwise, cap at 1500 ms). The final pause-snap always
uses full quality, so committed text is never degraded.

### 10.7.5 Guards against mis-transcription and message loss

This is the highest-density set of hard-won lessons in the whole part. Each guard exists because of a specific
observed failure.

1. **Gate every end-of-speech signal on real microphone silence.** Model-derived signals (gap detection, word
   stability) are computed on audio submitted seconds ago. When the model is slow, they fire while the user is
   mid-sentence. The microphone is ground truth: stamp a last-speech timestamp from a live 100 ms level timer,
   and let no model signal finish the capture unless the microphone has *also* been quiet that long.
2. **Make the pending finish retractable.** If the microphone hears the user again after a finish was armed,
   retract it and clear the fallback timer.
3. **Compute gate on finish.** If a partial is still transcribing, defer the send until it returns, with a
   ~2500 ms hard fallback that **re-checks the microphone** before firing.
4. **Merge the final decode with committed streaming text.** The single-pass high-quality decode is better
   overall but can regress on project proper nouns. If the final result omits a committed prefix of **two or
   more words** that the streaming text contains, prefer the streaming text. Requiring two words avoids false
   positives on short utterances.
5. **Respect the model's context window.** For a 30-second window, use a segmented partial window of roughly
   75 chunks — and advance the window start in **whole hops, not continuously.** Exceeding the context grows
   latency linearly and silently truncates the front, so the agreement algorithm sees a different word at
   position zero each cycle and committed words never grow. A continuously sliding start trips the
   stabilization reset on every pump past 30 seconds.
6. **Prepend the container header to every mid-stream slice.** A media-recorder stream is one container and
   **only chunk zero carries the container header.** A headerless mid-stream slice is rejected by the decoder.
   Before this fix, *every* partial past ~30 seconds failed server-side — freezing the caption, killing
   end-of-speech signals, and truncating long mobile dictations.
7. **Promote each finished segment into a permanent prefix.** When the window hops, promote the finished
   segment's *previous* words — not just the committed ones, because the settling tail's audio is not covered
   by the next window — into a monotonically growing prefix. Without this, a 60-second recording loses its
   first half whenever the final pass times out.
8. **Scale silence and stability thresholds with message length.** Above 12 committed words, extend the pause
   and stability windows; above 30, extend them further. The same constants cannot serve a five-word command
   and a three-minute dictation.
9. **Use a fixed speech floor and an adaptive noise floor.** Let the measured background level pick the *pause
   window* (short in a quiet room, longer in a noisy one), but **never** let it gate speech detection — speech
   uses a fixed threshold, or the detector mis-calibrates in a loud room and refuses to ever end the recording.
10. **Hard recording cap of 5 minutes, not 60 seconds.** A 60-second cap fires "every single time" for anyone
    dictating ten lines, because speaking pace is remarkably consistent. Silence detection ends normal
    recordings far sooner; the cap is a true last-resort backstop.
11. **Scale the final-transcription watchdog with audio length** — roughly `min(60s, max(12s, chunks × 500ms))`.
    A flat 6-second watchdog preempts real results on anything over ~12 seconds, especially when an in-flight
    partial holds the inference lock.
12. **Retire the emergency backstop once the normal stop path fires.** A finalize-time backstop exists solely
    for "the recorder never stopped." Leaving it armed preempts any final transcription slower than the
    backstop, sending the lower-quality live transcript and discarding the real result.
13. **Make the send idempotent** with a sent flag, so the backstop and the stop handler can both call it
    safely.
14. **Never drop a message.** An empty, failed, or timed-out final result falls back to the last full live
    text. **The only thing that may discard a message is an explicit ✕ cancel.** State the principle
    explicitly in your code: *pre-emptively sending is acceptable; dropping is not.*
15. **Re-query the input element by id at send time.** The input bar can re-render mid-capture, swapping the
    textarea node. Writing to the captured, now-detached node produces the infuriating "send animation plays,
    message vanishes" bug.
16. **If submit throws, leave the text in the input and say so** — "Your dictation is ready — press Enter to
    send." A failed auto-send must never silently swallow a message.
17. **Distinguish empty results.** If at least two chunks were captured but the model returned nothing:
    "Didn't catch that — try speaking louder or closer to the mic." Never vanish silently.
18. **Prime the audio context synchronously inside the tap gesture on iOS**, before requesting the media
    stream. iOS resumes an audio context only from a real user gesture; the analyser normally lives inside the
    media-stream promise, which on *first* use runs only after the user taps "Allow" — no longer a page
    gesture. The result: the very first recording never auto-stops, and every later one works, which reads as
    nondeterministic flakiness.
19. **Use one shared audio context for the application's lifetime.** Creating and closing one per capture is
    flaky; never close it, only disconnect the source.
20. **Do not show a different, worse engine's text as a live preview.** Painting browser-native interim text
    during a local-engine capture looks broken mid-speech and then snaps to a different result. Show honest
    signal instead: the microphone glows with real audio level.
21. **Guard the input-bar rebuild during capture.** If the input bar re-renders while a capture targets it,
    the submit closure captured at build time goes stale and the message is dropped every time a session
    finishes its turn mid-dictation. Four properties make this guard correct:
    (a) the active-capture reference must exist in the bar-rendering module at all;
    (b) the guard checks that the bar still *contains* the capture's target element — not bare truthiness,
    which would block bar updates forever if the reference lingered;
    (c) the guard returns **without** updating the bar's render key, so a post-send refresh still sees a stale
    key and re-renders;
    (d) it sits adjacent to the symmetric guard for the browser-native engine — the two must be kept in sync.

**Testing technique worth stealing:** a source-pattern guard suite. A test file reads the production
JavaScript as text and asserts that specific patterns exist, with failure messages that name the regression
each pattern prevents. It is unusual, but it is the only practical way to protect JavaScript invariants from a
backend test suite, and it makes the reason for each line permanently discoverable.

### 10.7.6 The Chromium-only constraint — a hard rule

**HARD RULE: the browser-native speech recognition API is Chromium-only. If the system default browser is
Firefox, the microphone button silently disappears with zero error messages anywhere — no console warning, no
toast, no log line. The user reports "the mic is gone" and there is nothing to debug.**

**Therefore: on all three platforms, the launcher must find and launch Chrome or Chromium before falling back
to the system default opener.** This regression already shipped to users once on Windows.

| Platform | Finder | Launch mechanism | Fallback |
|---|---|---|---|
| Windows | Registry app-paths entry under machine then user hive, then Program Files, Program Files (x86), and local app data | Shell-execute via the OS API — **focus-safe even when the parent process is minimized**, which the simple start-file call is not | System start-file |
| Linux | Path lookup over `google-chrome`, `google-chrome-stable`, `chromium`, `chromium-browser`, and beta/unstable channels; then standard bin directories, snap, the vendor install directory, and **Flatpak system and per-user exports** | Direct process spawn | `xdg-open` |
| macOS | System and user Applications directories, for both Chrome and Chromium | Direct process spawn | `open` |

**Isolated instance.** Pass an app-mode URL flag plus a dedicated user-data directory inside the application's
own data folder. Without isolation, the launcher-spawned window **wedges the browser's focus state** — windows
opened from outside the application silently no-op until the browser is fully closed and reopened. The
dedicated profile also bypasses session restore, which was the original reason a new-window flag existed. The
profile directory must be gitignored; if it cannot be created, fall back to a new-window launch rather than
failing to open at all.

**Two mutually exclusive bugs, resolved by a running-state check:**

- **Browser already running** → open a bare URL → a new *tab.* A focus wedge requires a launcher-spawned
  *window*, and session restore already ran on the browser's own startup, so there is nothing to swallow the
  URL.
- **Browser not running (cold start)** → new-window flag with the URL, which forces the URL to display; there
  is no running browser for a new window to wedge.

**Bias the running-state detection toward "running" on any detection failure.** A wrong "running" costs at
most a rare cold-start bare-URL open; a wrong "not running" wedges focus, which is by far the more annoying
failure.

Finally: **gate the browser launch on the server actually answering.** Poll the URL (60 attempts, 1 second
apart). If the server never answers, do not open the browser. Never open a broken tab.

### 10.7.7 The optional local engine, and wrapping a package you cannot edit

The local speech engine is opt-in, off by default, enabled in preferences, with a one-time model download of
roughly 150 MB and a machine-fitness check before installing. Nothing is installed for users who do not opt in.
Every failure path degrades to the browser-native engine and toasts "unavailable" rather than throwing.

The engine ships as a separate package with its own enable/install modal — but the application **wraps** it and
delegates only the real work (start install, refresh status, get status, set enabled, is-ready,
is-supported-browser, transcribe-blob), because a pip-installed package cannot be edited and its boot logic had
three first-run gaps:

1. **The resume gap.** After a web-layer restart and automatic page reload, the browser comes back *enabled*
   with an idle phase and dependencies not yet installed. The package's own resume logic only fires when the
   phase is already installing/downloading/loading *or* dependencies are importable — this exact state matched
   neither branch, and the install silently never restarted. This was the "dead screen, had to refresh
   manually" bug.
2. **The frozen-looking progress bar.** The engine reports coarse, jumpy progress while the two slow steps (a
   wheel build and a model download) sit at a single static percentage for minutes. No motion reads as frozen.
   Fix with a **continuous sheen animation on the progress track**, independent of the reported percentage.
3. **No success signal.** Completion was surfaced only by a toast from the polling loop — and when the page
   reloaded (bug 1), that loop died and nothing confirmed success or lit the microphone.

The wrapper's flow: browser-support check → enable → status → if a restart is needed, show a modal explaining
that **only the web layer restarts and running sessions stay alive**, with a button that persists the intent
and triggers a web-scope restart → poll status every 1200 ms → on ready, null the input bar's render key and
re-render so the microphone lights **without a page refresh.** A resume-on-load routine runs on every page load
and fills the package's two gaps.

Server side: mount the package's API routes and serve its web assets; default the model and virtual-environment
directories into a cache folder so a restart never re-downloads; and, because the package is a git dependency
rather than a registry package with no in-tree fallback, **have the launcher install it explicitly** — otherwise
non-technical users who never run a package manager silently lose voice.

**The general lesson:** when you wrap a third-party package you cannot edit, enumerate its state-machine gaps
explicitly and own the transitions it misses — especially the state that exists immediately after a restart.
